Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover

BBC News Sun, 06 Sep 2026 09:18:37 GMT

Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.

His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.

Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.

In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.

In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.

Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.

The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.

When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening."

"I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film.

"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.

"Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."

The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate.

Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.

Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.

But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics.

"They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said.

He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy".

Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.

Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations.

He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."

Speaking after watching the interview, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: "For a political party that don't like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash.

"We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them."

He added: "I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they're really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going."

There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case

BBC News Sun, 06 Sep 2026 08:05:22 GMT

Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges.

According to state-owned al-Ahram newspaper, they were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them.

They also had illegal firearms and munitions.

Khalifa, 39, is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues. She has denied the charges.

Nine fellow defendants have been sentenced to life imprisonment, while seven have been acquitted.

Khalifa's lawyer said she would appeal the death sentence.

The verdict was first announced last month.

However, it was only confirmed a month later after the court obtained a religious opinion from the grand mufti of Egypt - a legal requirement in death sentence cases.

During the trial, the court heard that authorities had seized more than 750kg (1,653lbs) of narcotics and the imported raw materials to make them.

Twenty witnesses had given statements to the prosecutors, al-Ahram said, in addition to electronic evidence that included conversations and video clips.

According to the state-run Akhbar al-Youm newspaper, when asked by the judge about her alleged role during a court appearance last September, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs until she was photographed with them inside the anti-narcotics authority offices.

According to a 2025 Amnesty International report, there were 492 death sentences in the course of the year, 23 of which were carried out..

The defendants were found guilty of drug trafficking and rape, "crimes that did not amount to 'intentional killing' to which the use of the death penalty must be restricted under international law and standards", the report said.

Diana fountain shut all summer by technical fault

BBC News Sun, 06 Sep 2026 07:01:46 GMT

The Diana Memorial Fountain in Hyde Park - which has long been a popular place to cool down in hot weather - has been kept dry all summer due to a technical fault.

Royal Parks, the charity that maintains the central London park, apologised to visitors who found it without water "particularly given the prolonged high temperatures we've been experiencing".

The fountain opened in 2004 in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales who died nearly seven years earlier.

The closure was initially triggered by a mechanical breakdown in the pump that draws water from the local borehole. The pump was fixed, but software used to control the system then failed, preventing the water supply from being restored.

The closure was publicly announced by Royal Parks on 1 July.

The charity's spokesperson acknowledged that the fountain had "remained dry for longer than we hoped" while specialist teams worked to resolve the software issue.

The same water supply network feeds several other locations across the capital's Royal Parks, compounding broader operational pressures faced by maintenance staff over the summer.

The memorial undergoes regular year-round maintenance and investment, with officials expecting water to begin flowing again "in the next few weeks".

It is not the first time the £3.6m memorial fountain, which was officially opened by the late Queen Elizabeth in July 2004, has had to shut down.

Just weeks after it opened, it closed temporarily after three visitors slipped and hurt themselves while paddling.

In January 2005, the memorial closed for four months' renovation work, primarily to tackle problems of flooding and waterlogged ground around the site.

The following summer, ministers blamed members of the public who littered and caused drains to block. This caused a 10 day closure.

Additional reporting by Ewan Somerville.

Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'

BBC News Sun, 06 Sep 2026 00:22:07 GMT

When it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion.

"I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says.

"If I'm sat in a chair, I get nothing.

"So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"

Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.

Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.

On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause.

"It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness.

"I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."

Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger.

"You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'

"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."

Things came to a head on tour, where her stage fright went into overdrive and she suffered "just terrible, terrible anxiety".

"I become sensitive to sound, so it feels like you're screaming at me if you're talking normally," she says. "I can't process questions very well. I act twitchy and weird, and it seemed to get worse with perimenopause."

She says her behaviour became a "nightmare" for her team. Pressed for an example, she explains: "If you asked me whether I wanted still or sparkling water, I'd say, 'That's a question, and I can't answer questions right now'.

"How diva is that?"

Well, it's not exactly Mariah Carey demanding baskets of puppies and forbidding eye contact, but Imbruglia was shaken up.

The day after one concert, she told her co-writers David Sneddon and Anu Pillai, "Guys, I think I'm going to have to quit my job because I can't cope with how I'm treating people before the show."

They helped to talk her down, putting her fight-or-flight instincts into context.

"What they helped me realise is that I was trying to stop the behaviour with willpower, and if I just relaxed into it and said to myself, 'You know, you're about to perform in front of a lot of people, it's natural that you're nervous', maybe I wouldn't be resisting it as much."

The impromptu therapy session inspired a new song, Upside Down - but Imbruglia is understandably frustrated that perimenopause isn't more widely understood, saying many women are rejected by their GP when they seek HRT treatment.

"My mum never talked to me about it," she reflects, "but looking back, I know she had a really bad one.

"Her anxiety was off the charts, too, and I have a lot more compassion now, because she had four kids. I've only got one."

As a child in Sydney, Imbruglia was drawn to performing. She'd squeeze lemon on her hair to make it blonder, and put on concerts of Whitney Houston covers for her neighbours.

Before long, she was cast in commercials for Coca-Cola and Twisties, and spent her Christmases singing carols in shopping centres.

"But when you turn 15 or 16, and you're into boys, you're like, 'Oh, that's really naff. I don't want to be doing that any more'," she laughs.

From that point onwards, Imbruglia became "basically unparentable".

"I was sneaking out and sleeping in someone's car on the beach, then getting busted.

"My parents were really strict - and my mum would turn up at parties with my picture, going, 'Have you seen this girl?'

"Socially, it was a disaster."

Music continued to be her solace. Dating a drummer, she switched allegiance from Whitney Houston to Tom Waits and Tori Amos, but the urge to sing remained.

You can see that hunger in a recently rediscovered photograph of a pre-fame Imbruglia, pressed up against the barriers of an INXS concert in 1992.

"It was my first ever concert," she says. "I was 15. I had white, tight jeans on."

In the photo, "everyone else is screaming but I'm looking at (Michael Hutchence) with this determination in my eyes.

"I'm studying him, like, 'How can I be up there too?'"

She got her chance in 1997 after quitting her role as builder's apprentice Beth Brennan in Aussie soap Neighbours.

Moving to London, she signed a deal with RCA Records and immediately scored an international hit with her first single, Torn.

Famously, the song was a cover – a fact journalists never let her forget, even though she co-wrote every other track on her debut album, Left of the Middle (lifetime sales, seven million copies).

"Yeah, I got famous on a song that I didn't write," she says now, "but there's more to what you bring to a song than whether you wrote the lyrics."

She still loves the song – "Torn was a beautiful gift" – but the furore around it fuelled her insecurities.

As a result, she essentially self-sabotaged her career. The lead single from her second album, That Day, was a free-verse stream-of-consciousness that sounded like a manic inner monologue.

"That was my rebellion against Torn," she says. "It doesn't have a chorus.

"That was my way of going, 'Can I get on with my life now? I've just started learning the craft of songwriting, I'm young, I didn't ask for this'."

In the midst of the madness, she auditioned for the lead role of Satine in Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge – which counts as one of the stranger experiences of her career.

"The audition was, pretty much, 'Have an orgasm'," she grimaces. "Because I think that happens in the movie." (Indeed, Satine delivers a breathy boudoir monologue as she tries to seduce Ewan McGregor's character, Christian.)

But Imbruglia stresses it wasn't a creepy casting couch situation.

"It's Baz, that doesn't really fit," she says of the soft-hearted director.

"But I remember leaving and feeling really icky. Like, 'Ohhh, that was awful. Where's my mummy?'"

Back in the world of music, Imbruglia returned to more commercial sounds on hits like Wrong Impression (2002) and Shiver (2005). But sales dwindled and her fourth album was shelved by her label.

In the years that followed, she joined the Australian version of The X Factor and appeared in a UK production of Alan Ayckbourn's play Things We Do for Love, before making a tentative return to music with covers album Male (2015); and the more personal, introspective Firebird (2021).

"It was quitting music and coming back to it that gave me an appreciation of my abilities," she says.

"I might not be the best songwriter, even now, but there's only one me, and when I go inside myself and feel the emotion of what I'm writing about and deliver it, that's what my fans resonate with, and that's enough."

She certainly has a lot to say on Algorithm. As well as the frank discussion of mental health, the title track talks about her flirtation with internet conspiracy theories.

She won't say which ones ("I think it's irresponsible") but stresses the danger is omnipresent.

"There's a voice in my head that says, 'You don't want to click on that', and I'll click on it. It's like this compulsion.

"You have to change the settings. Don't allow yourself to be in a situation where your stress relief is scrolling on a phone in bed. It's just not healthy."

Ultimately, however, the album ends on a note of positivity.

Beautiful Love, co-written with Snow Patrol's Gary Lightbody, is a soaring hymn to embracing your flaws and making peace with life's highs and lows.

"I've always made the joke that I'll never be a Buddhist because it's a middle path," she smiles.

"I like the pendulum to swing. Whether it's extreme joy or extreme pain, I like to feel the experience of life."

The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered

BBC News Sun, 06 Sep 2026 00:06:10 GMT

James Bond is special. Playing him propels an actor into an exceptionally elite group of performers. From Sean Connery to Daniel Craig, only six people have ever played him in the official film series.

In the last decade alone the UK has had more prime ministers, and twice as many people have walked on the moon than have played the British secret agent.

The last announcement of a new Bond was 21 years ago in 2005. So it's inevitable for Bond fans to want to have their questions answered about the future of one of cinema's most sought after roles, in one of cinema's biggest franchises.

This is, of course, the big question fans have been talking about for the last six years. And with an announcement edging closer and closer, the speculation has intensified recently.

Many of the same well-known faces have been bandied about for months, if not years. Those names have generally included Henry Cavill, Harris Dickinson, Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden, James Norton, Jack O'Connell, Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

More recently, other names have also been thrown into the mix.

Earlier this year Variety reported that stage actor Tom Francis had auditioned for the role. And in late August Page Six claimed there will be more auditions this month, and that Gladiator 2 star Paul Mescal and Heartstopper and SAS: Rogue Heroes star Jack Barton are also on the audition list.

The announcement about the next film's producers referred to keeping Bond's spirit alive "as he embarks on his next adventure", seemingly confirming that Bond would remain male.

However, it's never been clear whether the rumoured names have been well-sourced inside information, or merely guesswork and speculation.

Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way. But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right."

It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet."

Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy."

His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussie…"

The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career.

The audition process is likely to have been carried out in a similar way to previous castings.

The scene that many would-be Bonds have traditionally had to peform is taken from From Russia With Love, where 007 comes out of his bathroom to find Tatiana Romanova in his bed. It's a scene where an actor relies on their physical presence, movement and charisma. No explosions fights or gadgets.

As GoldenEye and Casino Royale director Martin Campbell explained to entertainment website Gold Derby: "The word is effortless. You never see Bond fumble, he is very economic, efficient and effortless. That scene covers all the bases, basically."

And for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen. As the 007 team themselves have explained in the past: "Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors."

Generally, the unveiling of a new Bond has taken place at a London press conference in front of the world's media. But for the first time creative control of the franchise is in the hands of a studio like Amazon MGM.

Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond. And they're reported to have paid at least $20m more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future.

Having paid such eye-watering amounts, it seems more than possible that Amazon MGM might well wish to drive fans towards their streaming service, with any reveal of the new Bond being exclusively announced on Prime Video.

It would almost certainly see a surge in streaming subscriptions. And such an announcement would still inevitably be covered by the world's press.

Global James Bond Day on 5 October, the 64th anniversary of the release of the first film Dr No, is fast approaching. So this date might be a good day for fans to mark in their diaries for a possible announcement.

We don't yet know what it will be called, or have a confirmed release date. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight is currently writing the script, and Dune's Denis Villeneuve will direct. They and the team may well already have a title in mind. Or, of course, they may just be calling it Bond 26 for now.

Most of the series have taken titles from the original Ian Fleming stories. Four of those remain unused - The Hildebrand Rarity, Risico, 007 in New York, and The Property of a Lady. Although elements from those stories have already been used in previous Bond films.

Fans have also been busy putting forward their own suggestions for potential titles. Since the accession of King Charles III in 2022, those suggestions have included On His Majesty's Secret Service, and King & Country.

As for a release date, it's been widely reported that the next film is likely to be released in 2028. That means it's almost certain that this will be the biggest ever gap between films, more than the six years and four months between 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

Only the Bond team themselves really know this.

But Amazon MGM do have the financial resources to plan well ahead, and explore various issues, such as how Bond will operate over multiple films; will there be an overriding arc that will cover his journey over the next decade etc; will there be a film every two years, every three years, every four or five?

Additionally, with such a huge investment, AmazonMGM will undoubtedly be keen to learn from Disney's experiences with Star Wars, and Marvel's experiences with its Marvel Cinematic Universe, in how best to use the Bond franchise.

While there might be appetite for multiple Bond spin-offs, eg Young Bond, the Miss Moneypenny adventures etc, they will also be wary that they don't over-saturate the market, and damage the films which are at the core of the Bond franchise.

The below contains spoilers for No Time To Die

Daniel Craig's farewell at the end of No Time To Die saw him on the island lair of the film's villain, Rami Malek's Safin, as it was struck by a volley of air strikes, with the super spy apparently finally meeting his demise.

Rumours have indicated that the next film might well reflect Bond's early years at the start of his MI6 career, in effect a reboot, which means that there won't be any pressure or sense of disappointment that the story won't reflect No Time To Die's conclusion.

And in any case, Bond fans have been reassured by the message that has appeared at the end of almost every Bond film - "James Bond will return".

It looks like soon we'll be finding out who that James Bond will be.

Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts

BBC News Sat, 05 Sep 2026 23:54:07 GMT

Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

"The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy.

"With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."

But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov.

"Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.

Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk.

Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.

But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.

Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.

Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee.

"This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.

Barsky has been able to continue to perform in Russian because it is a private theatre.

The new language proposal - similar to one already in force in the capital Kyiv and some other cities – would urge but not require private premises including shops and cafes to adopt the ban.

Odesa's state-appointed language ombudswoman, Anna Nerush, who inspects premises to check on alleged violations of the rules, thinks if passed it will put pressure on them to comply.

"All businesses interact in one way or another with local government," she told the BBC. "They rent premises, they need advertising permits, and so on. So for many entities it's important to comply with a council decision, even if doesn't provide for sanctions for non-compliance. "

Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.

Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.

Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside.

"But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.

Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Photographer Natalia Mykhailenko switched even earlier. She has led tours of Odesa highlighting non-Russian elements of its history.

These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.

A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists.

"We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."

Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage.

"In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said.

"Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"

It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.

Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.

One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world.

Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.

Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian."

"Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."

You can hear more about the language controversy in Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it

BBC News Sat, 05 Sep 2026 23:31:14 GMT

"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

In a survey looking into the mental load that involved 3,000 US parents, academics at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne found that mothers handled 71% of household tasks that required mental effort, such as keeping track of when sheets and towels needed to be washed and remembering by when food in the fridge needed to be eaten.

The study found that fathers handled many of the tasks researchers described as "episodic" - things that happen less often, such as remembering when to get the car serviced.

University of Melbourne Prof Leah Ruppaner describes the mental load as being invisible, enduring and without boundaries. "You don't bring your dishes to work, but you bring the mental load everywhere," she says.

The mental load is a popular topic on forums like Reddit and Mumsnet, where women seek advice about how to talk to their partners about the exhaustion of trying to juggle so many different responsibilities.

Mums told BBC News they were often added to school WhatsApp groups - where parents discuss things like non-uniform days, school trips, birthdays and lost property - as the "default parent", while their partners never joined.

Sophia, a 35-year-old mum of three in Portsmouth, pays for school trips and makes lunch orders on her children's school's app on her phone, but says her husband has never downloaded it.

Sophia says she tried multiple times to explain the concept of the mental load to her husband - but feels he didn't understand and dismissed her concerns as "quick tasks".

"They are quick tasks if you could just do the task," Sophia says, "but I have to plan for the task, I have to anticipate the task, I have to be 10 steps ahead all the time."

Sam Berry, a deputy headteacher, content creator and married dad of two in London, says when his wife first raised the idea of mental load after his eldest was born, he "didn't really get it" and was "a bit defensive" because he thought he was doing a lot - changing nappies, feeding the baby and more.

He would ask what he could do to help, but he says that still puts the burden on the other person to do the thinking.

As Stacie explains: "I always say to my partner: 'If I have to ask you to do something, that's just adding to my mental load'."

It took a few months of talking and listening for Sam to understand that it was not only about completing the task, but the thinking around it - not just cooking dinner, but what food was in the house, planning the meal, and doing the shopping.

Clinical psychologist Natasha Wallace says some women come to her feeling stressed by the pressure they feel to organise their households.

"It's often, for them, not one enormous stressor," she says. "It's when they realise that they have hundreds of tiny demands on them and their brains and bodies just can't switch off."

Many women are running on autopilot, she adds, so they often don't realise the extent of the cognitive load they're carrying, and this constant low-level stress can have an effect on the nervous system. In turn, this can cause poor sleep, irritability and decision fatigue, she says.

Anita Cleare, parenting expert and author of The Work/Parent Switch, said the overall cognitive drain spills over into our work lives and leads to unsustainable burnout.

One piece of research found that men who earned more did less physical and cognitive labour related to the household, but that when women's earnings increase, they do less physical housework but still the same amount of cognitive labour.

Women very seldomly feel it is a choice to opt out of family life, so the choice then becomes whether to decelerate their career, go part-time, or stop and stay home - with more and more women making that decision, Cleare says.

"If you lower the domestic load, if you lower the mental load, you will create energy, capacity, interest in being able to perform more and better at work."

Many of the women the BBC interviewed said they believed the disparity began with maternity leave.

Wallace says that because women typically take much longer for maternity leave than dads do for paternity leave, they become the "default parent" very early on.

"If you become the person who knows everything, knows where everything is and has in the past done everything, everybody starts coming to you for everything," she says, "so you remain that central person even if you return to work."

In the UK, mothers can take up to 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave, 39 of which can be paid, while fathers can take up to two weeks of leave with statutory paternity pay. Parents can also take shared parental leave.

Some employers offer extra parental leave to their workers, but most people earn less when on maternity or paternity leave, which affects how much leave many fathers take.

Cleare says workplaces can help by making examples of fathers taking paternity leave, not just offering it, and by setting expectations around when employees are contactable, and supporting career conversations for women.

It can also come down to what are seen as traditional roles.

Zach Watson, a married father of three and coach in the US on sharing the mental load, says his grandfather might never have cooked a meal in his married life, while his father did only a little.

In the first five years of his marriage, his wife cooked most of the time. If he offered to cook, he would ask her what she wanted - a question that could actually add to her mental load.

He learned he could come to her with options for dinner, having already looked in the fridge, and give her a default if she wanted to opt entirely out of decision-making. And if he needed help, instead of just asking "Where's the ketchup?", he could explain where he had already looked.

Sam Berry says while some men do not care, a big group - his audience online - "actually are really good husbands, are really good dads, they are trying their best and want to do the best they can, but almost haven't seen it or don't have the language".

Many women the BBC spoke to were keen for their partners to take ownership of certain tasks.

Sam calls this taking on "a category of tasks" - so dad might handle all the school admin, while mum manages the food.

However, he says equality is not necessarily about splitting everything 50/50 - because one partner might work more and another might like cooking - but about finding what works best for both partners.

And if you traditionally hold more of the mental load, you might need to accept that your partner may do things very differently, and it might not always go smoothly, says Afua Williams, 40, a mother of two in London.

Pig kidney kept a man off dialysis for nine months in world first

New Scientist September 03, 2026

A genetically modified pig’s kidney kept a man with organ failure off dialysis for nine months while he waited for a suitable human donor’s kidney to become available. This suggests pig kidneys could act as a temporary measure amid lengthy organ waiting lists, but they may also work as a permanent replacement one day.

“I think it’s incredible in terms of the science behind it and what they’ve achieved,” says Michelle Willicombe at Imperial College London, who wasn’t involved in the work.

Are genetically modified pig organs the future of transplants?

Rapid climate change brings wildfire threat to new corners of Europe

New Scientist September 03, 2026

Summer in Europe is no longer just a season of heatwaves and holidays. It is also, increasingly, a season of fire.

Following the pattern of recent years, 2026 saw huge fires break out across the continent, fuelled by weeks of hot, dry weather. Fires in France and Spain hit the headlines, but the UK, Belgium, Germany, Portugal and Italy have all also seen fierce blazes sweep through forests, grasslands and nature reserves.

Since the start of the year, almost 650,000 hectares of land have burned across the European Union, according to the European Commission, the result of over 1913 separate large wildfires across the bloc.

Advertisement

Canadian wildfires are reducing solar power generation in Europe

“Europe’s wildfires this summer have been extremely severe and destructive, and reached new corners of our continent,” Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, net zero and clean growth, wrote on LinkedIn at the end of August. “The scale of what is happening is hard to ignore.”

On both sides of the Atlantic, the fire season has been far more severe than normal. In Europe, the area of land burned so far this year is almost double the long-term average. It is a similar story in the US, where the area of land burned so far this year is 163 per cent of the 10-year average.

But although this year has been bad by past standards, it still doesn’t come close to surpassing the devastation wildfires wreaked in 2025, still by far the most severe year on record for Europe, with more than 1 million hectares burned.

Instead, what has been notable about this year’s blazes is where they have appeared. Fires have burned across the European continent, but in southern Europe, traditionally the most fire-prone region, it has been relatively quiet. Northern and western European countries, however, like France, Belgium, the Netherlands and the UK – which aren’t used to dealing with severe wildfires – have suffered intense burns. For some, these have been larger and more widespread than what has been ever seen before.

Free newsletter

In England and Wales, for example, fire and rescue services have responded to 1132 wildfires so far this year, outstripping the total for the whole of 2025, which was itself a record year. The fires tore through homes, closed major roads, and crept perilously close to a nuclear power plant, all in a country better-known for its rain than its heat.

“I think what is particularly interesting for this season, in 2026, is not the total area burned… but how quicky conditions developed, and how geographically widespread the fire danger became,” says Francesca Di Giuseppe at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

The conditions in Europe this year have been perfect for wildfires. An unusually wet winter encouraged rampant growth of grasslands, shrublands and forest understories. In May, the weather then shifted abruptly, bringing heatwaves in rapid succession and very little rainfall across swathes of the continent. The ground dried out, vegetation withered and a flash drought emerged on a grand scale. That left a dry, hot landscape littered with fuel. Add in high winds, and it was only a matter of time before fires broke out.

Will burying dead trees after a wildfire keep their carbon locked up?

“If you have 30 per cent of Europe fire-prone, somewhere it is going to happen,” says Di Giuseppe. “And if those conditions are sufficiently extreme, it will be very difficult to suppress the fire.”

This summer’s weather may have been unusually extreme, but it will become the new normal as global temperatures rise. Europe is one of the fastest-warming regions of the world. Across southern Europe, the number of summer days with fire-prone conditions has more than doubled since 1981, and the threat of catastrophic fires will only increase on the continent as the climate continues to warm, scientists predict. “The increasing frequency of hot, dry and windy conditions is consistent with the broader trend we expect under climate change,” says Maik Billing at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Research in Germany.

And, as we have seen this summer, in northern Europe the risk is rising rapidly from what was a low baseline. Managing the growing threat will require a significant shift in mindset, warns Alexander Held at the European Forest Institute. “When people outside of the UK think about the UK, they think of rain,” he says. “It you look at Ireland or Wales, where in a good year you have 2000 millimetres of rain, it is difficult for people to grasp that these landscapes are now burning.”

Why the extremes of climate breakdown will continue to take us by surprise

Much comes down to adopting common-sense behaviour in a fire-prone landscape – behaviour that is probably second nature to most citizens of southern Europe. In May, a major fire broke out at a Dutch military training ground, after the army trained with explosives during dry weather, prompting calls for training exercises to be halted at times of high fire risk.

In the UK, disposable barbecues were banned in August after they were found to have started fires in London, Staffordshire and Cheshire this summer. Simultaneously, the UK government sent out a nationwide alert to citizen smartphones, warning of a “very high risk of wildfires nationally” – the biggest use of the alert system to date – in the hope of curbing risky behaviours such as lighting barbecues or letting off fireworks.

Managing population movement from the countryside into cities is also a factor. In the US, urban sprawl has been blamed for bringing residents of cities such as Los Angeles into closer contact with the wildfire-prone countryside. But across Europe, rural abandonment is having the opposite effect; experts have warned that abandoned farmland provided plentiful fuel for the 2025 wildfires that swept through Greece, Turkey and Cyprus. The pruning, bush clearing and grazing that comes with managing a working farm is essential for fire suppression – policy-makers will need to find new ways to entice people back into the countryside to manage the fire frontiers.

The devastating wildfires in Europe demand urgent measures to make landscapes more resilient, but without action to reduce use of fossil fuels, the danger is only going to increase

Fire prevention can sometimes take the form of more unusual action – such as deer culling, says Held. In countries like the UK and Germany, earthworms are vital for clearing up leaf litter in forests before it becomes fire fuel in dry weather. But offering them the right species of leaf litter is important. In Germany’s Black Forest, for instance, earthworms love maple, cherry, lime and oak litter, but dislike conifer needles and beech litter. Unfortunately, the wild deer which roam the region’s woodlands have the same preference. As they graze and kill saplings, they are leaving the forests full of beech and conifers.

“You can see that in areas where we have too many deer, the decomposition of the [leaf] litter is not happening,” says Held.

In a similar vein, work is also needed to reshape forests to reduce monocultures and encourage native, broadleaf species which are more fire resistant. “It makes a big difference if you have a pine plantation with grass understory, where you have sunlight, wind, high temperature, drought, everything, or you have a very close to nature forest where you have shade, moisture, low temperature, no wind,” says Held.

Technology can also help. In May, a SpaceX rocket carried four new satellites into space, designed to help Greece better detect and track wildfires across its territories. FireSat is the same idea on a grander scale. Run by the non-profit Earth Fire Alliance with the help of Google, by 2030 it aims to have a constellation of 50 satellites scanning the most fire-prone spots on Earth, able to spot a fire as small as a beach bonfire. Three satellites entered orbit in July, joining the pilot satellite launched last year.

California bets on iron-salt battery power to protect against wildfire

Meanwhile, at ground level, feeds from camera networks can be monitored by AI software to spot the first signs of smoke. In California, a network of more than 1300 cameras covers fire-prone areas across the state. AI technology is used to scan the feeds and alert emergency services if fire is detected, with the aim of stopping fires before they have a chance to gather strength.

The system has helped firefighters react quickly to smother blazes that would have burned thousands of acres, according to Neal Driscoll at UC San Diego. The same technology is now arriving in Europe: in the Gironde, a region of France hit hardest by wildfires this summer, firefighters are now employing AI-assisted cameras to raise the alarm on emerging blazes. Solar-powered patrol drones could be next.

Yet fire management can take us only so far. Research published in August warns that by the end of this century, the area burned by wildfires in Europe will increase by 39 per cent even under a low-emissions scenario, and could almost triple under high emissions. Improvements in fire management could reduce these increases by more than 70 per cent, but not eliminate them entirely, the study found.

To reduce the growing risk of intense wildfires, California is cutting and burning the areas that fuel them – but these efforts may be moving too slowly

Some researchers think the fire risk is already beyond our control, particularly in southern Europe, which normally bears the brunt of “fire weather”. Raul Cordero Carrasco at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands points out that the burned area in southern Europe has been rising since 2018. He thinks this is a sign that investment in suppression and management is hitting its limit. In southern Europe, he argues, “climate change is making fires unstoppable”.

“When the temperature is very high and the winds are very strong, there is nothing you can do to stop the fire,” he says.

But for northern Europe at least, where large fires are still a mercifully rare event, there is plenty of work that can and must be done to mitigate further risk. Not every summer will be like the hot, dry days of 2026. But the threat is advancing, and this summer has been our amber warning to prepare.

“James Webb is discovering many more black holes than most of us theorists predicted in our most optimistic models,” says Priyamvada Natarajan at Yale University. “The universe is just littered with black holes.”

An existing idea is that primordial black holes formed in violent space-time spasms in the early universe before any stars appeared. Theorists have had to propose complicated new physical laws to make the explanation fit.

They call these black holes “not-quite-primordial” and argue they provide an explanation for the black holes spotted via the JWST that doesn’t require drastic changes to cosmologists’ picture of the early universe.

The researchers reached out to Natarajan, a theoretical astrophysicist, to help confirm their logic.

“This is a case where you could actually have a black hole forming before the stars. And that I found really exciting,” says Natarajan.

“What’s nice about the model is that it invokes less speculative physics than traditional primordial black hole physics,” says John Regan at Maynooth University, Ireland, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Having says that, what we need ultimately will be concrete observations. Their next step will be to simulate the new process and see what it implies about the spectrum of light that should be emitted from around a not-quite-primordial black hole. They can then compare these predictions more closely to data from JWST.

New Scientist September 05, 2026

AI company Anthropic has created a formalised proof of Fermat’s last theorem. It took just 11 days for a group of AI agents to complete the task, confirming that the human-found proof proposed in the 1990s is correct.

Fermat’s last theorem puzzled mathematicians for centuries until it was proved in 1995 by Andrew Wiles. It states that there are no whole numbers a, b, and c that satisfy the equation aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ, where n is a whole number greater than 2.

The theorem, though easy to state, was fiendishly difficult to prove. Mathematician Pierre de Fermat posed the puzzle in the 17th century and famously alluded to a proof that he claimed to have discovered, saying that it was too large to fit in the margins of the textbook he was writing in.

Advertisement

Mathematics is undergoing the biggest change in its history

Many mathematicians tried and failed to find a proof. Wiles worked on the problem for seven years in secret before announcing his breakthrough in 1993. Proofs often involve lengthy logical arguments that build on each other. If a single step contains an error, then the whole thing can collapse. This happened to Wiles when a flaw was found in his proof, which took him and collaborator Richard Taylor around a year to fix.

Formalising mathematical theorems is a solution to this problem. It takes them out of the realm of pen and paper, and puts them into a configuration – computer code – that allows machines to grapple with them, methodically working through the logic and exposing any flaws. There are already 2 million lines of formalised mathematics stored in a central repository called Mathlib.

Earlier this year, a conference of AI experts, computer scientists and mathematicians was held in London by Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, who was – until Anthropic’s announcement – working on a five-year project to formalise Wiles and Taylor’s 100-page proof in a programming language called Lean, so that it can be formally checked for correctness and used as a foundation for further research.

Buzzard said at the time that when his project began he was confident of success, but that recent advances in AI had convinced him that the project would be complete much faster than he previously thought possible. Anthropic’s announcement has now overtaken that effort and wrapped up the problem.

Buzzard said in a statement published by Anthropic that the company’s proof leaves “no assumptions other than the axioms of mathematics”. In short, the problem is solved.

Mathematicians put AI to work on Fermat’s last theorem

“Along the way we see autoformalisation of algebra, harmonic analysis, geometry and number theory, and we learn that AI autoformalisation artefacts are now robust enough to be built upon; the proof is multi-layered,” said Buzzard. “If the automatic formalisation of FLT is possible now, then we have taken a big step towards automatic formalisation of the modern mathematical literature.”

In its blog post announcing the result, Anthropic wrote that its Claude model worked continuously and autonomously for 11 days to write the proof. Numerous separate AI agents were involved, with different tasks, like tackling smaller chunks of the theorem, being assigned to each.

Free newsletter

Human experts occasionally issued “high-level instructions” to keep the work on track, the company says. Several times, the agents “lost track of the project’s state and stopped collaborating effectively”. Interestingly, the company said that success came after it began using a tool designed for human mathematical collaboration called Prove2Me, which helped different agents track their work and decide on next tasks.

Anthropic’s formalisation runs to 13 million lines of Lean and covers roughly 29,500 intermediate theorems that were necessary stepping stones towards completing the overall work. That makes the proof over five times the current size of all previous work on Mathlib, which also makes it the largest Lean proof ever written.

The species can transmit many different pathogens, including the dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya and Zika viruses. It commonly feeds at dusk and dawn, indoors and in shady areas.

According to the UKHSA, the mosquitoes and larvae were found breeding in residential properties in east London. They were spotted and reported under the government’s Mosquito Watch scheme, which aims to detect the presence of invasive mosquitoes.

The UKHSA said the larvae have been destroyed and promised the area will be monitored closely to eradicate any further mosquitoes and larvae that might emerge.

The UKHSA insists the threat to public health remains very low. There is no evidence the A. aegypti mosquitoes found in London have transmitted any infections to people, and so far no more mosquitoes or larvae have been found in nearby public areas.

César López-Camacho at the University of Oxford said in a statement to the Science Media Centre that the discovery of their presence should be seen as an “early warning rather than an immediate public-health threat”.

It is worth noting that the UK is home to many species of native mosquitoes, but these generally don’t carry serious infections, and are largely an annoyance rather than a public-health threat.

Jolyon Medlock at the UKHSA said in a statement that the mosquitoes were likely to be “accidental importations”, having “hitchhiked” in vehicles, in suitcases or via imported plants.

The UK has just had its hottest summer on record. London has seen some of the highest temperatures in the country, as heatwaves are usually amplified in cities due to the urban heat island effect.

That may mean the mosquitoes have been able to successfully breed over the summer months this year. But Medlock said the UK’s climate is still too cold overall to enable the mosquitoes to breed over the long term – for now.

Free newsletter

Mosquitoes are expanding their range north as the climate warms. Warmer weather also increases the rate at which viruses replicate in an insect’s body.

That means mosquito-borne viruses are rapidly becoming more common in Europe as the continent warms. In late August, French authorities reported cases of locally transmitted dengue, West Nile and chikungunya viruses across the country, including Paris.

And a study published earlier this year found that the Asian tiger mosquito, another invasive mosquito species in Europe, can transmit chikungunya over several months of the year on the continent. The study authors said Europe’s rapid rate of warming was enabling virus transmission to become more widespread across the region.

Over time, the threat of mosquito-borne disease to the British public is also expected to rise. Last year, West Nile virus was detected in the UK for the first time in mosquitoes in Nottinghamshire. For now, authorities hope to keep invasive mosquitoes out of the country for as long as possible to prevent disease transmission.

For most people in the UK, a mosquito bite is an annoyance but nothing to worry about. It will usually produce a red, itchy swelling that will subside within a few days. If you develop a fever or become unwell, and have recently travelled to a location where dengue, chikungunya or Zika is circulating, you should seek medical attention.

Scientist say it is important to minimise the chance of mosquitoes breeding in the UK, to try to prevent invasive species gaining a foothold on UK shores. A. aegypti mosquitoes are well adapted to human environments and can breed in small quantities of standing water, so the most important action people can take is to eliminate, as far as possible, any standing water around the home. That could include emptying water trays under houseplants, clearing rainfall from containers, keeping lids on rain barrels, washing out pet bowls and flower vases regularly and keeping shower areas as clean and dry as possible between use.

If you spot a mosquito in the UK, you can report it to the Mosquito Watch scheme.

The unprecedented El Niño gathering strength in the Pacific Ocean could upend forecasts for UK weather this winter, bringing continuously wet, stormy conditions until spring.

El Niño is a natural climate phase that happens when easterly trade winds weaken, allowing the warm water they had piled up in the western Pacific to wash back across the central and eastern Pacific. This swathe of warm water heats the atmosphere and weakens the winds further in a feedback loop.

The phenomenon’s impact on the weather in the UK and north-western Europe is notoriously tricky to predict, because weather patterns in this region are strongly affected by weather phenomena in the North Atlantic.

Advertisement

Under an El Niño event of normal intensity, the UK is more likely to experience wetter, windier, stormier weather in the late autumn and early winter, potentially followed by a colder, drier end to winter.

However, the sheer size of the current El Niño – already one of the largest on record and still intensifying – could mean that the end of winter and start of spring continue to be wet and stormy, says Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s national weather service, who leads the agency’s long-range forecasting.

“We found that the big events show a slightly different response over the Atlantic,” he says. El Niños usually increase the likelihood of cold easterly winds prevailing over the UK during late winter. But a very strong El Niño may reverse that trend, leading to prevailing westerlies late in the season. The weather under those conditions is “still cold, but it’s not extreme”, he says.

Scaife first reported this effect of strong El Niños in a 2006 research paper he co-wrote with Thomas Toniazzo, now at NORCE Research in Norway. The study assessed the weather in the North Atlantic during El Niño years and found that very strong El Niños produced this mild and wet pattern in late winter.

Free newsletter

The El Niño in 1997-1998, for example, was one of the most powerful on record. It saw high pressure developing in the North Atlantic to the west of the UK over the late winter, leading to westerly prevailing winds that blew milder, wetter, stormier air over the UK and northern Europe. The same pattern appeared in the 2015-2016 El Niño, when the UK had one of its mildest and wettest winters on record.

“We think that’s a real effect [of strong El Niños],” says Scaife. “We’re looking for that at the end of this winter.”

A prolonged wet and stormy winter could saturate soils and make parts of the UK more susceptible to severe flooding. But it would also offer an opportunity to replenish reservoirs and groundwater after an exceptionally dry summer.

Intense fires are already burning in Indonesia, and there could be much worse to come as the Super El Niño ramps up

However, Scaife warns it is very difficult to tease apart the effect of a strong El Niño compared with that of a standard-strength one, in part because there are only a few very strong events in the historical record for which we have good data.

El Niños – and their opposite pattern, La Niñas – also vary hugely from year to year and decade to decade, so it can be fiendishly difficult to separate out a signal from the noise in the system. What’s more, it is very difficult to predict weather patterns months in advance, and there is still huge uncertainty over what late winter will hold for the UK.

This week, the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) warned that the El Niño is still intensifying in the tropical Pacific and is set to be the largest on record, fuelling drought, floods and extreme temperatures around the world. In most cases, a stronger El Niño brings more pronounced impacts globally, such as severe drought in Australia, the Amazon and Indonesia, and heavy rain in parts of South America, East Africa and the southern US.

The pattern is likely to peak in November, but will persist until at least February 2027, the WMO said, bringing extreme impacts that will last well into next year.

Lucid dreams induced via multisensory stimulation

New Scientist September 04, 2026

Scientist Tobi Matzek has breathed underwater, explored outer space and even transformed into a dragon – in their dreams. “I pulled a purple-and-white pill out of my pocket and swallowed it, and immediately, I had purple dragon wings,” they say.

These adventures occurred during lucid dreams, when a person is aware they are dreaming and can often influence what happens. Matzek, at the University of Montreal in Canada, has now found that lucid dreams can be induced in some people via cognitive and multisensory stimulation.

Epic dreaming is leaving people exhausted and distressed

Fascinated by the concept of lucid dreams, Matzek and their colleagues recruited 60 adults with no known health conditions who had experienced at least one lucid dream before. The frequency of these dreams varied, with 15 of the individuals experiencing them less than once a year and others having lucid dreams several times a week.

Advertisement

The participants came into one of three labs – in Italy, Canada or the Netherlands – on two mornings to nap for up to 2.5 hours. Immediately before each nap, they were given half an hour of lucidity training.

This involved lying in bed with their eyes closed while the ZMax EEG headband, a sleep-tracking device, delivered red-light flashes, played a short melody and administered a few soft vibrations on their forehead.

At the same time, a soundtrack guided them to focus their attention on these sensations and asked them to be aware of any differences between the sensations they were feeling during this experience and what they felt during normal wakefulness.

Free newsletter

“This may train people to pay closer attention to changes in their sensory experience and make them more likely to recognise the odd or inconsistent experiences that occur in dreams and realise ‘I must be dreaming’,” says team member Claudia Picard-Deland, also at the University of Montreal.

During one of the two naps, these sensory stimulations were repeated when the participant entered the rapid eye movement (REM) stage of sleep, when we have our most powerful dreams.

Earlier, the researchers taught the participants to move their eyes from left to right to signal that a lucid dream had started and was ongoing. Overall, just over half of the participants gave this signal while the headset readings confirmed they were asleep, usually in the REM stage. After waking, these participants also reported that they’d had a lucid dream.

“The training led to a relatively high rate of lucid dreaming, even in people who rarely had lucid dreams before,” says Matzek.

Kristoffer Appel at the Institute of Sleep and Dream Technologies in Hamburg, Germany, calls the results “remarkable”. “They suggest that lucidity is far more trainable on short notice than the spontaneous and rare reputation that it usually has,” he says.

People who are terminally ill are commonly reunited with lost loved ones in their dreams and have visions of doors, stairways and light, which are said to help them accept the dying process

The lucid dreams were no more likely to occur during the nap in which the sensory stimulations were re-applied during the REM stage. However, the gap between the participants’ first and last eye signals indicated that they lasted around twice as long in this condition.

Longer lucid dreams could be useful because they are being investigated as a way to boost creativity and problem-solving, and to treat nightmares in people with post-traumatic stress disorder, says Matzek.

However, only about 55 per cent of people have experienced lucid dreams, and it is unclear if this approach can induce them in individuals who have never had one.

bioRxiv DOI: 10.1101/2024.06.21.600133

Nations and big tech to train AI using ‘gold dust’ data from Ukraine

New Scientist September 04, 2026

Global superpowers and giant technology firms are scrambling for real-world data from the war in Ukraine to build next-generation AI models that will empower militaries in future conflicts. Videos of drone strikes and other sensor data are like “gold dust” for training AI, say experts.

Last month, Ukraine signed a deal with the UK to share a vast treasure trove of data collected from drones, cameras and sensors since Russia staged its full-scale invasion. It is claimed that the deal will make the UK the first foreign state to have access to Ukraine’s so-called “Avengers AI” model, which is already being used to identify adversaries and their equipment in real time and slash the time taken to stage attacks.

The UK claims that the first fruits of this deal are about to be tested through a project that is turning buried fibre-optic cables into sensors to detect hostile intrusions at an unnamed UK defence site.

Advertisement

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

Peter Lee at the University of Portsmouth, UK, says the varied data will be immensely valuable in creating a wide range of defence and military tools, which will make both the UK and Ukraine more secure.

“This is the gold dust that allows the UK to enter the autonomous age of drones,” he says. “You can’t really put a price on the data they’re going to get access to. Add up everything that the UK has given to Ukraine over the last several years – this data is worth all of that and more.”

Ukraine flies thousands of drones a day, both in the war zone and penetrating deep into Russia, and has a vast array of sensors on the front line. This data has long been fed into a government department known as Brave1, which analyses it with AI to find strategic weaknesses and opportunities. It feeds that information back to troops on the front line and defence contractors.

Subscriber-only newsletter

AI models can be used to autonomously steer drones to their targets, monitor thousands of video feeds and other sensors for tell-tale signs of adversaries’ movements, or analyse footage of attacks to spot design flaws in military hardware. The models can even plan strikes and pick targets.

Numerous efforts are under way in Ukraine to use AI to eke out an advantage in all sorts of areas, including at the defence ministry’s “A1” organisation – which the Ukrainian government launched with UK government support in March, long before this latest announcement.

Lee says the possibilities are so compelling that it is almost certain that China is doing the same with Russian data, taken from the opposite side of the front line – and they probably had a head start. He thinks that, in the earliest stage of negotiations between Russia and China about military and intelligence support for the invasion, China will have raised the issue of data sharing.

“China understands that data is king when it comes to AI, and that the more data you have, the more powerful your systems are likely to be,” says Lee. “It would be a strategic oversight of grotesque proportions [if China hadn’t sought data].”

Solar-powered ambush drones can wait for targets like land mines

Joe Burton at Lancaster University in the UK says that despite the UK’s support of Ukraine with weapons, training and intelligence since the full-scale invasion, it is unlikely that raw data has been shared on a wide scale until recently. But a deterioration in relations with the US may be an incentive for Ukraine to create stronger ties with other allies.

“The Trump presidency has been very volatile in its approach to Ukraine and, if you’re in [Kyiv], it makes sense to have a broader set of partnerships around AI data, which can help support you in what will probably still be a long-term war,” says Burton. “I would not be surprised if Ukraine are hedging their bets.”

Big technology firms are also getting involved. Ukraine has long worked with AI company Palantir, and signed a data-sharing deal with the firm months before the agreement with the UK was announced. US company Clearview AI’s face-recognition technology has been used to find Russian spies operating in Ukraine, while another US firm, Scale AI, has used satellite data to identify Russian troop movements and detect building damage across Ukraine.

Injuries from the war in Ukraine have forced the country to develop highly advanced prostheses and fit them in record numbers. What can the rest of the world learn from its efforts?

“All these companies are competing for data. If you have access to actual, real, credible battlefield data from Ukraine instead of simulated data that you’re generating in a lab, that’s a big commercial advantage,” says Burton.

In short, if you are pitching your product to states looking for AI tools to protect national security or support their militaries, then having a battle-tested product is a strong selling point.

But despite the vast expansion of data collection, AI analysis and high-tech weapons systems, the day-to-day reality for troops in Ukraine remains a muddy trench, not dissimilar to those dug in the first world war.

“It’s still attritional. It’s still horribly violent. This idea that you can deploy a load of robots to the battlefield and you don’t need to send soldiers into harm’s way, it’s not [happening] in Ukraine,” says Burton.
