Waikato surgeon Stephen Adams takes specialist skills to Samoa

New Zealand Herald September 06, 2026

Dr Stephen Adams in surgery. Photo / Supplied

At Waikato Hospital, Dr Stephen Adams performs routine operations several times a week.

In Samoa, he found children who had waited years for surgery.

Adams, head of paediatric surgery at Waikato Hospital, travelled to Apia in June this year with a six-person Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (RACS) team.

Over five days, they assessed more than 50 children and performed 26 operations.

Some were procedures familiar to Adams in Hamilton. In Samoa, they carried a different weight.

The team treated children with conditions including Hirschsprung disease (where nerve cells are missing in a baby’s large intestine), anorectal malformations, hernias, undescended testicles and tumours.

Adams had wanted to become involved in Pacific outreach surgery for several years.

A colleague was unable to attend the trip, and Adams led the team. It comprised two surgeons, two anaesthetists and two nurses.

The mission is part of an annual RACS programme providing specialist surgical support across the Pacific.

The work starts well before the visiting surgeons arrive, with Samoan clinicians identifying and preparing patients throughout the year.

“They’re a really good medical team,” Adams said. “It’s just that they have no available resource to achieve it.”

The team began work on the Monday with a clinic of more than 50 children before moving into theatre that afternoon.

They operated until about 8pm and ran two operating theatres each day for the rest of the week.

For Adams, the differences from Waikato were quickly apparent.

A steam steriliser could take four or five hours to process instruments, and the hospital had limited supplies of some medicines.

The team also had to decide which operations would use the specialist paediatric instruments they had brought.

Adams decided against several operations because the equipment or circumstances were not suitable.

“We did have an ethical obligation to provide correct care, not just make do,” he said.

For Adams, one of the most striking aspects of the trip was how familiar many of the surgical problems were.

The team saw conditions he treated routinely in Hamilton, including hernias and undescended testicles, alongside more complex bowel and anorectal conditions.

The difference was how long some children had lived with them.

One patient had been dealing with the same problem for four or five years.

In another case, Adams removed a kidney that had been infected for a long time.

“It’s unusual for that to happen in our setting,” he said.

Several children were severely anaemic and needed blood transfusions.

Adams said some families struggled to afford necessities, including infant formula.

One young boy with an anorectal malformation underwent surgery to correct the condition.

“He was just smiling, happy and lovely,” Adams said.

“He was just delightful to look after.”

Not every case had a surgical solution.

Adams also reviewed children with serious illnesses that could not be corrected surgically. In some cases, the team could assess the child and reassure families that the local care was appropriate.

“Heartbreakingly, in a couple of cases, there really wasn’t anything more that could be offered.”

Local doctors and trainees worked alongside the surgeons, while the visiting nurses provided formal and informal education.

“It’s not really about us kind of parachuting in and doing stuff,” Adams said.

“It’s about supporting and developing and growing teams as well.”

The relationship continues from New Zealand.

Adams remains in contact with Samoan clinicians.

He hopes some of the trainees he worked with will come to New Zealand for further training.

Adams said greater funding could allow the team to spend two weeks operating rather than one, giving them more time to treat patients and train clinicians.

“The funding is probably the biggest barrier to care,” he said.

“Surgery is one of the most impactful things you can spend one dollar on.”

Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade was the major funder of the latest mission.

Adams said the most important outcome was not the number of operations completed.

“Probably the real outcome is that we’re increasing our ability to work with these guys and to develop them and improve them.”

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Dean Fifield’s killer Elizabeth Smith makes first appearance before Parole Board

New Zealand Herald September 06, 2026

Elizabeth Smith came before the Parole Board for the first time on Friday after serving half her sentence for the manslaughter of Dean Fifield (inset). Photo / Michael Craig / Supplied / Composite

A woman who ran over and killed her former partner has been told she’s lacking victim empathy and should try to find some within the next 12 months.

Elizabeth Smith was sentenced to four and a half years in prison last August for Dean Fifield’s manslaughter.

She ran him over after a tense night in 2024 when she returned to collect personal items from a home they shared in Massey.

As Smith was preparing to drive away, Fifield emerged from the house and hit the windscreen of a vehicle belonging to friends.

Smith then drove out of the driveway and directly into him.

On Friday, she came before the Parole Board for the first time, having served half her sentence.

Board chairwoman Ann-Marie Beveridge asked Smith why she had driven at Fifield, killing him that night.

“Why did this happen?”

“Because I got into a relationship really fast,” Smith answered. “And yeah, I didn’t leave sooner and I didn’t turn my car in the opposite direction and go left instead.”

Beveridge asked if Smith knew why she didn’t drive in the other direction.

“I was just scared. Very fearful. I wasn’t thinking right at that time.”

Smith was not seeking parole during her first appearance. Her lawyer Daniel Bousfield said there were steps she needed to take for that to be considered.

Beveridge asked Smith if she stood by what she told her probation officer before sentencing, that she had purposely hit Fifield with her car in self-defence, but it was an accident that she killed him.

Smith said she didn’t “purposefully” run Fifield over. However, after she hit him, she pressed the brakes, the car slid forward and Fifield fell under the front of the car.

“And I got out of the car and I just started screaming.”

She said because Fifield had kung fu experience she thought he would “roll off” when she hit him.

“Hadn’t he been hit by a car not so long ago?” Beveridge asked.

He didn’t seem like he was still injured, Smith replied.

Bousfield mentioned that what Smith said to her parole officer last year better reflected her intentions and mental state at that time.

He said rehabilitative prison programmes were one of the steps his client was keen to start.

Smith told the court she had started an alcohol and drug programme behind bars this week.

Parole Board member Pauline Hopa asked what she wanted to achieve at her appearance, to which Smith replied she knew she was not going home right now and needed to finish the course.

“That’s okay,” she told the board.

Contact the Open Justice team

Hopa asked what she wanted to achieve from the course, to which Smith said she wanted to learn how to make choices and be a better person.

She said the desired outcome for the course was to heal her own trauma, so she didn’t carry it on or make the same bad choices she had before.

Hopa asked if that was in relation to drug addiction, to which Smith replied, “yeah”.

The board went away for about 30 minutes. When they returned, Beveridge said “it won’t come as a surprise” that parole was declined.

“You have some work to do, which you yourself accept,” Beveridge said.

Smith would be before the board again in 12 months, Beveridge said, which would allow time for her to complete that work.

Beveridge said Smith’s conduct in custody was not always as good as it could be and that she needed this treatment.

She said next time Smith was in front of the board she would hopefully have a better understanding of why she committed her crime.

“Also, what would be good is a bit of victim empathy, which we seem to be lacking. So maybe through doing the programme, some victim empathy might come into play.”

Ella Scott-Fleming has been a journalist for three years and previously worked at the Otago Daily Times, Gore Ensign and Metro Magazine. She has an interest in court and general reporting. She’s currently based in Auckland covering justice-related stories.

Much of the North Island can expect heavy rain today, with flooding and dangerous driving conditions possible.

A storm making its way north caused flooding and slips, which closed several state highways in the South Island on Sunday.

Between 20-40mm of rain fell in lower North Island regions overnight, such as Kapiti, Manawatu and Whanganui.

MetService Meteorologist Dom Barry told the Herald a low-pressure system sitting near the North Island's east coast will move through the Waikato this morning, bringing rain for the majority of the island.

"Bands of showers passing through everywhere from Wellington all the way up to Cape Reinga, so it's definitely a wet one on the cards for everybody today at some point."

Rain will begin to ease for the lower North Island this afternoon, Barry said.

For Auckland, the heaviest rain will fall between 7am and 9am.

In the South Island, two drivers had to be helped out of floodwaters around the Murchison area early this morning. One had driven into flooding on State Highway 6, while another became trapped while trying to take a detour, Fire and Emergency southern shift manager Lyn Crossan said. The water wasn’t deep enough to send the vehicles floating down the road “but it obviously gave the drivers a bit of a fright”, Crossan said.

A tree had also fallen on the roof of a house in Richmond overnight. Fire crews had removed the tree and secured another to make it safe, with more calls after daybreak as people began to assess the weather damage.

He said the model was a type of mortgage-lender insurance, lowering the risk for banks of lending to low-deposit buyers.

About 7500 first-home buyers had applied for the scheme in the past nine months. However, around half of first-home buyers weren’t eligible as their incomes were too high.

“First-home buyers are up 29%, mortgage serviceability because of lower interest rates is up 61% under us. So, the real problem that people are finding is not servicing the mortgage – it’s actually getting the deposit together.”

National’s latest campaign promise would see buyers earning up to $300,000 eligible for the 5% deposit scheme.

Since 2003, the In Reach loan scheme – renamed the First Home Loan scheme – has helped more than 33,000 households to buy a home.

The current income cap is $95,000 for an individual with no dependents, or $150,000 for multiple buyers or a single person with dependents.

Announcing the policy on Sunday, Luxon and his housing spokesman Chris Bishop said the cap was too restrictive and hadn’t been updated since 2022, with around half of first-home buyers now earning more than $146,000.

The proposed $300,000 cap would not distinguish between single or multiple buyers.

National wanted home-ownership rates back to their peak in the 1990s, when almost three-quarters of households owned their own home.

Only two-thirds of households currently own their home, although first-home buyers have been buying a record share of properties as house prices have fallen.

The party estimated its policy would cost the Crown $4-$6 million extra per year.

Meanwhile, the Green Party has announced its plan to break up the supermarket duopoly by nationalising 120 supermarkets to create a new Government-owned supermarket chain known as KiwiMart.

KiwiMart would have a mandate to prioritise affordability. Greens co-leader Chloe Swarbrick said currently two companies controlled what almost everyone in New Zealand ate, while taking $1m daily in excess profits.

“That is money that should be in people’s pockets,” Swarbrick said.

The plan has been costed at $2.8 billion, which includes buying 120 Woolworths and Foodstuffs stores and two distribution centres, and capitalising KiwiMart to make it a commercially viable competitor.

Woman Unknown review – postwar paranoia with some deliciously dastardly Du Maurier touches

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 20:15:14 GMT

Venice film festivalA nanny becomes the new lady of a prosperous Copenhagen house as accused Nazi sympathisers are violently shamed in May el-Toukhy’s shrewd, painful portrait of survival

Here is an elegantly appointed drama-thriller from May el-Toukhy, about sexual shame and political paranoia in postwar Denmark, with something of Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca, which it consciously recalls. As director and co-writer, El-Toukhy has created a shrewd and painful movie about the terrible things you need to do to survive, and what it takes to forget those things afterwards.

The scene is a prosperous, upper-middle-class apartment in Copenhagen just after the second world war, when the Danish resistance was permitted the powers of a secret-police militia to detain and interrogate those suspected of having given assistance to the Nazis. Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund) is a ageing factory owner and widower who has evidently fallen in love with his infant daughter’s nanny: this is Marie (fiercely and convincingly played by Mathilde Arcel). Or at any rate, he sees that the child needs a new mother, finds Marie attractive and appreciates her submissive attitude. They are now engaged.

As for Marie herself, her fellow servants do not appear to resent her counter-jumper prominence as the new lady of the house; very indiscreetly, she sleeps with Christian in what will shortly be the marital bed. Marie has a reasonable working relationship with housekeeper Esther (Marina Bouras) who would otherwise be Rebecca’s stern Mrs Danvers figure but is in fact pleasant enough, though she disapproves of Marie’s friendly relationship with single-mother neighbour Mrs Berg (Sofia Nolsøe), whose worldly, sophisticated air she finds disagreeable.

But poor Marie’s ability to cover up her own secret fears and sins is tested to the limit when she is expected, in a pure Daphne du Maurier touch, to wear the wedding gown of Christian’s late wife at the ceremony. She has to carry it on public transport to the dressmakers to get it altered (another Hitchcockian display), which leads to a disastrous encounter with someone from her past.

And all the time, Danish women who are accused of having consorted with Germans are shamed in the street; their heads are shaved and swastikas painted on their back. The film also shows the great and underacknowledged truth of this, in postwar Denmark as in postwar France: shaming women was a convenient way for men to divert attention from their own far more substantial and far-reaching Nazi collaboration. This includes Christian, whose factory would have gone broke without Nazi customers.

The shadow of suspicion closes in on their well-appointed household as the wedding day approaches and, as various ruses occur to her to make sure that the past does not rise up to overwhelm her, Marie discovers a new strain of cunning and ruthlessness and self-pity in herself. This is a very watchable, expertly managed drama about the return of the repressed.

The US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to Ukraine for the first time on Sunday for talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an attempt to end the war with Russia.

The Ukrainian president announced plans to widen peace discussions to include European countries in the near future, saying he wanted to do “everything to ensure that trilateral meetings take place” with Ukraine, the US and Europe.

Witkoff said he was hopeful such meetings would be announced “in short order”. The British, French and German national security advisers briefly joined Sunday’s talks.

Witkoff said the talks with Zelenskyy had been “very constructive and substantive”. Kushner said the conflict between Russia and Ukraine was “a long, hard and emotional war”.

There were otherwise few details from the highly anticipated talks between Washington and Kyiv, which came a day after the US envoys met Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow.

Kushner and Witkoff were forced to arrive in Kyiv by train after Russia bombed the city’s two main airports on Friday. Both countries pledged to refrain from attacking each other’s capitals over the weekend to ensure the US envoys’ safe passage.

Zelenskyy joked that the delegation should come more often to “protect our citizens who are in the capital”.

But the president’s mood was generally sombre. He said Ukraine was “really counting on a winter package” from the US and Europe to enable it to withstand another war-torn winter.

“We specifically discussed this with Steve and Jared, as well as with our European partners: air defence, energy support, and as you know we are counting on the serious use of LNG, American LNG,” he said, referring to liquefied natural gas.

Zelenskyy greeted the US envoys earlier in the day in Sophia Square, in front of Kyiv’s historic cathedral.

The cathedral is a few hundred metres away from the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency, which was hit by a Russian drone on Friday afternoon, marking an escalation in a conflict that has dragged on for more than four and a half years.

Kushner said his team was in almost daily contact with Ukrainian officials. “Just because we haven’t travelled out, it doesn’t mean we haven’t … been communicating,” he said.

Expectations going into the talks were low. US-backed mediation has stalled over the past few months as Washington has been focused on the war with Iran. Many Ukrainians are also sceptical that Trump is committed to a peace agreement that is acceptable to Kyiv. “People don’t trust the Russians and people don’t trust Trump personally,” said Artem Bronzhukov, a political analyst.

Talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending the war have focused on a 20-point peace plan put forward by Washington and Kyiv in December. But the two sides have failed to reach common ground on several sticking points, including control of territory in east Ukraine.

“People mostly understand that if you step back from the Donbas, the next day or the next week, Putin will push for another condition,” Bronzhukov said.

A White House official said on Saturday that the talks with Moscow “discussed substantive plans for next steps” for ending the war and that an announcement would follow in the coming weeks.

The senior Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the talks as “extremely frank” and said there was an acknowledgement of the need to address “the root causes of the conflict”.

Kyiv and the surrounding areas have been hit by a barrage of daily drone strikes for more than a week, the most sustained attack on Ukraine’s capital in months.

The capital is now enjoying a reprieve from strikes and air raid alerts that had become a daily occurrence, but other parts of the country are still being hit. Ukrainian authorities reported on Sunday that at least eight people were killed and 69 injured across Ukraine in the past day.

Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles that can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones that can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept.

Many Ukrainians are worried about the war dragging on into a fifth year and are anxious about the winter ahead. This week, Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov, told the Guardian that the government should consider evacuating elderly people from Kyiv as Putin had ordered the Russian military to “prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities.

Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent weeks in an effort to sap morale in each other’s countries.

There were eight minutes of stoppage time indicated for the end of the second half, so the substitution in question came with merely seconds remaining. The consequences could be significant for Palace, depending on the outcome of the investigation and the verdict of any potential tribunal.

The WSL's rules regarding the fielding of an ineligible player list the potential punishments in rule 7.13.2, which include the possibility that the points gained from the match be deducted or that the match be replayed. It is understood that the team of match officials who worked on that Palace-Everton game will not be appointed to the next round of games in WSL/ WSL2 on the weekend of 12-13 September, in light of this incident.

Teams are permitted to use no more than three substitution opportunities per match, in addition to being able to make replacements at half-time and for concussion substitutions. Tom Garry

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 18:13:29 GMT

Exit poll shows Alternative für Deutschland on 44.4% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being counted

The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has emerged as the winner in a crucial state election in Germany, exit polls have projected, securing a historic result and more than doubling its support. The AfD now appear on the brink of becoming the first far-right party to gain power in Germany at state level since the second world war.

Initial exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.4% of the vote, a larger share than predicted, and decisively larger than that of the Christian Democrats (CDU) of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world. However, it still remains unclear as to how and whether the AfD will be able to form a government, having ruled out entering a coalition and being refused any form of cooperation by the mainstream parties.

The CDU was trailing massively on around 18.4% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.3%, with the Social Democrats on 8.4% and the Greens on 8.7% by around early evening. The smaller BSW reached the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament, against expectations. The party, an offshoot of Die Linke, has agreed to cooperate with the AfD on issues such as energy price reform.

Participation was at a record high of 76.5%.

Votes are still being counted, but it appeared initially that the AfD might have failed to secure an absolute majority – the condition it has said is central to it taking power, given its refusal to govern with another party.

The CDU and all other mainstream parties have also refused to collude with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer, or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.

Addressing jubilant supporters, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said: “We have made history in this country”. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD, he said his party was ready to ⁠reach out ​to ‌all powers ‌that ‌strove for political change.

“We extend a hand to all ‌democratic forces that wish to pursue ​better policies,” a beaming Siegmund said after ⁠exit polls had been published. He said themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate.

The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with the AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out.

Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era.

She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Siegmund on Sunday evening called Merz “a very good campaigner for the AfD”.

Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how the AfD could rule.

About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents.

Final polls had shown the AfD to have around 40-41% of support, and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%.

The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.

The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.

The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter.

In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.

If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms.

He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.

Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.

Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.

Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.

On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”

The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.

The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.

Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

Ødegaard fires winner as Arsenal complete comeback win over Chelsea

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 17:53:08 GMT

The first heavyweight encounter of the Premier League season was previewed in some quarters as the immovable object versus the irresistible force. Arsenal do not give an inch. Chelsea have been fun and free-scoring under Xabi Alonso. Yet that overlooked something pretty fundamental. The percussive force of Arsenal’s game when they have the ball and want to make something happen.

Chelsea landed a significant blow after 77 seconds when Morgan ­Rogers put them in front with a nicely executed volley from the edge of the area. It was not only the first goal that Arsenal have conceded this season but one with rich narrative strands. Rogers was chased by Arsenal over the summer only to join Chelsea for £117m.

The story here was about Arsenal’s reaction. The sheer fury of it. For a blistering spell that culminated in Kai Havertz’s equaliser on 25 minutes, they threatened to blow Chelsea off the pitch. Arsenal’s confidence shone through. They had not lost to their cross-town rivals in 11 previous ­meetings in all competitions, winning eight, but it was rooted in more than that. They had too much for Chelsea and they knew it.

Martin Ødegaard’s goal shortly after half-time proved the dif­ference – after a stunning feint by Havertz – and it continued Arsenal’s perfect start to their title defence. It is now three wins out of three. They will take some stopping. Then again, everybody already knows this.

It was possible to feel a blast from the past as Alonso lined up with three central defenders. Almost exactly 10 years ago, Antonio Conte brought Chelsea here and trailed 3-0 at half‑time. Cue the manager’s switch to three at the back, a click and a bolt towards the title. This was the acid test for Alonso and his team could not have made a better start. They had scored very early in the Spaniard’s first two league matches against Fulham and Brighton and it was the same again.

Arsenal offered £80m to Aston Villa for Rogers but no more. ­Chelsea went much higher and there was an inevitability about him ­showing up when it mattered. Arsenal did not clear their lines after a Reece James free-kick and when Jorrel Hato outjumped Ødegaard, the ball broke nicely for Rogers. The volley was threaded into the bottom corner. Could David Raya have done better? It felt that way in the moment.

Arsenal’s response was ferocious. It was the intensity and the physical levels. The Emirates sounded like a bear pit as the home crowd yelled after what felt like every coming together, every time an Arsenal player tumbled over. The equaliser was extensively trailed and it came when Havertz was allowed to drift along the edge of the Chelsea area from right to left. There was no challenge and his low left-foot shot beat ­Emiliano Martínez inside the near post.

It was a soft concession and out of keeping with the resilience that ­Chelsea had shown up to that point. Especially Martínez. The former ­Arsenal goalkeeper had thrown himself into a thicket of legs to keep out a low Ødegaard free-kick delivery, taking a boot to the head from Gabriel Magalhães for his ­troubles. He also saved brilliantly from the Arsenal ­centre-half shortly ­afterwards, ­keeping him out at close quarters after João Pedro had failed to clear a Declan Rice free-kick. On the rebound, Ezri Konsa hit the post before Riccardo Calafiori lashed the loose ball home. The goal check showed Konsa was offside and it was disallowed.

Arsenal created a staggering number of openings before the Havertz goal. Chelsea put their bodies on the line. Martínez got his angles right to deny Bukayo Saka; Wesley Fofana made a big block to thwart Havertz. After James had worked Raya from distance, Arsenal stormed to the other end and Hato leapt into a ­saving block on Ødegaard.

It was breathless stuff and it was as if Arsenal exhaled after the ­equaliser. This kind of tempo was surely unsustainable. Chelsea kicked out a foothold. Arsenal cleared their heads for the second half and they were in front almost immediately. ­Ødegaard started and finished the move but it was all about the dummy from Havertz, who knew where his captain was when Christos Tzolis sent over a low ball from the left. We’ve obviously managed to develop a few players and give some opportunities throughout, so it feels like a really positive end to the summer.”

Edwards also seemed satisfied with the results of her experiment involving Alice Capsey as keeper. Capsey added two stumpings on Sunday to her glovework highlights reel – the second a very decent effort standing up to a Ryana MacDonald-Gay bouncer, as Ireland subsided to 177 all out.

“The idea of this was to see where she’s at,” Edwards said. “There’s a real chance [for her to keep] in T20 cricket. We want competition for places and she’s certainly put her hand up in that department.”

Neither of England’s two young picks – the 21-year-old left-hander Jodi Grewcock and the 19-year-old Tilly Corteen-Coleman – have yet made a decisive contribution. EU faces 300,000 factory job cuts as China ‘colonises’ supply chains, industry warns

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 17:00:10 GMT

Protest using 10 coffins to symbolise struggling manufacturing industry to take place in Brussels

Job losses in EU manufacturing will rapidly increase unless Brussels stops the “colonisation” of industry by Chinese component manufacturers, a leading industry trade body has warned.

Eurometal predicts 300,000 job losses in manufacturing in the rest of 2026 because of expanding competition from China, which is now enjoying a record €1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.

On Monday, Eurometal will bring its concerns to decision-makers in Brussels, staging a protest using 10 symbolic coffins in a procession around the European Commission headquarters.

The coffins will be marked with phrases such as “EU competitiveness”, “industrial jobs” and “European factories”.

European manufacturers fear that the commission is not fully alive to the cannibalisation of their industries as China becomes embedded in supply chains through the sale of components.

Alexander Julius, the president of Eurometal, told the Guardian: “China has made no secret of what it is doing. It is in their five-year plan.

“China doesn’t want to be a raw material supplier, it wants to be a finished product supply. They want to be in key product supply chains because they know that once they control the supply chain, they own the complete value chain.” He wants the commission to understand fully the impact of Chinese exports at component level, including metals and chemicals used in 90% of manufacturing.

The EU has already taken action on electric vehicles by imposing tariffs on Chinese imports in 2024, and in June introduced higher tariffs on imports of foreign steel. The bloc’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, has also said the EU’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance with China is “not sustainable”, with both sides agreeing to hold three months of talks, ending in October, to try to avert a trade war.

“You look at the job losses stacking up in industries in places like Germany. The media, the politicians can see the consequences, but they don’t go after the virus that is causing it,” Julius said. “They don’t see why it is happening or ask why companies are either relocating to China or India or going bust.”

Among the conditions allowing the “virus” to spread is the increasing costs borne by European metal manufacturers with tariffs on steel imports and carbon emissions taxes for those high-energy sectors.

Components manufactured in China face none of those levies, said Julius, and that, combined with the undervaluation of the Chinese currency, the yuan, makes it challenging to compete with Chinese rivals, he added.

Education in prison is key to tackling the crisis

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:58:43 GMT

It would be better for the government to focus on rehabilitative programmes, rather than turning laundry rooms into extra cells, writes Jon Collins. Plus letters from Margaret Carey, Simon Hamilton and David Evans

Turning laundry rooms into cells, as the justice secretary has proposed, will put even more pressure on our understaffed and overcrowded prisons (Burnham warned running prison capacity near limit is ‘big risk’, 1 September). This will, in turn, make it even less likely that people in prison will be able to access the education and training that will help them to turn their lives around.

Education in prison is proven to reduce reoffending and get more people into work. But we’ve already seen provision slashed by a quarter in prisons this year. Just this week, an inspection of a prison in northern England found that there were not enough places in education and many men were frustrated at the lack of opportunity to progress in their sentence.

Rather than investing in converting offices and laundries into cells, we should be properly funding education so that prisons can focus on rehabilitation. That would enable people to spend their time in prison purposefully and ensure they don’t come back. Jon CollinsChief executive, Prisoners’ Education Trust

I have worked in prison-linked charities for over 30 years and am tired of saying that evidence proves that prison does not “work” in respect of preventing repeat offending, except, of course, when the offender is inside. Some offenders clearly need to be taken out of circulation, but building more prisons, at vast public expense, is not the answer to changing the behaviour of the majority of them.

We should be using that money on structured and rigorous programmes, within the community, which promote behavioural change, personal development, literacy and employability, and maintain whatever family and community ties existed.

Andy Burnham should think again. The government should spend the money on numeracy and literacy programmes, vocational and relationship skills, restorative justice, healthy living and keeping people in touch with their communities wherever possible. That way we won’t need to spend precious tax money on ever-more hugely expensive prison places. Margaret CareyHurstpierpoint, West Sussex

Nowhere in the debate about prison overcrowding have I seen any discussion about a blindingly obvious solution: reform of drug policy. Many people in jail are there as a result of the relentless thieving required to support an opiate habit.

So, isn’t it time to get rational, follow the evidence and start treating addiction as the health problem it so obviously is, rather than a moral failing to be punished? Decriminalise drug use as they did in Portugal in 2001 (without triggering societal collapse), and suddenly there would be plenty of room to lock up all the people who actually deserve it. Without building any more prisons. Incidentally, you’d also reduce crime and provide relief to thousands of addicts and their families. Simon Hamilton Kington, Herefordshire

Zoe Williams (Why are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloids, 31 August) states that “the purpose of prison itself has always been threefold – punishment, public protection and rehabilitation”. Not quite so. There is a fourth major purpose, which is deterrence. If a hard or lengthy sentence can be acknowledged to act as a deterrent, then it follows that a lenient sentence or very early release would have little deterrent effect, if any. David EvansMarket Harborough, Leicestershire

Wellens had started the final stage in Earlston 21 seconds ahead of Lewis Askey but extended that advantage to 42sec by the finish. The British rider finished second overall after riding impressively through the earlier stages, while Ben Wiggins, the 21-year-old son of Sir Bradley Wiggins, placed 10th overall.

The Belgian rider’s German teammate, Nils Politt, took a rare win in the final stage on Sunday, as Pogacar’s team celebrated another well-executed overall victory after a select group, which included five of their riders, broke clear of the peloton in the Lammermuir hills.

“It was a very successful week,” Wellens said. “We came here for the GC and today we also have this stage victory, so everything’s been perfect.”

The 165-kilometre stage on Saturday from Helmsley to Leyburn was won by Cees Bol of the Netherlands, but the Tour de France stage winner Wellens did enough on the short sharp climbs of the Yorkshire Dales and North York Moors, to distance the overnight leader Askey and take what proved to be an unassailable lead.

“Today we just wanted to defend the leader’s jersey,” Wellens said of the final stage through the Scottish Borders. “We didn’t want to attack, we didn’t want to make a hard race, we just wanted to ride defensively. But then suddenly, in the crosswinds Netcompany Ineos started to ride very hard, so we just followed.”

The British team, whose hopes were frustrated once again by inopportune punctures earlier in the race, took the initiative on the windswept moors, in an attempt to crack UAE Emirates XRG’s hold on the overall standings, but race leader Wellens was well protected and never really looked at risk.

Politt’s stage-winning move from a leading group that included Wiggins, came with less than 10km remaining. A race that began with a tribute from the peloton to Fin Tarling, who died last month in the Volta a Portugal, ended with another poignant moment as Politt pointed to the sky when he crossed the finish line in memory of his grandfather.

Downside of Burnham’s devolution drive

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:48:09 GMT

Areas will remain excluded, and nothing is gained from making local government units larger and more anonymous, write Steve Leach and Colin Copus

John Harris correctly recognises that “England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance”, but justifiably points out how areas remain excluded from the new arrangements, or are at best a poor fit (Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England?, 30 August).

Allowing for a further batch of city region-based authorities over half of England’s population does not suit this model. Where are the city regions and “strategic authorities” in most of rural Devon, Surrey, Hertfordshire and much of Kent and Essex?

If Andy Burnham goes ahead with the local government reorganisation (LGR) he inherited from Steve Reed, we will be faced with vast tracts of non-place authorities with names such as Devon Coast and Countryside and North West Essex, which do not make sense as strategic authorities. They are what remain when the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has completed its long-term aspiration of reducing the number of English councils and councillors.

We estimate that when this LGR is completed, 90% of councillors and 75% of councils across England could have disappeared, eliminating almost all authorities based on real places and communities. Germany, with its Basic Law, much admired by Mr Burnham, operates with about 11,000 municipalities in a tiered county-municipality structure, and retains municipalities based on real places. The equalisation elements of the Basic Law, which sparks the PM’s interest, have been achieved without the introduction of huge anonymous unitary councils across Germany. England already has the largest units of local government across Europe; nothing is to be gained from making them larger and more anonymous. Steve Leach Emeritus professor of local government, De Montfort University; Colin Copus Emeritus professor of local politics, De Montfort University

Lessons for the aid sector

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:35:47 GMT

USAID’s closure was abrupt, but no PR campaign will bring it back, says Monica Kappiantari

Jeremiah A Carew argues that USAID fell because of poor storytelling rather than poor work (How misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easily, 1 September). Having spent decades in a recipient nation working at the final point of delivery, I see a different lesson. The primary problem was not the story USAID told, but the architecture behind it.

Aid money passes through a heavy supply chain: from prime contractors down through international and local NGOs, with administrative costs absorbed at every layer. Meanwhile, project success is too often measured by easy outputs, such as workshop attendance, rather than long-term systemic impact. There is also a quiet truth: aid workers, including local consultants like myself, often benefit when projects extend, creating incentives to prolong processes rather than complete them.

Comparing USAID to Nasa is equally unhelpful. Nasa delivers visible, binary moments of engineering triumph. Aid involves slow, complex and contested social change shaped by local politics. No amount of polished marketing can package that like a rocket launch.

USAID’s closure was abrupt, but no PR campaign will bring it back. The real lesson for the broader aid sector is to focus less on telling a better story and more on structural reform: shortening the supply chain and funding local actors directly, as some Nordic donors already do, measuring genuine outcomes, and rewarding work that truly finishes. Monica KappiantariDevelopment specialist, Jakarta, Indonesia

Therapists should never play God in people’s lives

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:34:34 GMT

Karin Blak responds to an article by Nicholas Purcell, in which the relationship psychotherapist said he sometimes advises couples to end their marriages

Nicholas Purcell’s article concerns me greatly, not because he recognises that some relationships are abusive and dangerous, but because he appears to place the decision about whether a relationship should “die” in the hands of the therapist (As a therapist, here’s why I sometimes advise couples to end their marriage, 31 August).

As a psychosexual and relationship therapist, I would never presume to know whether a client should leave their relationship. Our role is not to make that decision for them but to help clients understand what is happening within their relationship, explore patterns of behaviour and coping strategies, recognise coercion or abuse where it exists, consider the options available to them, and understand the possible consequences of those choices.

Where abuse is present, couples therapy may be entirely inappropriate. We may need to talk explicitly about risk, a safety plan, involve specialist services and support a client through separation if that is what they decide. But the decision remains theirs, not the therapist’s.

That distinction matters because of the considerable power the client invests in therapists, who often come to us at their most vulnerable. If we begin to regard ourselves as knowing which marriages should live and which should die, we risk replacing our clients’ judgment with our own.

Indeed, in relationships where someone’s sense of self has been diminished through coercion or control, one of therapy’s important functions can be to help restore agency. It would be a troubling tragedy if, in attempting to free a client from someone else’s certainty about what is best for them, the therapist substituted their own. Karin BlakPsychosexual and relationship therapist; author of The Essential Companion to Talking Therapy

The Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up call to us all

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:30:09 GMT

With thousands dead across Europe this summer, it’s time to recognise heatwaves as the major natural disasters they are

The numbers are now trickling in: nearly 2,900 dead in the UK, at least 35,000 dead across Europe. That’s how many people are believed to have lost their lives in this year’s early-summer heatwaves – the death tolls for the August heatwaves have yet to be counted. In a sense, these people died in a series of natural disasters, similar to the hundreds who died last month after flooding in Nepal, or during the 2024 floods in Valencia, Spain. And yet we do not process these events the same way. Increasingly deadly heatwaves are the most direct and damaging effect of the climate crisis felt in Europe, but they are rarely framed as such.

There are some obvious reasons for this. Heatwaves by definition unfold over longer periods than other disasters, they are less dramatic, the majority of those who die are elderly or otherwise vulnerable, and their deaths often take weeks or months to be catalogued and reported, all of which make heatwaves seem less immediate and visible. But while heatwaves will probably never provoke the same visceral shock as earthquakes or tornadoes, it should still be possible to shift the way the public thinks about them, which could save lives and lessen their damage.

The first and most obvious change is in the way heatwaves are reported on. The tendency to use images of “fun in the sun” should be balanced by serious examination of disrupted transit and the dangers of living in sweltering buildings. Perhaps the immediate fallout could be made more legible: heatwave deaths might be made more granular with personal detail. Ultimately, governments should report the death tolls and other fallout closer to the actual event – recall that during the Covid-19 pandemic the UK government statistics reporting was tweaked to reflect weekly Covid-specific deaths, which the media and public followed with close interest.

More could also be done to make heatwaves feel like a major collective experience, similar to other disasters. Research shows that over time the British public have come to regard heatwaves as a serious problem, one linked to the climate crisis. But at the same time, most people think that they are personally unlikely to suffer any health consequences. Worryingly, work by the British Red Cross showed that a majority of those aged over 75 did not consider themselves vulnerable to extreme heat.

It would help to better communicate the risks and potential adaptation measures to vulnerable people, but equally good would be fostering a sense of community responsibility. Currently, the UK government has an excellent system to warn specific sectors – such as medical and care services – about extreme heat. This messaging should be expanded, and voluntary and local groups should be further encouraged to help people at risk. Again the pandemic gives a model here – the Scottish and Welsh governments in particular fostered a sense that we were all in this together.

At a society-wide level, a pilot project in Seville, Spain, to name specific heatwaves and give them a categorisation system like hurricanes made early warnings more effective, and also provided an important anchor for news coverage. This simple intervention should be considered in the UK. Changing the way we talk about extreme heat seems a minor thing. But if the public can be helped to recognise heatwaves as the major disasters that they are, lives would be saved and people would be convinced that the difficult work of adapting to the climate crisis is urgent and necessary.

The Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutiny

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:25:09 GMT

Vital accountability mechanisms have withered as English devolution has evolved. The government should take note

Andy Burnham has criticised Britain’s “unaccountable state” that is at once too powerful and too distant from everyday life. He has made English devolution the central idea of his premiership, but his plan to give England’s mayors unprecedented power and money will have to confront a number of tricky realities, not least a landscape in which scrutiny of local government is vastly diminished.

As England’s devolution map has evolved, vital accountability mechanisms have withered. The abolition of the Audit Commission in 2015 deprived Whitehall of information about local government spending. The decision, taken by the then Tory prime minister David Cameron during his “bonfire of the quangos”, coincided with a period when cash-strapped councils were selling off assets and making risky investments. A succession of bankruptcies and scandals have since exemplified the dangers of governing in darkness, including the questions raised at Teesworks, the development led by Ben Houchen, a Tory mayor, where a “culture of excessive confidentiality” has prevailed, according to a damning 2024 government report.

There is wide recognition that greater accountability is needed. But Westminster has tended to create top-down mechanisms where accountability flows upwards and local scrutiny is infantilised. The “trailblazer” deals in 2023, for example, gave the mayors of Greater Manchester and the West Midlands greater flexibility over spending, but made them answerable to quarterly select committees of MPs. Under the current public accounting regime, the Treasury appoints an “accounting officer” to each government department, who answers to parliament for their department’s use of money, including that spent by local authorities. Located in Whitehall, these officers lack knowledge of the places such spending impacts.

Mr Burnham is right to try to wrest power back from the Treasury and recognise that those closest to a community best understand its needs. His government’s recent pledge to appoint the chief executives of mayoral strategic authorities as “local accounting officers” is welcome. But its plans to give England’s mayors a share of income tax generated in their area (a power that Lord Houchen has said he will use to fund rebates) will demand deeper forms of accountability. The English devolution bill in 2026 created a new Local Audit Office and introduced new powers for scrutiny committees. Both are improvements.

A fine place to end up would be the creation of “local public accounts committees”, an idea suggested in the Starmer government’s white paper in 2024. These could be modelled on Westminster’s public accounts committee, whose reports have exposed flagrant misuses of public money. The prime minister wants to take a “place-based” approach to public service delivery. Such local committees, if properly resourced and empowered, could be integral to scrutinising these initiatives.

Yet scrutiny isn’t solely the job of officials. The decline of local media poses another problem. Although new local reporting outlets have flourished in cities like Manchester and Birmingham, an estimated 4.4 million people in Britain live in areas without a dedicated news outlet. A robust solution, once mooted by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, would be a tax on social media giants to fund local journalism. When mayor, Mr Burnham had a media capable of holding power to account. The same cannot be said for too many places in Britain.

Biopsies, aerial drills and a personal pizza: a day in the life of a shark scientist

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:00:09 GMT

Jasmin Graham, a shark scientist and science communicator, also makes time in her day to practice her hobbies and play music bingo with friends

“Sharks are not monsters, they just need better PR,” writes Jasmin Graham. And she should know: Graham is a shark scientist and science communicator.

Here’s what a day in Graham’s life in Sarasota, Florida looks like.

Do you have a morning routine?

I usually wake up around 8am, but I woke up at 7am because I had to go to the dentist. I got a head start on some emails and took a fundraising phone call in the car.

After the dentist, I got home and did my drills. I’m an aerialist, which is basically all the things you see in Cirque du Soleil: lyra [aerial hoop], pole and silks. Breakfast was Honey Nut Cheerios.

I went to the office to meet with an artist in residence [with Graham’s nonprofit Minorities in Shark Sciences]. They’re helping build props and sets for our theater shows. One is an immersive experience about the mass extinction of sharks. It’s a combination of a whodunit and an escape room.

What did you do for lunch?

I get delivered meals because I don’t have time to cook – it was some sort of pasta thing. After that, I was working on a grant for grassroots organizations working on the environment in the south-east. I’m co-chair of the Priorities, Projects, and Campaigns committee of the America the Beautiful for All Coalition, a coalition of organizations that want to protect nature and also center justice and access. Then I worked on prepping for our shark survey next week.

What does a shark survey entail?

Surveys have different goals, with the overall mission of understanding our local shark populations and assessing their health and stability.

We are targeting bonnethead sharks, but we also get stingrays. We bring them on board and measure them. Then we take a little fin clip, which is like taking a fingernail, so we can see who’s related to who. We also take a little muscle biopsy to look at the toxin load in their body. We’re particularly interested in brevetoxin, which comes from red tide, a harmful algal bloom that we unfortunately have here in Florida a lot.

For the bonnetheads, we make a quick incision and we put a transmitter inside them and suture them up. That transmitter can track their movements for up to three years. Then we release them, and they swim off.

What did you do to unwind?

I came home and had a little personal pizza. Then I drove to Beerbusters, a Blockbusters-themed bar, for music bingo. One of my friends hosts, and it’s always fun – our prizes are just things that people want to get rid of. I ended up winning a printer and a 3D puzzle. Someone brought a fire pit. On the way home, I listened to the KPop Demon Hunters soundtrack.

What time did you get to bed?

I usually go to bed between 11pm and midnight. It’s very important for me to get eight hours of sleep. Otherwise, I become a monster of a person. I usually pet my dog and watch silly things like Kevin Langue videos in bed. I check my Google Calendar for tomorrow so that I can mentally prepare, and make sure I don’t need to wake up any earlier.

‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:00:09 GMT

Georgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in future

Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double in rush for support

Georgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock.

Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting.

Under the government’s proprosals announced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send).

The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system.

“What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans.

Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.

“Of course, schools want to do everything in their power to support children and it’s important that they get a blueprint to be able to do that.”

The hope is that the new tiers of support and national standards will be in place by 2030, when the government wants education, health and care plans (EHCPs) – which many families now use to access support – to be narrowed down to those with the most profound educational needs and disabilities.

But the government’s white paper will allow existing EHCPs to remain in place after 2030. In doing so it may have created a surge of applications from families who fear missing out if they don’t get in before that deadline. That surge means the legacy of EHCPs will absorb funding desperately needed by the new system of support that does not require parents to jump through legal hoops.

“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight and battle and go through a bureaucratic process,” Gould said, highlighting evidence she has seen from Rochdale schools that offer early intervention for speech and language difficulties.

“They’ve seen an 85% reduction in referrals for speech and language support because they were able to meet much more of that need at a universal level earlier on, and then those children who did go for an assessment were ones who really needed that specialist extra support. There are models that show this is possible, so we want that early support to be available to everyone.”

Simon Essex, the executive head of Thomas Lord Audley, said the school had earned the trust of parents in Colchester so that it is now oversubscribed.

“We want to serve our community,” he said. “We don’t want any young people who live nearby who can’t come here because we can’t meet their needs.

“That’s our goal, and if that attracts others then we will work hard with the local authority to make it work. That’s why I’m hoping that the funding the government will bring will enable all schools to have the same mindset that we have for these young people.”

Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 16:00:09 GMT

Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision

‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision

Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.

Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.

The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029.

Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets.

School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications.

One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.

Bill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February.

“Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded.

“This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.”

EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million have identified special needs, according to official data.

The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid many local authorities becoming technically bankrupt.

Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to its white paper, which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030.

During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries.

“I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families.

“That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes.

“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.”

Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.”

Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”.

Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.”

Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced.

Madeleine Cassidy, Ipsea’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.”

The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029.

William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures.

Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.”

Long-term allies and verifiable reality must make way for Saving Private Nige

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 15:42:10 GMT

Has Farage’s brain been hacked? Has he started talking in his sleep? There’s no shortage of explanations for this scandal

We’ve all been there. It’s a lovely summer’s day and you just want a bit of me time. A quiet lunch of champagne and oysters. As you do. Anything to get away from having to pretend you are interested in the people of Clacton. Hell, it’s bad enough being expected to actually visit Clacton – who in their right mind would want to do that? – let alone having to talk to the little people who live there.

So, you’re just minding your own business when who should turn up but two of your closest mates in politics – or contractors who you’ve barely heard of, as you prefer to call them – saying they have been having meetings with an American donor and his son who have already given you more than £30,000 for an opinion poll you have commissioned and now want to bung you another £500,000. And these guys would like to meet you.

The cheek of it. Two strangers, one of them even a foreigner, who want to take up an hour of your time. And all you’re going to get for it is half a million quid. Who do they think you are? Don’t they know the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne stumped up a £5m gift? Admittedly, several hundred Cameo users have bought you for £80 a pop, but that was at least a few months ago. Things have changed. Besides, that wasn’t really being bought. More a short-term rental.

These wasters are basically insulting you. But you’re a tolerant kind of guy. You choose to indulge them. If you have a fault it’s that you’re never chippy and are unfailingly polite. Everyone tells you that. So you go along with them even though they have nothing of value to offer you. Yes, Yes. That’s fascinating. Thank you so much. But all along, you’re not really listening at all. You’re just zoning out. Trying to chill out in the sun. All you’re really thinking is of getting the first train out of Clacton.

Over the past few days, Reform have been in a tailspin over the Channel 4 News sting that appeared to show the party was intensely relaxed about breaking the law by taking money from overseas. First, they tried to style it out. It was a hoax. Nothing to see here. It was an establishment plot carried out by anti-establishment climate protesters. Go figure. Then, as the net closed in, they started to panic. No one had a clear line on anything. Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s long-term protege, and James Orr, the lawyer turned Cambridge academic turned Reform head of policy, left the party. Anything to buy some breathing space. All that mattered now was Saving Private Nige. Everyone else was expendable.

So for his interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that was recorded on Saturday but broadcast on Sunday morning, Nige was keen to distance himself from any allegation of wrongdoing. That person in the film that people said was him? It was actually an avatar. Who knows how many versions of Nige might be in play at any one time? He’s a very busy man.

But whichever Nige it had been, he was certain that he hadn’t been listening as the people around him were discussing in some detail not only how they exactly planned to break the law but how they had done so in the past. I mean, that was just pub talk. Who doesn’t like to boast about apparently criminal behaviour over a couple of drinks?

Laura K seemed rather taken aback by this. She wasn’t the only one. Because it turns out Nige is capable of holding down his part in a conversation when he isn’t even listening. What a gift that must be. Most of us distinctly remember him saying, when the talk turned to the polling, that Nige insists he had no idea he had been funded by foreign money, that the polling had been “amazing”, had provided “bang for buck” and “it had worked – boom”. Perhaps he was just talking in his sleep. Or had had his brain hacked by the establishment. He even made a point of thanking the donors.

Not that they were donors, of course. Maybe that was the bit that hurt the most. The realisation that the offer had never been genuine. Then came the distancing. Jukes and Orr had been “injudicious at best”. That would suggest that at worst they might have been … maybe that’s one for the lawyers.

What you had to remember was that Nige had never been close to Dan. Had never really liked him. Come to think of it, he had no idea why he had allowed him to be his right-hand gofer for the last 10 years. As for James, he was just an ingenu. A dreamer. It was totally unreasonable to expect someone who had trained as a finance lawyer to know anything about … er, the law concerning party funding. And it was just daft to think that a Cambridge ethics professor should behave ethically. Orr’s thesis had been on “divine lawmaking”. Perhaps breaking the law had been God’s will.

Dan and James had just been freelancing. They didn’t really work for Reform. So any alleged law breaking was one step further removed from Nige. Besides, as Reform leader, it wasn’t his job to be the compliance officer. Even though no one apparently knew the rules governing party donations better than him. He was the world’s leading expert. That was by the by. His job was just to be the frontman. To smile and shake a few hands. He had just been doing what he had been told.

Yes, said Laura, by now totally confused. But you did appear to be up to speed as the potential donor outlined how a scheme like that would be breaking the law and told him, “it’s all above board”, she said. Worried that she might be losing the plot. No, said Nige. What he had said was: “Is it all above board?” Except he hadn’t. He had definitely said it as a statement. Still, that cleared up one thing. The reason he hadn’t been listening was because he had hearing difficulties. One that made him turn every sentence on its head. Hopefully the police will take that into consideration if they get round to starting an investigation. Nige could do with a break.

Kindness of strangers: A hall-of-fame athlete helped my 94-year-old mum buy a vacuum cleaner

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 15:00:09 GMT

A woman in the queue said she was happy to drive an hour, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house. I was worried – but how wrong I was!

Read more in the kindness of strangers series

For a 94-year-old woman, my mother is still very busy and active. So when a vacuum cleaner she liked the look of went on sale at a national electronics chain, Mum drove herself to the nearest store to buy it.

Unfortunately, the shop in her area had sold out by the time she got there. The sales assistant told her it was still available in another Melbourne store – but that store was an hour’s drive away. As active as she is, Mum pointed out that at her age she really could not manage a drive of that length. She asked the sales assistant if they could transfer the vacuum to this store and was flatly told no.

Just as Mum was feeling a bit taken aback by the poor customer service, the woman in the queue behind her interjected. She told Mum that she was happy to drive all that way, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house for her.

The woman in the queue seemed to be a genuinely nice person, so Mum allowed the vacuum to be ordered for her and gave the woman her address.

As Mum recounted this story to me later, my heart sank. I couldn’t envisage a good outcome. But how wrong I was!

The stranger was as good as her word. The next day, she drove all the way to pick up this vacuum cleaner and bring it to my mother’s house. Finally, having delivered the vacuum, the stranger asked if Mum was OK with putting it all together. Of course she wasn’t, so the woman did it for her.

They kept in touch and even later went out for coffee – Mum doesn’t let anyone go that quickly! It was only later that Mum discovered the woman was actually a very well-known Australian sportswoman: basketballer Michele Timms.

Neither my sister nor I live in Melbourne, so Mum relies on friends and family there for help. That a stranger would step up like that made me feel that there is real hope for the world. The generosity of it is mind-blowing, and something that is unexpected in this day and age.

From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.
