Let your mind wander, don’t retire and stop worrying: surprising ways to help save your brain from the cognitive cliff

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 15:00:09 GMT

In his new book, The Brain Cliff, Dr Norman Swan outlines the science of brain ageing and strategies for staving off cognitive decline

You write that “changing the way you think about the brain cliff can literally change the way you think and remember”. How?

Dr Norman Swan: There are three things you need to know which are not widely known.

Think cognitive change not cognitive decline: one way people think about our cognitive function is by comparing it to what it was like when we were in our 20s and it’s not a valid comparison. It leads to an assumption that we’ve declined into deficit. That’s not actually what’s happened, especially when we’re in midlife (40s and 50s). Our brains have changed, not deteriorated. Focusing on what that “change” looks like can make the task of maintaining cognitive function and perhaps even improving it, much clearer. Sure, our fluid intelligence – which is about speed and problem-solving – peaks in our 20s, but unless you’re a maths whiz or a gun lab researcher, that is less important than what’s called your crystallised intelligence which can actually improve with age. It’s the wisdom of knowledge and experience.

Secondly, as the years pass, our thoughts move address.

This is about a phenomenon in the brain called scaffolding. To protect our cognitive abilities and perhaps even enhance them as the years pass, our brains build out networks of nerves which act pretty much like the scaffolding inside a skyscraper. It’s the infrastructure around which the brain works. The more successfully we scaffold, the further away we push the brain cliff. This scaffolding initially moves across the brain then into the frontal lobes – the all-important prefrontal cortex which brings our thoughts and memories together and is involved with judgment, decision-making and emotional control.

The third idea is that we should do as much as possible to encourage the scaffolding and as little as possible to get in its way.

I interviewed seven cognitive super-agers, who are as different as you could imagine – from the illiterate 95-year-old shoemaker to the woman who taught Mick Jagger statistics and the 94-year-old woman who still works in McDonald’s in Kyushu, Japan. But underneath, they’re remarkably similar and they’re all protecting their scaffolding in several ways. One example is how they respond to stress. They get over it. They problem-solve. They don’t ruminate. And where do you think we ruminate? Yes, in our prefrontal cortex. So you’re occupying valuable brain space for cognitive function with unproductive circular thoughts. As we move through life, the prefrontal cortex becomes more and more important and anything that distracts or damages it potentially brings the brain cliff closer. Depression affects the prefrontal cortex. Alcohol does too.

You mention that the time to start helping our brains adapt is in our 40s and 50s. What should you be doing at that age and is it ever too late to start?

It’s never too late to start.

Exercise enhances our brain plasticity, which in turn encourages brain scaffolding. An anti-inflammatory diet – with low amounts of red meat, high diversity of vegetables including leafy greens, fermented foods such as yoghurt and fruits such as berries – can change the microbiome and aid direct absorption of bioactive compounds, both of which support brain scaffolding.

What’s also thought to be part of scaffold building is what’s called the default mode network – what our brain gets up to when it’s supposedly at rest. When the default mode network fires up, parts of the brain that don’t normally talk to each other make connections. How do you know if your default network is at work? Your mind wanders. Mind wandering looks as though it’s good for your brain.

An associated activity is mental time travel: reliving the past, being well anchored in the present and imagining the future. When you’re in midlife you’re in a good place when it comes to mental time travel. When you’re young, there’s not much past; when you’re much older, the past tends to dominate. Mental time travel and mind wandering seem to encourage our scaffolding.

What was the thing about cognitive super-agers which most surprised you, having interviewed so many of them?

One of the important findings from research has been that genes don’t play a large role in whether we’re on a journey to the brain cliff or when we might reach it. That means the environment and how we live matter hugely and that’s what the cognitive super-agers I interviewed illustrated.

There was only one of them where you could convince yourself that his family history mattered, and even he – a neuropsychiatrist from New Jersey aged 100 – was doing the things that maintain your brain. He had learned a new skill – pencil drawing – and through the classes had made new friends and was well connected with other people beyond his family.

What have you changed in your own life or daily habits since going on this deep dive into cognitive decline?

I’ve become much more aware of when I might be ruminating and how I respond to stress. I work hard at problem solving and “getting over it”. I’ve really cut back my alcohol intake – not that it was ever high. I’m much more assiduous about my coronary risk factors like cholesterol and blood pressure. Leafy greens, berries and yoghurt are more prominent in my diet, and moderate to vigorous exercise is not an optional extra in my life. Oh … and I’ve no intention of retiring. Retirement is bad for your brain. So the ABC will have to sack me.

You say that rumination and stress may accelerate cognitive change. How, and how can people best try to counteract this?

For some people these are disabling and it’s hard to change by yourself. There are variations on cognitive behavioural therapy which can help in the hands of a well-trained clinical psychologist.

You have a chapter titled “Don’t Retire”. Should we all be working until we drop?

Work is mostly good for our brains. The evidence is strong that cognitive decline speeds up after retirement. Now some people with hard physical jobs simply can’t keep them up. The point here is what retirement means. If you move from your job to other work such as volunteering, new leisure activities, learning new and complex skills, then that’s actually not retirement. You’re still at work. Retirement to the couch and Netflix is a bad idea.

The Brain Cliff by Dr Norman Swan (A$34.99, Hachette Australia), is out 8 September

There are three ways to shut down an annoying conversation – but are they too brutal?

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 15:00:08 GMT

We’ve all had meetings that could have been emails. Often, this also applies to casual chats with your friends

The last thing you need in a meeting that could have been an email is attachments. Sadly, it’s sod’s law that there’s one oblivious person in every work gathering who raises extra, unnecessary queries using as many words as possible, and holds everybody up. Now, Forbes magazine has helpfully supplied three phrases business leaders can use to stop rambling questions from hijacking or lengthening proceedings, without embarrassing the hijacking lengthener.

But obviously it’s not only the office where we encounter those seemingly hellbent on derailing interactions, so can we steal Forbes’ gameplan for boring chat in real life?

Many conversations are DOA, too dull to rescue, but others – at a party, the school gates, a random bump-into – can be going fine until a third party ruins it by asking for or providing superfluous details that stymie the story. Sometimes you’re not married to that party, so you can’t give them a Paddington hard stare or pinch them. What does Forbes advise?

“Phrase one: route the tangent somewhere else. Say, ‘Let me pause you there. That’s worth discussing, but it’s more than we can cover here … Send me the rest, and I’ll follow up after the meeting.’” Clearly too formal for a casual natter, but there’s still gold in them thar hills. “I’d love to hear all about this when there’s time – text me later,” may be the most artful get-out-of-chat-free card ever played. Next?

“Phrase two: close a question you’ve already answered. Say, ‘We covered that earlier, so I’m going to keep us moving.’” Bit brutal, so IRL maybe reply, “But, anyway …” and then steer the convo in the direction you want to go (presumably towards the exit).

And finally: “Phrase three: give the floor to someone else. Say, ‘I want to make sure we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet. Let’s take the next question from someone new.’” It was good while it lasted, but unfortunately every technique has its limits. There’s no way of saying this, whether in the pub or at the conference room table, that won’t be loudly and clearly received as STFU.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 13:26:51 GMT

Leon Panetta tells Guardian US is risking ‘forever war’ and says Pentagon ‘turmoil’ sending message of weakness

Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict.

Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.

“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”.

“I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.

Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings.

US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.”

He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries.

“And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.”

In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership.

“The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.”

The White House was also contacted for comment.

In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure.

Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said.

Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing.

The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender.

That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East.

The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability … to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint.

“So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play … this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said.

Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.”

He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open.

“So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.”

Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran as a “war”. And asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”

Panetta told the Guardian he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it.

He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health aboard.

“Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said.

“So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”

Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ – but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly rich

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 13:00:07 GMT

Our US friends may pity Europeans for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport – but they’re forgetting the really important stuff …

I’m sorry to break this to you, but you may be “Europoor”. This is, apparently, what proud American patriots (the kind who describe themselves in those terms on their flag-forward X profiles anyway) are calling us Europeans, mocking us for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport.

GB news presenter Tom Harwood declared this dig “entirely accurate”, but is it? Well, sort of. US post-pandemic GDP growth is more than double that of the eurozone (15.6% compared with 7.2%; the UK is even worse on 6.3%). As for wages, once you adjust for national differences in the cost of essentials such as housing, food and services, the US average is $86,977 compared with the UK’s $66,299, Germany’s $76,286 and France’s $60,483, according to the OECD. A Sunday Telegraph investigation of the “Europoor” question highlighted astronomically powerful growth of the US tech sector supercharged by AI, making it easy to raise and make big money unencumbered by “old world” regulation and taxation. “We don’t want to be like what Europe has become,” said the Republican pollster Brent Buchanan.

There are massive, obvious caveats. GDP is a wholly inadequate proxy for quality of life or even prosperity: the UN’s proposed alternative dashboard of 31 indicators includes the likes of “respect for the planet” and wealth inequalities, against which the US would surely take a beating. US mortality rates are higher than European ones and life expectancy is lower, so, when a medical diagnosis or accident could bankrupt you, how rich do you really feel?

But, actually, this Europoor stuff is hitting me where it hurts: my New York-based grad student son out-earns me, and his junior nurse girlfriend is paid six figures – that’s more than I made in a city law firm. Quite right – nurses should earn more than corporate lawyers – but it’s hard to imagine them ever choosing to live here in the UK (an NHS nurse’s starting salary is £32,073).

To console myself as I contemplate years of getting even Europoorer, flying long-haul to hug my son, I’ve been counting the ways we’re Eurorich. Sure, healthcare, social protections, holidays, blah blah – but what about the really important stuff?

Cheese“The United States offers over 1,000+ cheese varieties and styles,” the Cheese from the USA website claims, to which I would counter: “But do any of them taste of anything?” I doubt a single Freedom Cheese can clear a train carriage like a ripe époisses.

BikesApparently, Americans buy 130m bicycles a year, but I suspect that’s thanks to a handful of legmaxxing California billionaires. Anyway, 130m also feels like the number of bikes parked outside Amsterdam Centraal station on any given day (in 2019, 41% of Netherlanders said the bike was their main mode of transport).

SaintsThe US has 11 saints – pathetic. I’ve seen the remains of more than 11 saints in a single European mini-break; Ireland alone has an estimated 1,000.

Wholesome foodLet’s take stock of this summer’s US food safety scares. Lettuce, blueberries, jalapenos, fruit bars, granola, eggs, alfalfa sprouts, mangoes, sourdough, tofu … basically anything healthier than Flamin’ Hot Cheetos is a gamble; Gwyneth Paltrow is probably claiming asylum in Puglia as I write.

Weird rulersSure, they have their stable genius, but nothing can match absolute monarchy and centuries of inbreeding for floridly unhinged leadership. Charles VI of France thought he was made of glass; the future Peter III of Russia court-martialled a rat for eating one of his toy soldiers.

Characterful teethThe US has, I read, “entered the age of veneer regret”, with people rueing their decision to drop big money on massive, gleaming, Hollywood teeth. Not over here! We’ve still got teeth Breugel the Elder would recognise (in the UK it’s partly because we can’t access affordable dentistry, but sssh).

Disturbing folkloreScratch the surface of any European country and some weird, sinister custom emerges. At Belgium’s Matî l’Ohê festival they mourn a bone by waving celery; Austria’s demon-chasing Perchten festival involves dressing like a horned haystack; in Wales’s Mari Lwyd, people take a horse skull on a pole from door to door singing for midwinter. In the name of carnival, we throw herring in northern France, execute a pretend mare in Czechia and hunt people dressed as bears all over the place. And really, what’s better – purchasing power or an annual opportunity to wave celery at a bone? I know my answer.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Meera Syal looks back: ‘South Asians weren’t seen as funny. We sold you fags or served you curry’

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 13:00:06 GMT

The actor, comedian and writer on idolising Victoria Wood, being fuelled by rage and injustice after a sexual assault, and ​t​he life-changing impact of Goodness Gracious Me

Born in Wolverhampton in 1961 and raised in Bloxwich, also in the West Midlands, Meera Syal is an actor, comedian, novelist and playwright who was awarded a damehood in the 2026 new year honours. Her first novel, Anita and Me, won the Betty Trask award in 1996. She rose to prominence as a writer and performer on Goodness Gracious Me and starred in The Kumars at No 42. She has two children and is married to the actor Sanjeev Bhaskar. Her memoir, Vigilauntie: A Memoir – Innit?, has just been published, and she is starring in The Children, at the Lyric Hammersmith, London, until 3 October.

I have no idea why I was posing with my hand on a pillar in a professional studio in Wolverhampton. My parents must have thought, “Let’s preserve the era of the only child before her brother comes along.” As it was the late 60s, I’ve got marriage-age shoes on and a slightly uncomfortable, sticky-out skirt. As for the hair, my mother clearly cut it with the kitchen scissors.

This was not a typical look for me. I spent most of my days in trousers and a T-shirt, rushing around Bloxwich on my bike. I had total freedom – if only my parents knew the things I fell off, climbed up, cut myself on, nearly drowned in or got impaled on.

We were the only Asian family in Bloxwich, and I was the only Asian girl in my school. There were a couple of Asian boys, who got bullied horribly, but I had a protective bubble around me because my mum was a teacher at the infant school. It got harder as I got older. It was the 70s and we were the visible wave of immigrants, so the reception wasn’t always friendly. I’m not proud of it, but I did have a brief fighting period. The school bully was a psychopath. If you looked at her the wrong way, she’d say, “I’m going to mash you out.” She’d stand at the side and let one of her little minions scrap instead – mostly hair-pulling, punching. I realised that being timid and running away made it much worse. The fact that you stood up for yourself made people think twice. They didn’t expect self-defence from a little brown girl.

My imagination came alive in my teen years, because I felt so out of place. I was surrounded by images of beauty in Jackie magazine – girls who were exclusively white, thin and blond. I had a culturally multifaceted life – at home I was very Indian, very cosy and warm, eating with my fingers, speaking my language. I’d code switch the moment I left: adopt a different persona, different accent, different walk. It’s no wonder I became an actor.

My one-woman play, One of Us, was a huge turning point. I developed it with my friend Jackie Shapiro at the University of Manchester, mainly because I thought, “If people knew half the stuff in my head, maybe they’d think differently about how they saw me, and people like me.” It got picked for the National Student Drama festival, then it went to the Edinburgh festival, where it won some prizes. Two weeks before I was due to take up an MA at Leeds to do drama and psychotherapy, a director walked in and said, “I’m about to do a new play by Sue Townsend. Would you like to be in it? And here’s an Equity card.” Until then, I had no idea how a person like me would get a foot in the door.

At the start of my career, I was sexually assaulted by somebody in the industry, somebody whom I trusted. That kind of behaviour was part of the culture in the 70s, 80s and even into the 90s. From remarks such as “Cheer up, darling” to the bum pinch, to what happened to me, everything was accepted as normal. But the sense of betrayal and shock almost made me give up. I thought, “I don’t have thick enough skin. If this is the way it’s going to be, I can’t do it.” Instead of being defeated, I got angry. Instead of shrinking, I tried to get bigger. It led me to meeting a bunch of women at the Asian Women Writers’ Collective who lifted me. I found my tribe. I got politicised. I started writing properly. I was fuelled by so much rage and injustice, and realised the corrosive part of assault is the silence around it. It was an awful thing to go through, but it changed the trajectory of my life.

I’d been working in theatre for years when I got my first TV job. It was on The Bill and I had to run down Whitechapel High Street in London shouting, “There’s a bomb in the restaurant!” My uncles and aunties thought my career was a waste of time, so for me to be able to tell them I was on television – even for 10 seconds – was the marker of something.

Victoria Wood was my absolute idol. I looked up to her completely. Then one day I got a call, “Victoria is doing a new sitcom called Dinnerladies. She’d like to see you.” I rehearsed the part a million times; I knew it inside out. And yet … I did the worst audition of my life – just a bad Mrs Overall impression. I learned that when you want something too much, you’re going to screw it up. Shobna Gulati went on to play the role of Anita and she was brilliant, but I couldn’t watch it for a long time as the memory was too painful.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

From 1991 to 1996, I worked on a series called The Real McCoy. It was a black sketch show, a huge success, and undoubtedly opened the door for Goodness Gracious Me. We decided to approach Jon Plowman at the BBC about the concept, who said, “I don’t really know what south Asian humour is.” Neither did we. It was hard to explain as we were never thought of as funny: we were the people that sold you fags in the corner shop or set your bones in a hospital or served you curry in a restaurant. We weren’t seen as observant or ironic or absurd. But we knew what made us laugh, and we were given a chance. We assembled a team of writers and actors, and threw together a night at the Riverside Studios. The roar of the audience who finally felt seen was intoxicating. We had to hold on to that feeling throughout the commissioning process, which took years. But it eventually transformed our lives.

In my 60s, I’ve realised this career is a marathon, not a sprint. The actors I admire most are the women who have survived through the dead zone where you’re not considered attractive or relevant. There was a time when you hit 50 and had to get the slippers out, because there was going to be very little work until the batty old grandma parts came up. That has changed over the last few decades, thankfully. It’s not perfect but it is better – and the juicy roles for women come more from theatre than television.

Sometimes I wish I could save that seven-year-old version of me from the fear and insecurity that’s ahead. I also wish I could tell her: when you are 39 you are going to meet Donny Osmond – the boy whose poster you kiss every night. Most of all, I wish she could know that one day other Desis will come up to her and say, “I grew up watching you. You made a difference to the way I walked down the street and felt about myself.” All of the loneliness, the bad experiences, will transform into stories – stories that change people for good.

The sleeping x eating secret: 15 ways to better rest, a healthier diet – and a happier life

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 13:00:06 GMT

We all know tiredness can lead to hunger, and vice versa. But there are so many other ways our habits in these areas are linked. Here are some easy tweaks to help us feel properly refreshed

A study published in the journal Nature Health last month found that food choices and meal timings have “immediate and measurable effects” on sleep. It was just the latest in a growing body of research into the link between diet and rest. Here is the latest science on what to eat for better sleep – and how sleep deprivation can affect your dinner the next day.

While there isn’t “a special sleep diet” that will guarantee eight undisturbed hours, a Mediterranean-style diet comes closest, says Dalhia Campbell, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for the British Dietetic Association. She describes it as “a balanced, varied diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, wholegrains, lean proteins and healthy fats to help stabilise energy and support the hormones involved in sleep”.

Prof Marie-Pierre St-Onge is the director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University in New York, and the author of Eat Better, Sleep Better. Her research into “plant-forward” diets, including the Mediterranean diet, is investigating why they are beneficial for sleep. She says this could be due partly to the phytonutrients in plant foods, which have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compounds, and partly to nutrients that feed the gut microbiome and are involved in gut-brain communications. “That could play a role in improving sleep through helping people quiet their minds,” St-Onge says.

“It is best to look at your overall diet rather than focusing on one particular food,” says Campbell. “The latest UK diet and nutrition survey shows that fewer than 17% of adults meet the ‘five a day’ recommendation. Improving fruit and vegetable intake supports general health and sleep.”

But once you’ve nailed your five a day, are any fruit and veg better than others? “There’s quite a bit of research showing tomatoes, tropical fruits such as bananas and pineapples, and oranges have benefits for sleep,” says St-Onge. “Nuts and seeds, especially pistachios and walnuts, and wholegrains can contribute to better sleep as well.”

Emerging studies show that kiwis may have some benefits, says Dr Sammie Gill, a senior nutrition scientist at the British Nutrition Foundation, but the evidence is limited so far. There is also early research into tart cherries: “A recent systematic review indicated that consumption may help improve sleep duration, sleep efficiency or sleep onset time,” she says. “That said, the science remains limited and inconsistent.”

Diets higher in protein have also been associated with better sleep. “Proteins are important because they provide a source of tryptophan, which is essential for producing serotonin and melatonin, which are important for sleep,” says St-Onge. Tryptophan is one of the nine essential amino acids that your body can’t make on its own, so it has to come from your diet. All animal proteins and many plant proteins contain tryptophan. “In the US, people talk about turkey all the time, like, ‘That’s why you fall asleep at dinner on Thanksgiving,’” says St-Onge. “But food is not an instantaneous process – it’s not like you pop a pill and two hours later it gets to exactly where it needs to get.”

If you do want to try tryptophan-maxxing, Gill says other sources are “dairy, eggs, fish, seafood, meat, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and legumes. Tryptophan-containing foods have been linked with improved sleep outcomes – such as total sleep time and sleep efficiency – compared with controls.” So having a warm milky drink before bed makes sense? “There isn’t strong research showing that warm milk helps with sleep, but that shouldn’t stop you from having milk as a bedtime option,” says Gill.

“Foods that are low in nutrients and high in fats and sugars are less likely to support good sleep,” Campbell advises.

St-Onge conducted research on this topic in France. “We showed that people who consumed more ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of insomnia symptoms. We’ve also shown that women who consume foods that have a higher glycemic index – the types of foods that tend to raise your blood sugars to a greater extent than others – have a higher risk of developing insomnia.” According to Diabetes UK, high GI foods include refined carbohydrates such as white bread, potatoes, doughnuts, bagels, sweets, sugar-sweetened breakfast cereals and sugar-sweetened drinks. As well as added sugars, St-Onge would avoid foods high in salt.

“Caffeine is a double-edged sword,” says Gill. “Plenty of studies have shown that caffeine in moderate doses [up to 400mg/four cups of coffee a day] can have a positive effect on cognitive performance, memory and alertness. But at higher doses, it can trigger anxiety, irritability and restlessness.”

Four coffees may sound an awful lot to some. “The effects of caffeine vary from person to person – some people are more sensitive to its effects. How you respond to caffeine is partly determined by your genetics,” she says. But however much you drink, the main thing is to do so in the morning. “Caffeine has a quarter-life of around 10-12 hours, meaning that if you consume it at lunchtime, a quarter of the caffeine is still in your body close to midnight, which can disrupt sleep.” Cutting it out by lunch “can lead to noticeable improvements in sleep quality and quantity”.

As you get older, you may find the after-dinner espresso you once enjoyed is now keeping you awake. “Your ability to metabolise caffeine changes as you age,” says St-Onge. “It’s important to keep track and evaluate every so often. If you’re starting to see that your sleep is changing, you might want to make adjustments related to intake of caffeine or timing of the last caffeinated beverage.”

Many people think a drink or two helps them fall asleep – and they are right. But that doesn’t mean it’s a sleep aid. “Alcohol is a sedative – it does not prompt natural, ‘true’ sleep,” says Gill. “While it may help you fall asleep faster, it significantly disrupts the quality of your sleep. Alcohol, even in low amounts, reduces REM sleep, which is important for emotional processing and memory consolidation.”

What’s more, “alcohol interacts with several neurotransmitters that are important in the regulation of sleep and can trigger awakenings during the night, which can make you feel tired the next day”. It can also make acid reflux worse, adds Campbell. So much for the trusty nightcap.

“Studies have found that later meals are generally linked to lower-quality sleep,” says Gill. “A recent trial found that eating dinner one hour before bedtime was linked with reduced sleep continuity and stability.” And you may find it harder to drop off in the first place, says Campbell, as your body is busy digesting your meal.

St-Onge cautions that going to bed on a full stomach also increases your risk of heartburn and acid reflux. “As a general rule, wait two to three hours after a meal,” she says. If you already suffer from acid reflux, NHS advice is to avoid food for up to four hours before bed. Beware of that late-night cuppa, too, says St-Onge: “If you’re drinking much too close to bedtime, you’ll need to wake up to use the bathroom.”

“It’s OK to have a light snack after an early dinner if you’re feeling hungry – going to sleep on an empty stomach can disrupt sleep, too,” says Gill. “The key message is: don’t go to bed too full or too hungry.”

“Choose a light, nutritious option such as yoghurt with fruit and nuts, or wholegrain toast with nut butter and banana,” says Campbell. “That’s better than grazing on biscuits and chocolate.”

This is partly down to your body’s hunger signals. “Some research suggests that sleep loss can alter appetite hormones such as leptin [which signals fullness] and ghrelin [which stimulates appetite],” says Gill. “One study showed that one night of inadequate sleep can increase ghrelin levels and decrease leptin levels.” As a result, “poor sleep is associated with increases in energy intake, mainly from snacking, especially on foods higher in fat and carbohydrates. One review found that people who are sleep-deprived consume an average of 385 calories extra the following day compared with controls.”

St-Onge’s research has found this hormone effect varies by sex: “Ghrelin tends to rise before a meal, signalling hunger. We’ve shown that it increases to a greater extent in men who haven’t had sufficient sleep.” In sleep-deprived women, on the other hand, leptin – “the satiety signal” – is suppressed. But the result is the same: overeating.

It’s not just about ghrelin and leptin. “I always tell people that we don’t necessarily eat because we’re hungry, right? People have many reasons to eat, and eat despite lack of hunger,” says St-Onge. She says our brain reward centres are affected by how much sleep we’ve had the night before, and the “hedonic signals – the things that make food more appealing – tend to be more intense after a period of short sleep. So you’re more susceptible to reaching for appetising or pleasurable foods.” Who hasn’t chosen the pain au chocolat over the porridge after a bad night?

In the long term, it certainly increases the likelihood. “Studies show that people who regularly sleep less than six hours tend to gain more weight over time, and increasing sleep to seven or eight hours can help with appetite regulation,” says Campbell. As well as disrupted hunger hormones, there are a number of explanations. “Observational studies show those who don’t get enough sleep tend to eat less fruit and vegetables, more sugar, less protein and less fibre. Staying up late at night also means that you might get peckish and be more tempted to snack. And when tired, we may be less motivated to be active and to cook from scratch, relying more on quick, less nutritious foods and fizzy, sugary drinks.”

“Most of the research focus is on chronotype [your body’s natural preference of when to sleep and wake] – if you have a late chronotype versus an earlier chronotype,” says St-Onge. So is it better to be an early bird or a night owl? “Typically, people with earlier chronotypes tend to have more healthful diets and exercise more,” she says. Plus, “people who have an earlier chronotype have an easier time getting adequate sleep duration because their sleep is more aligned with the societal clock”. Unfortunately for late risers, chronotypes are thought to be largely genetic.

“Shift workers report less healthy diets compared with day workers, and shift work is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes,” says Campbell. She suggests “eating the main meal before a night shift, and choosing lighter, nutrient-rich foods overnight”. This is easier said than done, says St-Onge. “It’s difficult because it’s a whole culture that needs to change – people tend to bring in treats to have in the middle of the night.”

“Try science-backed sleep strategies first, focusing on regularity, timing, temperature and lighting,” says Gill.

Campbell agrees: “Rather than looking to supplements, it’s more helpful to look at the bigger picture. Take a look at sleep routine, stress levels, alcohol and caffeine intake, activity levels, and any underlying health issues that might be affecting rest, such as sleep apnoea, menopause symptoms or frequent night-time waking.”

If you’ve sorted your diet, exercise, sleep hygiene and general health, however, there is some weak evidence that magnesium may help. “Observational studies have linked magnesium with sleep-promoting effects, whereas limited gold-standard trials report mixed results,” says Gill. “A recent randomised controlled trial in adults with self-reported poor sleep quality supplemented with magnesium glycinate found modest improvements in insomnia severity. Another study showed that supplementation with magnesium threonate improved sleep quality and daytime alertness in people with self-reported sleep problems.”

B vitamins and vitamin D are also commonly believed to help with sleep – are supplements advisable? “B vitamins are abundant in the diet – typically, people don’t have any deficiencies in those,” says St-Onge. “Vitamin D is something that could be problematic, especially if you don’t drink fortified dairy products. We can produce vitamin D from sunlight, but in some populations the sun is not sufficient, so that could be something that could be supplemented.” In the UK, government advice is to consider taking vitamin D in autumn and winter.

“Melatonin is a hormone that helps regulate the body’s sleep-wake cycles,” says Gill. “It’s often called the ‘hormone of darkness’ because its levels increase as evening approaches, signalling to your brain and body that it’s time for sleep. Rather than acting like an on-off switch, melatonin works more like a dimmer switch – preparing your body for sleep without directly causing it.” So should insomniacs take supplements? “Melatonin supplements are most effective for shifting the timing of your sleep, rather than as a routine, everyday sleep aid,” says Gill. “Melatonin can also be really helpful for managing jet lag. When used at the right time, melatonin can help fool the brain into thinking it’s night-time.”

Mind games and a ‘toss master’: world stone skimming contest returns to Scotland after cheating scandal

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 11:20:55 GMT

More than 400 competitors battle windy conditions on Easdale, a year after tampered-with stones made headlines

“Want to touch it?” Jonny Jennings asked, clutching the World Stone Skimming Championship trophy in his arms as he waited for the ferry. The mind games from the 2025 men’s champion had started hours before this year’s competition had even begun. The 38-year-old had travelled from Kentucky to Easdale island just off the west coast of Scotland to defend his title. He was not giving it up without a fight.

On Saturday, more than 400 of the world’s best stone skimmers descended on the tiny island in the Inner Hebrides, normally home to just 60 residents. From Argentina to India, Hong Kong to Jamaica, more than 30 countries were represented, ferried over in groups of 10 from the mainland.

Easdale is home to stone skimming’s colosseum: a former slate mine flooded by a ferocious Atlantic storm in 1881, forming a natural amphitheatre for the tournament. Competitors get three throws across the 63-metre (207ft) stretch, which is marked off like a swimming lane. Stones must be made of Easdale slate and can be no wider than 7.6cm (three inches). The ultimate aim is to hit the back wall, the equivalent of a nine-dart finish that sends the crowd into raptures.

From the “skim of destiny”, the stone plinth from which all skimmers have to throw, the back wall of the quarry does not look far away. But looks deceive on Easdale. The wind, the rain and shadows in the water combine to make it one of the toughest places to compete for skimmers in the world. Many elite male skimmers can throw more than double the distance of the quarry in calmer conditions. But at the world championships, they often crumble.

“It’s the magic of Easdale,” said Lucy Wood, the six-time female champion. “It’s different, very different. You have got hundreds of people watching you throw. It’s completely insane. Some people say that the island is not the best place to host the competition because of the back wall, and you cannot really throw that far. But most of these skimmers have never even hit it.”

On Saturday, a vicious wind played havoc with the competition, blowing stones off course as it swirled around the quarry. To combat conditions, many skimmers changed their style to try to avoid the gusts. Some bent their knees more than usual, others wound up their arms and used brute force for their throw. But nothing seemed to work. Stones whizzed off course in all directions, disappearing into the depths of the quarry far short of their intended target. By the halfway stage, just one competitor had hit the back wall.

Last year, the competitive spirit boiled over. Two competitors were caught cheating after fashioning stones into perfect circles in an attempt to improve their chances of a better throw. The scandal made international headlines and organisers had a geologist on hand this year to check stones if any questions were raised.

“To win at Easdale, you need to have guts,” said Dr Kyle Mathews, the competition organiser, known as the “official toss master”.

“You need distance, consistency and accuracy. You need to be able to stand up and throw when it counts. We are often put in the same category as cheese chasing down the hill or the conkers championship. But these skimmers have genuine sporting talent. The world record for the javelin is nearly 100 metres. The record for stone skimming is much further than that,” he added.

When it was time for Jennings to throw, the packed crowd around the colosseum fell silent with expectation. Dressed in his signature colour, the “Green Giant” finished his pint of beer before taking the plinth, still wearing sunglasses. “Now that’s aura,” one young spectator whispered.

Jennings had to hit the back wall if he was going to retain the title. His first attempt was superb, delighting the crowd, but the stone disappeared into the water just before it could produce a satisfying “clink” with the back wall. The second skewed left, caught by the wind. He waited for the gust to die down for his final attempt. Bending his knees, the champion unleashed the throw with all his might. But it was short again: 2026 would have a new men’s champion.

By late afternoon, Liam Knight from North Carolina was still the only competitor to hit the back wall. Nobody could beat him. “I came here two years ago and I got the bug. I had to use a technique that nobody else was using to get it out past the wind. It was brutal. It ruined everyone’s day,” said the 32-year-old. “It was kind of a trick shot really. But it worked.”

At the award ceremony, Jennings had to watch from the crowd as Knight lifted the trophy. He would return to the mainland empty-handed. But he would be back next year to try again.

Farage says overseas donation row ‘looks bad’ but denies Reform broke law

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 11:12:09 GMT

Robert Jenrick says party has followed legal protocol ‘at all times’ as Met police consider launching investigation

Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks bad” for his party but denied it had ever taken foreign money in breach of electoral law.

The Reform leader, who is battling to contain the fallout from the allegations, was asked if he could categorically rule out that foreign money had ever been funnelled to his party. He replied: “I can. Never happened.”

Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation apparently plotting to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Farage described their comments as “injudicious at best” and admitted the optics of the undercover filming were problematic for his party, which has in the past tried to suggest it would do politics differently.

“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations,” he said. “We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations.”

The questions overshadowed the start of Reform’s party conference in Birmingham, where numerous hecklers were removed from the hall during Farage’s keynote speech.

Footage has emerged online of one of the women being dragged by her hair, with a man also appearing to hit female protesters with his crutch.

When questioned about the incident by Jon Sopel on Sky News’s Sunday Morning programme, Robert Jenrick said: “Oh, boohoo. We’re now in a country, Jon, where somebody who is – whatever she is – a far-left protester, goes into a party conference, tries to wreck the leader’s speech, and cries foul if a pensioner knocks her over the head with their Zimmer frame.

“I mean, come on, get a life,” Reform’s treasury spokesperson added.

West Midlands police said they were aware of the footage, adding: “We would ask the woman involved to come forward. Anyone with any information should contact us on 101 quoting log number 924 of 5 September.”

After an official complaint that Farage and his aides had broken political funding laws, the Metropolitan police said it was assessing the evidence, with sources suggesting a full investigation is expected. They all deny wrongdoing.

Scotland Yard could extend an existing investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.

Farage is already facing intense scrutiny about Reform’s finances, as well as about his £5m gift from a crypto billionaire shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election, which he has since said was intended to pay for security.

In an earlier extract of the BBC interview, Farage also claimed he “wasn’t even listening” during the meeting at the centre of the controversy, and that he knew donation law “better than anybody”, as he sought to limit the damage caused by the allegations.

Jenrick said on Sunday that he had seen legal advice that the party had not in fact broken electoral law over foreign donations but that lessons would be learned from the episode.

“We’re going to investigate exactly what happened,” Jenrick told Sky News. “It’s right to have due process. But this is not the way that Reform conducts itself.

“Like any political party, we seek to abide by the law at all times, and we believe we have in this case. In fact, I’ve reviewed the legal advice from the KC who’s advised the party in the last 48 hours, and it shows that, yeah, we did.

“But do we want for the best version of ourselves? Yes, absolutely. And no doubt there will be lessons to be learnt from this.”

Speaking after the BBC interview, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “For a political party that don’t like foreigners much, they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them.”

He added: “I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they’re really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going.”

Air conditioners are our best bet in the fight against extreme heat – whether we like it or not

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 11:00:03 GMT

Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis

The greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.

Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation over air conditioning.

If the atmosphere were to warm more than 3C above the average temperature in the preindustrial era, a prospect that looks ever more likely given the lackluster efforts to reduce carbon emissions, one in six of the world’s largest cities would suffer at least one heatwave per year lasting more than a month, according to the World Resources Institute. Low-income countries would suffer, on average, 6.9 heatwaves per year. Delhi would suffer at least 140 days with temperatures hitting at least 35C (95F).

Demand for AC around the world will inevitably accelerate as the atmosphere continues to warm. Ninety percent of households in the US and Japan enjoy artificial cooling. But in Indonesia, the share is only 9%. In India, it is 5%. Of the 2.8 billion people living in the hottest parts of the world, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), only 8% currently possess AC. These countries are populous, they are generally poorer and they will get particularly hot as climate change progresses.

The global stock of air conditioners in buildings is expected to mushroom to 5.6bn by 2050, up from 2.5bn today, according to the IEA. In India alone, installed AC inventory will rise from 48m units in 2020 to 1.1bn in 2050, a 23-fold increase. Even if the world met the emissions targets laid out in the 2015 Paris climate accords – which is not going to happen – an average of 40% to 50% of the population in many of the world’s warmest countries would still require AC.

This is going to require a lot of energy. Scientists at Harvard’s School of Engineering and applied sciences estimated that in India and Indonesia, demand for power just for cooling in 2050 could be as high as 75% of their current total annual electricity demand.

This poses a challenge for the climate. In 2022, energy for cooling, mostly for residential and nonresidential space cooling but also to maintain cold chains for food and pharmaceutical production, and to cool transport, accounted for roughly 2.5bn tons of CO2 equivalent emissions, according to a United Nations report, about 7% of total emissions. In the absence of further strategies to improve energy efficiency and improve passive cooling techniques, it would rise to nearly 8bn tons by 2050.

So what does one do? Apparently, 58% of the French would rather “suffer from the heat than install an air conditioner in order to protect the environment”. But these sentiments cannot drive the world’s response to a warming world. To fight the battle against climate change requires, in fact, facilitating access to AC for billions of people who are now at risk of facing a hotter planet without the technology to protect themselves and their economies.

This proposition doesn’t rest only on arguments from ethics – although there are plenty of those. For starters, there is substantial evidence that air conditioning reduces heat’s impact on health. One study of US data found that the lethality of days hotter than 80F (27C) declined by about 75% from 1900 to 2004, almost entirely due to the adoption of residential air conditioning. Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.

Another powerful reason is that limiting access to air conditioning will set back economic growth. There is abundant evidence that excessive heat in the workplace reduces labor productivity and that air conditioning mitigates the decline. Heat can also stymie student achievement, eroding human capital.

Those living in India, Bangladesh, Indonesia or other unbearably hot places wherever will not heed the call to resist AC. Demanding unrealistic policies that are detrimental to their development is a straightforward strategy to ensure these countries do not cooperate with the effort to slow climate change. Campaigns from the west to stop hydropower in Africa, (even as westerners also called to stop developing fossil fuels on the continent) delivered little and engendered ill will. Trying to limit their access to AC would do the same.

Whether it is to power industries, improve transportation, or cool homes and workplaces, achieving faster economic growth will require poor hot countries around the world to consume more energy. Their economic development is indispensable for the global battle against climate change.

Just as fans of depopulation must understand that innovation needs people, fans of shrinking humanity’s footprint on the planet to prevent climate change misunderstand how humanity has prospered despite environmental constraints: through innovation. The path to decarbonization requires figuring out how to produce zero-carbon energy on a vast scale everywhere. It will be easier to do this in a rich world with AC and refrigeration than in a poor hot one.

Dining across the divide: ‘He looked like a Green voter. As you get older you realise it’s unicorn politics’

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 11:00:03 GMT

A part-time musician and an office manager disagreed on benefits and work-life balance, but ​where did they stand on community responsibility?

Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how

Occupation Waiter and musician

Voting record Green. He describes himself as “left leaning”

Amuse bouche Jumped into a canal for one of his music videos. In January

Occupation Office management

Voting record Conservative in the UK. Democrat when she lived in the US

Amuse bouche Won the French prize at school, though she’s rubbish at French

Lynn The restaurant has beautiful views of rolling hills. I had roast chicken and potatoes, panna cotta and a couple of glasses of red wine.

Henry I ordered an old fashioned, and some white wine with the meal. I had a lovely peach salad, then a pizza. I told Lynn I grew up in Dubai, went to a French school, then uni in Paris with my final year in Bristol, which was my first taste of life in the UK.

Lynn Henry looks like a Green voter: flip-flops, pink trousers, bushy beard, earrings. My daughter might have voted Green when she was 16, because you think everything is free, but as you get older you realise someone has to pay. It’s unicorn politics.

Henry Lynn definitely had more facts and figures than I did, and is more opinionated. I’m still building my thoughts and opinions.

Lynn I’m a huge proponent of the benefits system for people who need it, but it is exploited. A business owner I know looking for a labourer offered someone £35,000 a year. The guy flat-out said, “Sorry mate, with my housing benefit, my child benefit and everything else, that’s not worth me getting out of bed for.” There’s something seriously wrong with that.

Henry I work in a restaurant, but when my hours go down I reapply for universal credit. I looked for other jobs, but ultimately didn’t find anything. Along with work, time for yourself and socialising with friends and family are the cornerstones of living. Without that, I wouldn’t have made my album, which is my passion.

Lynn I was raised on a poor council estate, and everybody worked and everybody’s gardens were nice. Go to those estates now and there’s no pride. People scream poverty, but they’ve got new iPhones, Sky TV, they’re getting their nails done. How can it be that you can’t afford to feed your children if you’re getting all that? The problem with Britain today is that it’s more about quality of life than working really hard, and Henry is part of that.

Henry I’m more likely to volunteer, help out a community, if I’m in a good place. Having a social life is also important to maintain mental health. I did feel there was a generational difference between us. I don’t know if it’s the optimism of youth.

Lynn We agreed politicians need to stop chasing votes and stand up for what they believe in. And there needs to be more pride in the country. Look at Europe: people there are clearing the streets. We have none of that here.

Henry There can be a lack of community. And I do agree cheating the system isn’t right. On immigration, Lynn did somewhat sway me that there might be a physical limit to the number of people we can take in.

Lynn I don’t agree with the full face coverings for Muslim women. It stops integration. How is it OK that someone on a motorcycle has to take off their helmet in a petrol station because you have to be able to see their face, but then you make different rules for different people? If you’re coming to a country, you have to assimilate.

Henry You should respect the culture of where you move to, but it doesn’t mean you have to ditch your own. Whether women should cover up is a different question, but they’re not a threat. Maybe because of where I grew up, I’m more comfortable around Muslims in full veils than a group of British lads in hoodies and tracksuits.

Lynn Henry’s lovely. He lives in an idealistic world and wouldn’t it be lovely if we could all live there? I don’t agree with his politics, but it’s good to hear other people’s points of view. We had a hug and went our separate ways.

Henry Lynn might have got more out of it if I’d had more facts, more debating power. There were a couple of times it got a bit animated – I said something and she repeated it, saying, “Are you serious?” But we had a nice dinner and a nice chat. A good, one-off experience.

Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 11:00:03 GMT

A Dr Seuss-style story written in seconds alerted me to the power – and perils – of the technology. But how can children embrace it without forgetting core skills?

When I was growing up, my dad and I often talked about a story we wanted to write together. It was called “The Day Nobody Went to Disneyland”. One day, the story goes, the weather is so perfect that everyone in the world decides to stay away from Disneyland because they expect it to be far too busy. But my dad, who has the same thought as them, sees the disappointment on my face that morning – and decides to risk it. We set off. And when we arrive, the park is completely empty. Nobody else was brave enough to visit. We have everything – the rides, shows, food – to ourselves.

I loved the idea of writing that story. But, as so often happens, we were too busy to do anything about it. Life ran away from us. I grew up, and we both forgot about it.

Thirty years later, I was at my parents’ for dinner with my own children (eight, five and two). For some reason, the idea popped into my mind again. I told my oldest about it – and she wanted to hear the full thing. We turned to ChatGPT, gave it the vague outline and asked it to have a go at writing the story in the style of Dr Seuss (one of our favourites). Within a few seconds, we had it. She read it out – and we laughed.

Of course, what this AI generated wasn’t perfect. A few lines didn’t quite make sense; a few Americanisms had slipped in (“sneakers”, “cinnamon buns”). But that night on the sofa we had great fun together tweaking the prompts, refining the story, adding more scenes, working with this strange new creative partner to do something that had escaped my grasp for decades.

For the last 15 years, I have been exploring the impact of AI on work and society. But becoming a dad of three small people has made these disruptions far more personal: it is clear that their future is going to look wildly different from my past.

For my wife, that realisation really sunk in a few weeks ago, on a journey to her parents’ in Suffolk. Three children, confined in a car, stuttering along the A12, is a combustible setup. So we were thrilled to find a rare podcast that everyone miraculously enjoyed: History’s Not Boring, a series of 15-minute bursts of conversation, on a kaleidoscope of subjects, narrated by two children.

As we listened, we started to speculate in the car about who these whiz-kids might be. Where were they from? How were they selected? How did they juggle this job with school? Eventually, I went to the website to find out. All our answers were wrong. The kids did not, in fact, exist. The entire podcast seemed to be generated by AI. None of us had realised.

It was a strange moment, learning that people we had grown fond of were not actually people at all. It was also remarkable that AI could create such high-quality educational content. But for my wife, a podcast and documentary maker, it was an unsettling moment as well: here was something that would have taken her and a talented team several days to make, and now it was being done without people.

My work on AI has taken me to boardrooms and conference halls, classrooms and government buildings. But wherever I go, one question is now asked more than any other: what should my children do?

Today, we are floundering. Teachers worry that the way they teach no longer seems to work. Parents, watching their children use AI to solve problems and answer questions, wonder what they really know. Employers doubt whether traditional educational achievements, awarded in time-honoured ways – coursework, exams, assessments – are still a useful guide to what young people can do.

Yet reacting to these new technologies by putting barriers up, as many instinctively want to do – banning, admonishing, punishing – just cannot be right. To begin with, this is the water in which the next generation will swim: we are letting them down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in, not the one they will actually inhabit.

How often, for instance, have you heard people accuse students of cheating if they use AI to help them with their work? But at what point are we cheating them by failing to overhaul the way we are educating them? If AI is making education “too easy” for young people, at what point does the burden shift on to us, the adults, to make their education more testing, to push them on, to stretch them?

More importantly, this dismissiveness of AI is also unimaginative. It stops us appreciating the astounding possibilities AI could create for the next generation as well. Of course there are risks. But at the same time, if we use this technology wisely, what difficult ideas might the next generation now grasp, ones that were beyond us when we were in their shoes? What hard problems might they now solve, ones that once required years of training and experience – if they were solvable at all?

A big part of the challenge of AI is that our traditional response to technological disruption in the working world – the idea of “future-proofing” people – no longer works. In 2013, the then prime minister David Cameron announced that England would become the first place in the world where all children in primary and secondary schools would learn to code. This, in the words of education secretary Michael Gove, would “equip every child with the computing skills they need to succeed in the 21st century”.

The idea seemed bold and clever: in the years that followed, it was hard to find an advanced country that did not follow our example.

Fast-forward to today. What does it turn out that the latest AI systems, such as ChatGPT and Claude, are best at doing? Writing code. In January 2026, Anthropic reported that 90% of the code for Claude Code – their AI-powered coding assistant – was itself written by AI. Skills that were meant to protect kids from technological disruption for their entire lives were largely redundant before they had even left school.

For politicians and policymakers, it is tempting to dismiss the coding saga as an unfortunate blip. But this is a mistake. The reason they slipped up was because they had believed in the idea of “future-proof” skills, the thought that there exists some valuable set of skills that AI will not be able to do for some time – and that by thinking deeply enough about the future, we can accurately identify them.

The truth is that we know only two things about what lies ahead. One is that it will be full of technologies that are far more capable than today. And the other is that we know little else. But rather than attempting to resolve this uncertainty, we have to accept it and instead ask a different question: how do we prepare the next generation to flourish in a future that we actually know surprisingly little about?

The first step is to get back to basics. Since 2009, literacy and numeracy have been falling among young people around the world, according to the OECD’s programme for international student assessment (Pisa); the same holds true for adults. In itself, this is worrying. But given the uncertainty that we face about the future, these trends are a disaster.

Why such a calamity? To begin with, while it might be hard to say precisely which more advanced skills will turn out to be most valuable in the future – creativity, judgment, something else – they will rely in some way on these basic skills. They are the foundations for everything else.

What’s more, AI systems are far from flawless. They make mistakes, often on simple problems; they hallucinate, providing confident and plausible answers that are completely made up. They are, as the computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton put it, “idiot savants”. That means we must use AI critically, not blindly, keeping our basics sharp so we can tell when AI is being a savant – or an idiot.

So, with both those reasons in mind, we should be focusing intensely on teaching literacy and numeracy, even if AI does them better, as it increasingly seems to do. Getting back to basics is what an economist would call a “no-regrets” strategy – we will never regret improving these basic skills, however the future turns out to be.

And we should try to be imaginative. When my eight-year-old grew bored learning her times tables the traditional way – long lists, learned by rote – I turned to ChatGPT to create various computer games, designed by her, to test what she knew. (Unicorns and rainbows featured in all versions.)

Then there was the time my five-year-old was tired of reading his standard-issue phonics books after school – there really is only so much Biff, Chip and Kipper a human being can take – and instead we used AI to generate some custom stories together, carefully tuned to his reading level and much closer to his favourite topics. (At the time of writing, HMS Belfast, TNT explosives and Bukayo Saka.)

Experimentation is important and we can learn so much from the creativity of others. Take Chris Moran, for instance, head of editorial innovation at the Guardian. His daughter had been reading Dracula at school but was struggling to place the sprawling novel in the real world. Together, with the help of AI, they built an app – PlotLines – which placed the story on an interactive 1890s Ordnance Survey Map, plotting the key scenes and character journeys around Europe, with the help of AI. (They have done it for many other books now, too.)

These are precisely the sorts of innovations we should be testing and embracing throughout education – rather than banning.

Despite the uncertainty we face, there is still one thing that we do know about the future: it will be full of technologies that are vastly more powerful than today. With that in mind, we must teach the next generation to use them. To do this properly will require us to dedicate a serious chunk of time to teaching people how to use AI.

after newsletter promotion

The challenge, though, is how to do this without also setting them up to forget crucial basic skills. An important, growing fear is that AI is making us stupid. Why bother reading a book if AI can summarise it? Why bother completing maths homework if AI will do the sums? And in my view the answer here lies not in Silicon Valley, but with a forgotten British maths professor, Wilfred Halliday Cockcroft, half a century ago.

In the 1970s, the quality of maths teaching in UK schools appeared to be collapsing and numeracy was reportedly low. Cockcroft, who had a longstanding interest in mathematics education, was asked by the government to look into it. And in 1982 the Cockcroft Report was published. It was enormous, forensic – and is now largely forgotten. But it may turn out to be the most important document written for thinking about the future of education, because of its response to the electronic calculator.

It is fascinating to read Cockcroft’s report and discover how the challenges of the calculator back then were so similar to the ones we face with AI today – from the fear that it would undermine “basic skills” to the intimidation many felt at the complexity of this strange new technology (“Some … had been discouraged by the large number of figures which had appeared after the decimal point”).

Cockcroft was realistic: “all candidates”, he expected, “will have access to a calculator by 1985”. And his proposal was revolutionary: overhauling mathematics education by splitting it into two parts, spending part of the time teaching students to use a calculator and the rest of the time learning to cope without one – and crucially, testing both. It caught on. Learning maths without and with a calculator is now the gold standard around the world, the former nurturing the basics and the latter applying them to more fiendish problems.

We should also be realistic and revolutionary, adopting this tried-and-tested principle – what I call “teach both, test both” – for AI now. Every subject, from history to English literature, should be divided in two: teach students to use AI in one part, teach students to flourish without it in the other – and, crucially, examine both. A teacher cannot monitor whether or not a student uses AI in the quiet solitude of their bedroom. But nothing can replace the feeling of sitting in an exam, looking at the paper, and feeling that cold sweat when you realise you haven’t prepared for both parts.

One of my worries is that we allow a legitimate sense of concern about the impact of social media on children’s lives to seep into how we think about AI, allowing good restrictions on the former to turn into kneejerk bans on the latter. Social media and AI are not the same thing, and whereas the former often dehumanises and distracts us from the real world, AI – used in the right way – can make our lives go far better.

There is another way to think about this: a debate is now under way about the “Goldilocks” amount of screen time for children – not too much, not too little, just the right amount. But this is not the right argument to be having. What matters is not so much the amount of screen time, but what is actually on those screens, what we are using this technology to do.

This distinction matters not only for thinking about what we teach, but how we teach as well. Consider a further example: personal tuition. It is often said an average student who receives one-to-one tuition will outperform almost all their peers in a traditional classroom setting. I saw this first-hand, as a tutor in Oxford for years, teaching mathematics and economics.

The problem, though, is that human tutors are too expensive to provide to everyone. But now, AI can finally provide high-quality personal tuition, tailoring the way material is taught to the unique strengths and weaknesses of each student, mimicking interactions with a human tutor but at a far lower cost.

In all honesty, AI provides a level of tailored instruction that I – and many other teachers I have watched over the years – have struggled to achieve. In part, it is the breadth of AI that is striking. I have used it to respond to my five-year-old’s bedtime-delaying tactic of asking vast questions just as I turn down the lights (in response to, “Daddy, where did the first human come from?” it drew up a short story about evolution), as well as to create step-by-step instructions to help graduate students solve hard mathematical problems in economics, such as the Ramsey growth model.

“I don’t think anyone has ever paid such pure attention to me and my thinking and my questions,” a student was reported as saying in The New Yorker in April 2025. “It’s made me rethink my interactions with people.” AI never gets tired or distracted. It doesn’t have fixed office hours or limited classroom time. It will always answer one more question, always provide one more explanation of a problem you don’t understand.

I am not surprised that students have been booing tech titans during recent US graduation ceremonies. The most resistant groups I have spoken to over the last 15 years are young professionals: they have spent a big chunk of their life, and sunk huge amounts of money, preparing to be a lawyer or doctor or whatever it might be, and they are understandably furious when they are told, just as they cross the finish line, that the world they were preparing to enter is over.

There is so much advice I would want to give them, worried at the start of their careers. But one of the most important bits is to choose a profession because the problem interests you, not the job. Bluntly, if you go into medicine because you like the look of doctors on House, or law because of Suits, or marketing because of Mad Men, then you are going to be disappointed. These jobs are soon going to look very different.

But the problems themselves – improving health outcomes, providing legal advice, selling products? They are not going away. It is the way we solve them, and the skills required to do so, that will look very different.

You could glimpse this well before the arrival of generative AI. Back in 2017, a team at Stanford University announced they had built a system that could tell whether or not a freckle was cancerous from a photograph as accurately as leading dermatologists. It was a remarkable moment, a lurch forward in AI-enabled diagnostics. Yet what was particularly interesting about this work is that the final co-author on the Nature article that announced this achievement was Sebastian Thrun – not a medical doctor, but a leading computer scientist who developed the world’s first driverless car. Here was a man who knew very little about medicine at all, yet with the skills that he had was able to build a system that could rival the expertise of the finest doctors.

What would I actually do if I were at the start of my career, back in the starting blocks of life? Without hesitation, I would run towards AI and science – not because it is protected from automation, but because it is where the most excitement is likely to happen in years to come. In the 20th century, the best ideas we had about the world came from the heads of clever human beings. In the 21st century, I expect they are likely to come from capable AIs instead.

We could catch a glimpse of that in late 2024, when the creators of an AI built by DeepMind – AlphaFold2 – won the Nobel prize in chemistry for solving the “protein folding problem” (one of the greatest unsolved challenges in biology, critical for understanding how diseases work and how to treat them). At the time of writing, frontier mathematics is next in line, new discoveries appearing at an impressive rate.

The more time I spend with AI, the more I realise the main constraint on its use in the world is the limits of our imagination. Even if we were to press pause on progress in the technology today, there would be vastly more uses for it than we have currently dreamed up.

Part of the imaginative task falls to us. But that night with my eight-year-old, crafting that story, reminds me that part of it falls to the next generation as well. “We look at the world once in childhood,” wrote the poet Louise Glück, “the rest is memory.” In that spirit, we need the next generation, with their sense of adventure and open-mindedness, their lack of world-weariness, to help us think wisely and freely, together, about what we can use these extraordinary technologies to do.

What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind is published by Penguin at £20. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.
