It felt as if the world had tired of rock music, yet Geese are the perfect soundtrack for this age of disquiet

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 10:54:07 GMT

This young American band, led by Cameron Winter, make music for a generation on the edge

“If you want me to pay my taxes,” sang the 23-year-old man on the stage, loudly accompanied by the thousands in front of him, “You better come over with a crucifix/ You’re gonna have to nail me down.”

Last Thursday night, I stood in a field in Dorset, and watched the headlining attraction on the first night of the End of the Road festival. Geese are a rock group from New York, led by the extremely talented Cameron Winter, who has a lot to say, and an often gnomic, veiled way of saying it. But the meaning of the most celebrated lines on his band’s most recent album – Getting Killed – might be clearer than a lot of the rest.

There are hundreds of different interpretations online of a song simply called Taxes, from death and martyrdom to the avoidance of responsibility. He may just, I suppose, be telling the Internal Revenue Service to go away in the cause of small-state libertarianism. But at the risk of ridicule, I’ll opt for the most literal and crowd-pleasing reading: that Winter is inspirationally updating the idea of rock music sneering at the powers that be and rejecting whatever it is they want. When I first heard those lines, in fact, I imagined him being cornered by Donald Trump, JD Vance and some or other Maga goon squad, wearily exhaling and sending them on their way.

For at least a decade now, rock – which is to say, stuff largely made with guitars and mostly delivered by bands – has been in an increasing state of cultural eclipse. Its presence in what remains of the singles chart is usually minimal-to-nonexistent; it tends to fare better in the albums rankings, but chronically lacks its old ability to push itself to the forefront of its era.

It’s striking, then, that Geese’s somewhat belated rise has been powered by an album that consummately embodies its time, has received praise to match and is evidently loved by younger people who were supposed to have long ago become largely rock-phobic (for proof, see the footage of Geese’s performance at this year’s Reading festival). Their current high profile has been powered not just by Getting Killed, but Winter’s much more intimate solo album – titled Heavy Metal – and a one-man performance at Carnegie Hall in New York, about to be released as a film directed by Paul Thomas Anderson. Seemingly as a matter of contractual obligation, all four members of his group (including guitarist Emily Green) have hairstyles like those of the early-1970s Rolling Stones, but the music they now make – their first album came out in 2018 – usually suggests something immeasurably more contemporary.

It is variously tender, soothing, angry and explosive, prone to tumble into lengthy improvisation, and sometimes shot through with knowingness that can be maddening, but is presumably the result of working in an artistic field now full of cliches that either have to be acknowledged or swerved around. But when they play live, power, ferocity and sudden snaps between loudness and calm take precedence. Some moments are redolent of Led Zeppelin, but taken somewhere completely different by the lyrical content. Radiohead are another oft-cited reference point, which feels more satisfactory, but only in the sense that Geese largely stay true to the idea that they should sound like no one but themselves and damn the consequences.

This is an age in which a huge amount of popular music is tailor-made for audiences assumed to be in a constant state of distraction, so songs often have the briskest of intros and the crassest, most earworm-ish hook lines. Geese’s music, by contrast, is often gnarly and difficult, and entails friction between the musicians and their listeners. It took me six or seven plays to even start to get my head around Getting Killed, but in an occasionally masochistic way, I enjoyed every minute.

And this, I think, is why. From its title onwards, Getting Killed is full of flickers and flashes of the volatile and frightening condition of both Geese’s home country and the wider world. Among the first words on the album, repeated five times, are “There’s a bomb in my car”, quickly followed by “My daughter is dead.” Other lyrics seem – seem – to reference the crazed ringmaster who has led the US into both internal conflict and disastrous entanglements abroad: “All people/In times of war/Must go down to the circus,” Winter sings on a piece titled 100 Horses, following that up with “There is only dance music in times of war/But we have danced for too long.” What you really yearn for is a zinger akin to Bob Dylan’s “even the president of the United States/Sometimes must have to stand naked.” But Winter’s facility with words suggests he will soon get there, even if he is currently too keen on bathetically bursting his own lyrical bubble and thereby avoiding the “spokesperson for a generation” deadweight that Dylan found so irksome: “There were hundred horses dancing/Maybe 124,” he sings at one point, which isn’t even that funny.

But such slip-ups are rare. At the core of what Geese do is something that is also sharply generational. It’s surely one of the identifying features of people their age that even comparative material comfort (all four were privately educated) doesn’t make the anxiety that comes with being the canaries in the coalmine of digital capitalism unavoidable. The title track puts this point plainly: “I’m getting killed by a pretty good life,” wails Winter. “Getting killed by a pretty good life/I have been fucking destroyed by the city tonight.” A track titled Half Real suggests twentysomethings so understandably confounded that they just want to switch off. On Thursday, Winter sang with such ferocity that any lingering suspicions about archness or humour instantly vanished: “I’ve got half a mind/To just pay for the lobotomy/And tell ’em get rid of the bad times/And get rid of the good times too/I’ve got no more thinking to do.”

On the face of it, there may be reasons to keep your distance: their comparatively privileged backgrounds, or a spurt of controversy about the ubiquity and craftiness of their (very common) online marketing. But their empathetic kind of excellence makes those things almost irrelevant. What they excel at is reflecting their audience’s experiences, feelings, passions and furies back at them. At End of the Road, evidence of that connection was consistently there on the giant screen next to the stage. The younger members of the audience pressed against the barrier at the front rejoiced in every note of Taxes, and sang along most loudly to that eternal rebuke to the hypocrisies of power and influence: “Doctor, heal yourself.” But what was most telling was the ecstatic exchange between the band and their core crowd triggered by a simple line from one of Winter’s love songs, which seemed to take on quite another meaning: “I see myself in you.”

They would doubtless hate me for saying so, but still: right now, Geese sound like the accidental representatives of a global demographic that may look sensitive and gentle, but that – in response to the impossibility of just about everything – may yet explode. In that sense, the simplest of messages is woven into what they do: look out.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

This is how we do it: ‘As carers, we have to be responsible. During sex, we relinquish control to each other’

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 10:00:02 GMT

Betsy and Felix have sex once a week when they are alone in the house – it frees up their minds just to be together

How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously

double quotation markI used to kick guys out of bed after any sexual encounters. But with Felix it was totally different from the start

Felix and I have separate caring responsibilities. I look after my adult son, who has disabilities, and Felix is his elderly mother’s full-time carer. We live in separate suburbs of the same city, and see each other three set evenings a week. We often feel stressed and preoccupied, and so we have a rule: for the first hour, we do a shared trauma dump, where we talk about the sad feelings weighing on our minds.

We have sex once a week because it’s the only time we are alone at mine without the people we care for. Felix tends to initiate more than I do because in the last year menopause has really dampened my sex drive. I worry about him feeling rejected. His love language is touch and I want to be able to give him that – so I hold his balls as we go to sleep, which makes him feel comforted.

When we met at a house party three years ago, we had an instant connection. Felix is covered in tattoos, with lots of earrings and a mohawk. He gave me a gentle kiss on the cheek. After that, I was on a trip for 10 days and kept thinking about that kiss. We spent that time texting and covered so much ground that by the first date, I felt I already knew him really well. He confided in me that he was creating a science fiction pornographic comic strip based on his own fantasies – in a universe where women dominate men – and invited me into his sexual desires.

I used to be quite cynical about sex. It was an itch I needed to scratch. I don’t find that intimacy comes very naturally to me. I hated sharing a bed and used to kick guys out after any sexual encounters. But with Felix it was totally different from the start. Our first sexual encounter was slow, intimate and caring. He really dissolved my boundaries. Unlike previous guys, I find him worth sharing a bed with, even if he disturbs my sleep. He’s always called me Lil Betzy – as though I am a rapper – which is hilarious, because I’m a middle-aged woman. I think of him as a gentle part of my life I can cosy into.

I met Betsy at a party and we spoke all night about culture and philosophy. We texted for a while because she went away and I found myself opening up to her, sharing things I would have never told other folks. For six years, I had been secretly creating a sexy comic strip based in a fantasy world where women dominate men. Betsy seemed genuinely interested in what excited me, so I felt safe to share it for the first time.

We have sex once a week on a set day. I live with my ageing mother and so when Betsy is here, we don’t have sex. We also don’t have sex at hers when her son is there, which leaves the one day a week I am at Betsy’s and her son is with his father. I think it works best for us to be intimate when we are completely alone, as it frees up space in our minds to just be together. In our sex life, we like to relinquish control to one another. I think that is because in our separate lives we both have to be responsible and make the decisions all the time.

Some of my favourite times have been when we were fooling around on the sofa and it evolved into something more. Those moments are harder to come by nowadays because of our caring responsibilities, which is a little sad. The other factor is that my sex drive is now higher than hers, because she’s going through menopause. I try to spend more time on slow foreplay to get her in the mood. Even if we don’t have sex, we’ve found if we kiss, cuddle or hold hands, I don’t feel as rejected by our mismatched libidos.

Betsy is not naturally a cuddly person. I know she used to kick other blokes out the bed, and I feel pretty special that she lets me stay over. I think of our time together as very important and never enough.

Burnham talks of radical change, but Treasury mood music says otherwise

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 09:48:54 GMT

Bond market volatility means John Healey will have to take tough decisions, soon, if he wants to meet spending pledges

In John Healey’s bright Treasury office, overlooking St James’s Park, the artwork has not changed since his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, selected a row of Bridget Riley prints in her feminist rehang. Judging by the signals emerging from No 11 about the chancellor’s 28 October budget, not much else has changed either.

Voters listening to Andy Burnham’s promises to overthrow 40 years of neoliberalism and vanquish the ghost of Margaret Thatcher would be excused for expecting a radical policy reset. Early signs suggest they may be disappointed.

Healey will give a speech about growth policy on Monday in his bluff, reassuring style, less than six months on from Reeves’s Mais lecture. He is expected to lean heavily on two of her favourite themes: investment and devolution.

That’s hardly surprising. The UK economy has been held back by decades of underinvestment, and growth has been far too concentrated in London and the south-east.

But the speech seems likely to be followed up six weeks or so later with a “steady as she (or rather he) goes” budget – with key decisions, including when the UK will be spending 3% of GDP on defence, deferred.

When he resigned in June, Healey was adamant that the UK should set a “headmark date” of 2030 for hitting the 3% target. Treasury sources indicate that he has not changed his mind, yet he has made clear he intends to defer setting out a timeline until next year’s spending review.

That suggests Reeves’s promise of one major fiscal event a year – the autumn budget – with a low-key forecast in the spring has been ditched.

Usually, the budget before a spending review would set out the “envelope” – the broad path of future public spending – and, where necessary, the tax rises to finance it, leaving the details to be hammered out later. But the priorities for 28 October appear to be more immediate. Healey will fill in the gaps in the defence investment plan – the one he resigned over three months ago.

There may be also modest further moves towards giving consumers “breathing space” from higher energy bills in January – though judging by the mood music, it will not be funded, as the Trades Union Congress has urged, by a windfall tax on banks.

Healey told the Financial Times this weekend: “People look at the banks largely as big profit-making multinationals, but their fundamental role is too often overlooked. That’s something that’s strong in my mind.”

There is some logic for projecting what the chancellor has called “steadiness”. He has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, where volatility in government bond markets was a hot topic.

Higher interest rates on the Treasury’s debt pile already appear to have wiped out up to half of the £24bn headroom Reeves left against her fiscal rules.

Up to another £4bn is expected to have evaporated as a result of lower-than-forecast migration, and Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills will have to be paid for, too.

It must be tempting to paper over the cracks and hope for the best. But the truth is that it will be all but impossible to raise defence spending to 3% by 2030 and avert the Whitehall funding squeeze pencilled in by Reeves for the back end of the parliament without raising taxes.

Last year’s spending review was predicated on generous increases in spending for key departments including the NHS and defence for Labour’s first two years in power, followed by a much tougher three years.

after newsletter promotion

That means, as Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies told me, “things are so tight that if the government knows for sure, for example, that they want to increase defence spending to 3% by the end of the parliament, that would mean that to stick within the current plans, you’d have to hold all other departments, including the NHS, flat.” She added with typical understatement: “That seems pretty unlikely.”

Miller said: “If you don’t want to do that, you probably want to find the money now, for the spending review next year. If you really want to get defence to 3%, that is a real challenge … the budget is the right time to be making preparations that would allow that to be possible.”

That’s an extremely tough message to announce for a government that claims to be “bringing back hope”.

One approach would have been to point to the fragility of the global environment – Iran, Ukraine, Donald Trump’s tariffs – and ditch some of Labour’s manifesto promises on tax and spend. But Burnham has already rejected that idea.

There is no doubt more to be done on reforming welfare – so that more young people are encouraged into work instead of left without help, for example, as Alan Milburn’s forthcoming review is expected to recommend. And certainly, Burnham’s erstwhile friend Lord O’Donnell is right that the triple lock pensions promise should go.

But that is unlikely to take Healey to the £10bn-ish additional spending he needs to get to 3% of GDP – let alone the 3.5% Labour has promised by 2035 – while still convincing the bond markets there is a plan for balancing the books.

As the Resolution Foundation pointed out this week, the 3.5% target looks impossible to meet without tax rises on middle-earners – who still face less of a burden on average than in many other major economies, but may feel otherwise.

Burnham’s choice of Healey as chancellor read like an endorsement of 3% defence spending by 2030. Postponing the decision will just unleash another six months of the destabilising speculation so depressingly familiar from Reeves’s tenure in No 11. Healey should bite the bullet at the budget and take the tough decisions now.

Aged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroom

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 09:00:01 GMT

I’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospect

You know those dreams when you’re back at school? And you’re sitting at a desk reading a GCSE exam paper? Only you don’t recognise anyone around you? Well, I am living that dream. Because, at the age of 41, I have gone back to school. And not just any school. I have gone back to my own secondary school. Only this time, I am allowed in the staffroom.

That’s right: a short 25 years after walking out of those concrete and carpeted halls, the smell of polyester jumpers and canteen chips heady on the early summer air, I am back. But now I’m training to be a teacher.

To some extent, this was inevitable due to the logistics of my life. Despite a few lessons, I have never learned to drive (my instructor asked my mum out on a date and things got so awkward so quickly I have never really been behind a steering wheel since). I also have small children at nursery and primary school nearby, which meant that I had to beg my training scheme to place me at a school I could easily cycle to.

But as I sit beneath the very ceiling tiles I once knew as intimately as the freckles on my own arm, I also wonder if this was somehow destined. If I, as someone who loved school, was raised by a teacher, and married a teacher who was himself raised by a teacher, was always going to join the family business. Or if, like one of those eels that swims all the way from the silty bed of some Essex river out to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, only for its larvae to wriggle all 10,000 salty kilometres back home, I have been slowly making my way back to school since I left.

It is undeniably odd to find myself walking across the playground on which I first tasted Um Bongo, and heard the name the Strokes, and hid my first love bite under a sticky layer of foundation. As I hustle to a safeguarding meeting, or am escorted by my mentor to pick up my new printing code, I can’t help but remember treading that same route at 15, wearing a skirt I’d sewn myself out of wetsuit material (I stretched the definition of our school uniform back then until the seams screamed), or with the initials of the boy I fancied written in ballpoint pen on the inside of my thumb, or on the way to my last ever chemistry lesson.

I’m also far from the only person I know hole-punching their way into a new career after decades in the arts, media or what we used to laughingly call “the creative industries”. I can count at least four former journalists from my contingent retraining as English teachers, another who is well on their way to qualifying as a plumber, a DJ working as a midwife, and a fair crop of writers, poets and journalists working towards jobs as therapists.

The old story used to be that ambitious people worked as teachers for a few years and then went into creative fields – Romesh Ranganathan, Philip Pullman, Joanne Harris, Greg Davies and so on. But it seems to me that publishing, music, broadcasting and all the rest are now losing scores of mid-career artists to the world of education and other public services. Or rather, if you’re lucky, the ambition to press your thumb on to the surface of the world, through writing or performing, one day gives way to a far greater urge: to unfurl the thousands of brilliant minds coming up behind you.

I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic moulded chairs, as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders. I am thrilled at the prospect of being able to dissect a novel over weeks in a classroom, rather than in minutes on the radio. I am delighted to be back in my old assembly hall, taking notes on a lined page, only this time with grey hairs, and two children down the road, and two decades of life in my rucksack.

The world is being driven to the brink by thugs and dictators, but there is a route to a brighter future

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 05:00:57 GMT

It’s no surprise some analysts say we are already in the midst of the third world war, but ordinary people have more power than we think

Don’t look up! The world is a mess. The sky could fall in any day. Unending wars, expanding humanitarian crises, rising authoritarianism, dysfunctional democracies, rampant racial and religious extremism, and unchecked lawlessness cast a dark cloud as the west’s new political year begins. Set all that against a backdrop of staggering global economic inequality, corporate and individual greed, irresponsible government indebtedness, dangerous AI gambles, climate breakdown and proliferating nuclear weapons, and a truly apocalyptic global outlook begins to take shape. It’s enough to make anyone shut their eyes, cover their ears and utter a Munch-like scream. And it’s only getting worse.

Democratic leaders who promise a better, safer, more optimistic future – what Britain’s freshly arrived prime minister, Andy Burnham, calls a “new era of possibility” – cannot escape this wider international context. Last week’s global bond market upheaval, sparked by external factors, left Burnham’s cash-strapped government struggling with sharply increased borrowing costs before he barely got started. The fact he chose Ukraine for his first overseas trip, while symbolically important, highlighted another grim reality. As a lead opponent of Vladimir Putin’s invasion, Britain now finds itself in a de facto state of war with Russia – and facing attack. Argentina, too, is eyeing UK defence vulnerabilities. These are not the sort of possibilities Burnham envisaged.

Little wonder some analysts believe a third world war has already begun. Those who say this is over-dramatic should consider the following snapshots of the state of the world in 2026. From Kyiv to Khorramshahr, Kordofan and Kachin, conflicts flare and subside but never seem to end. All-out Russian aggression in Ukraine, now mostly comprising daily attempts to murder and terrorise civilians, is into its fifth year. Trump has lost his Iran bet, but keeps killing and bombing with no end in sight. In southern Sudan, appalling atrocities go unchecked. In Myanmar, a people’s war against a brutal junta rages on. Israel’s response to the 2023 massacres has triggered an ongoing regional war embroiling Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Iran and the Gulf states. Worldwide, record numbers of people are displaced by conflict.

Increasingly interconnected, these wars threaten to merge into one uncontrollable global conflagration. The alliance system, key pillar of the post-1945 order, is eating itself. Donald Trump taunts Europe and Nato with tariffs, troop withdrawals, barbs and insults at a time of acute vulnerability. Canada and the US are at daggers drawn as the White House bully fatuously threatens Venezuela – or Greenland-style annexation. China aids North Korea, which also aids Russia, which aids Iran, which aids Hezbollah and the Houthis. In Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia, China looms menacingly as partnerships with Washington fray. In Taiwan, fears of invasion grow, aggravated by Trump’s obsequious appeasing of Xi Jinping.

Everywhere you look, humanitarian crises caused by war, the climate crisis or natural disasters are producing chaotic mass migrations, malnutrition and disease. Increasingly, the suffering overwhelms a UN-led aid system crippled by US and UK funding cuts. In the fertile West Bank, 900,000 Palestinians, their homes and farms besieged by settler extremists, are now food insecure, the World Food Programme says. In Somalia, millions go hungry amid record drought and predicted El Niño-related flooding. Colombia and Afghanistan face similar perils. Humanitarian and human rights outrages take individual form, too. In Hong Kong, for example, an ailing Jimmy Lai, brave champion of free speech, languishes in 23-hour-a-day solitary confinement, a tortured casualty of Chinese communism’s hatred of democracy and civil rights.

Skittish bond markets may be the least of the world’s economic and financial problems. Is a crash coming, reminiscent of 2008, only worse? The signs are ominous. The US just notched up a record $40tn in national debt. France, the UK, Japan and others are deep in the red, too. Unmanageable current-account deficits, rising inflation and the huge, draining diversion of investment into bloated AI tech companies all point to what market analysts cutely call a “disorderly correction”. By some estimates, the Nvidia chip-maker, plus Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, are “worth” about 23% of the entire US stock market. Meanwhile, unaffordable northern-hemisphere energy and food prices loom this winter, exacerbated by Trump’s Middle East forever folly. In the worst case, all this could translate into global recession and yet more political instability. It’s a gigantic bubble waiting to burst.

The existential hazards posed by the climate crisis and global heating should require scant elaboration after the terrifying Nepal-Tibet flood disaster. Similarly inimical to life on Earth, in an avoidable, human-made way, is the rapid proliferation of nuclear weapons, including so-called “battlefield” or tactical nukes that are more likely to be used in war zones such as Ukraine or Iran. All nine nuclear weapons states are expanding or modernising their arsenals, with China in the lead. Countries such as South Korea and Saudi Arabia weigh their nuclear options. And now this atomic arms race is expanding into space. There really seems no limit to humanity’s relentless, doom-laden drive towards self-destruction.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The fundamental values of post-Enlightenment liberal societies are everywhere under siege. The rule of law is routinely flouted. While Putin and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu ignore war-crimes arrest warrants, Trump and his unctuous lickspittle, Marco Rubio, actively work to destroy the international criminal court. Across Europe, far-right racists, loons and bigots make political advances, seen again this weekend in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt. Next year, France will approach its own fateful national reckoning. In the US, Trump, enabled by a supine majority in Congress and dishonourable supreme court justices, is constructing a “constitutional dictatorship” to subvert future elections, symbolised by a gross, 250ft-tall “Arc de Trump”. Let alarm bells ring: US democracy and the entire western democratic tradition are in dire peril.

What is to be done? Is any consolation to be had? First, key pillars of the post-1945 order, though badly battered, are still just about intact. The UN and most of its agencies, the international court of justice and collaborative, multinational western democratic alliances such as the EU, Nato and the G7 have so far survived the current tumult. Second, the age of tyrants is nearing an end. These angry old men are mostly headed for nursing homes, jail or the grave. May their legacies of fear and hate die with them. Last, younger generations in many “middle power” and developing countries, exemplified by India’s Cockroach youth protest movement, are making plain their revulsion and rejection of the way the world is now. Like Burnham, they believe passionately in the power of possibility and change.

The future lies not in the hands of political thugs and killers, of dictators and megalomaniacs, but in the hands of ordinary people everywhere. It depends on millions upon millions of individual daily acts of kindness, selflessness, faith and courage. So don’t lose heart. Keep your eyes open. Unblock your ears. And don’t look down!

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

‘The first half of my 20s was hell’: Maisie Williams on her tough childhood and why she’s been having more fun since Game of Thrones

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 05:00:56 GMT

After her role in the fantasy series, the actor felt lost. Now she’s getting relationship advice from Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, and following a Sex and the City star’s mantra: never be anywhere you aren’t enjoying yourself

Maisie Williams has dabbled in witchcraft exactly once. The actor was getting ready to audition for a part in a film. “I wanted it so badly that I went on to Etsy, and I paid a witch to manifest me the role,” she says, poker-faced.

“It didn’t work, and that was where my days of witchcraft ended,” she adds, breaking into an infectious cackle.

The spell may not have worked that time, but Williams will soon try her own hand at witchcraft on screen in Practical Magic 2. The sequel to the beloved 1998 romcom, about two supernatural sisters played by Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, it features Williams as Antonia, the youngest daughter of Bullock’s Sally Owens. She never did get her money back from her Etsy witch. “It was maybe, like, £16.50? Which is not going to break the bank, but good for her. Good for her, to be making money doing nothing!” Williams laughs again.

We meet on a sweltering afternoon at a posh pub in Belgravia in London where women in expensive-looking sundresses are drinking Aperol spritzes on the terrace. Williams arrives from a busy day of appointments. She removes a pair of oversized grey headphones and sets them down on the table (she was listening to the US singer-songwriter Slayyyter on the walk over). “I’m in my business outfit because I’ve had business meetings,” she explains. (It’s arguably a very gen Z take on corporate dressing: long, dark hair worn in a practical ponytail, white T-shirt, smart grey trousers with a matching grey miniskirt attached, chunky, don’t‑mess-with-me Prada boots.)

Today’s agenda has included two jewellery fittings for a red carpet event, an “important producing meeting, with me as the producer” and lunch with her former Game of Thrones co-star Hannah Murray. The pair were catching up and discussing Murray’s recent memoir, The Make-Believe, about her devastating experience with a wellness cult. The group promised spiritual healing through expensive, elaborate rituals; Murray experienced a psychotic episode and was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder. “I knew something was going on, but I didn’t know it was that,” Williams says. “I felt really upset with myself for not asking sooner.”

Williams says she hasn’t always been a sceptic regarding magic. “I used to indulge in the whimsy of the patterns of the universe and think, ‘Oh, it’s a sign that everything’s going to work out.’” She says, taking a sip of Diet Coke. But after reading Murray’s book, Williams decided that searching for symbols in daily life might not be so wholesome after all. “I realised it leaves your mind slightly malleable to seeing a sign because you think it’s a divine intervention, and not just a good, fun coincidence.”

The 29-year-old actor is probably still best known as Arya Stark from Game of Thrones, the baby-faced assassin who shot her to stratospheric levels of fame at age 12. I remember first seeing her in Carol Morley’s The Falling, in which she stood out as a prickly, stiff‑backed schoolgirl opposite a then unknown Florence Pugh. In the seven years since Game of Thrones ended, Williams has landed roles in Marvel spin-off The New Mutants, in Danny Boyle’s miniseries Pistol as punk icon Jordan, and in Apple TV’s The New Look, a glossy drama about Christian Dior and Coco Chanel in Nazi-occupied Paris. She has started her own production company, and co-hosts the Frank Film Club podcast with two of her friends. It has been a period of trying different things, of searching for light relief, after a long stretch dealing with some much darker stuff. Last year, she even got a new agent. “He was bringing me fun things and was calling me every day,” she says. One of those fun, unexpected things was Practical Magic 2.

Williams had seen the original once or twice, but rewatched it before her audition. “The first movie has a lot of different beats to it,” she says diplomatically. That’s one way to put it: tonally, the film is all over the place. Based on an Alice Hoffman novel, it tells the story of the Owens sisters, two witches doomed by an ancestral curse: any man who falls in love with an Owens woman is destined to die. It is a cult classic, with fabulous 90s costumes, Bullock and Kidman drunkenly dancing around their kitchen to Harry Nilsson’s Coconut and a jarringly dark domestic violence subplot. The sequel is much slicker. Directed by Susanne Bier, it sends Sally’s more rebellious eldest daughter Kylie (Joey King) to England as she tries to break the family curse. Bullock and Kidman go after her, bickering the whole way, while Williams’s character, a trainee neurosurgeon, holds the fort at home.

“Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman are real movie stars – from a time in cinema that is escaping us,” says Williams matter-of-factly. “I went into this film seeing them as otherworldly.” She recalls meeting the actors for the first time at the read-through. Later that day she was heading to Glastonbury festival. “I got back in my car, and I wound the windows up, and I was just like … ” Williams claps both French-manicured hands to her face and lets out a high-pitched shriek. “I had my dog in the car. He was probably thinking, ‘What is going on?!’ And then I drove to Glastonbury.” On set, in between takes, the veteran Hollywood actors imparted important wisdom to their younger co-stars. But it wasn’t about the industry. “We spoke about how being friends with your ex is a fallacy,” she says. Who said that? Was it Kidman, who is recently divorced? “We all said that!” Williams demurs.

In the film, Williams and King are an inseparable sister duo, snuggled under the covers at their mum’s house and whispering as if they’re at a sleepover. In real life, Williams has three siblings, including one sister who is five years her senior. “When we’re together it’s like no time has passed but we’re not … ” She pauses. “We don’t call every day,” she says. “We’ve had waves in our life when we’re a lot closer, but a lot of our connection now comes through the kids.” Williams takes her niece and nephew on camping trips. “We never went out partying together,” she says. And, anyway, when she would have been the right age, Williams was busy filming Game of Thrones. “I was away most of the time, and I’d moved out as well.”

Williams’s route to child stardom came via a curiously X Factor-themed school nativity play. “I played Sharon Osbourne, and had done such a good job that my friend’s mum felt compelled to tell my mum, ‘You should put her into classes.’ That was when I started taking it seriously, because they were taking me seriously.” Then things got very serious, with Williams barely in secondary school when she landed a role on Game of Thrones. The speed at which her career took off shaped her expectations of the film industry, she says. “I thought, oh! Whatever you want, you can get. Like that,” she says, snapping her fingers. “That was how I thought the industry was.” Her naivety, she reckons, was a good thing. “It informed the way I see life, and the way I threw myself into what turned out to be a huge responsibility.”

Those early positive experiences, she says, gave her the confidence to pursue her dreams. “I wasn’t knocked down as a child. I wasn’t knocked down by my mum. I wasn’t knocked down by teachers at drama school, and I wasn’t knocked down by the industry when I did start auditioning.” Williams wonders if she would have still been resilient if she hadn’t enjoyed early success. “I think that a lot of people have a gift, but they just don’t get cast in a huge TV show when they’re 12.”

Williams claims not to know about an Arya Stark spin-off movie that is reportedly in development with HBO. “I saw that, too! I was like, huh?” Would she be interested in returning to that character? “I don’t know, really. She would have to be developed in some way because I feel like I’ve changed so much, and I feel like what people loved about Arya is that she was always a child doing things that were quite grownup.”

In person, Williams is warm but somewhat guarded; she sits next to me on the leather banquette but maintains a cautious distance. She is good company, with a beaming smile and a glorious, trilling laugh, but several times in our conversation I sense her weighing up her words. When asked about her early life growing up between Bristol and Somerset she becomes visibly uncomfortable. She settles on an honest, abridged answer. “My mum and my siblings and I spent a lot of time with my auntie,” she says, adding that she was mostly raised by the two women. “My auntie was a childminder with loads of other kids, so my life was vibrant and silly and fun and playful.”

Williams describes herself as “not coming from a hugely privileged background”. I wonder how, on the brink of 30, she reflects on growing up with less. “When I reflect on myself as a child, I wish I could just tell her it’s going to be fine. It’s going to work out. I think the fear that I felt at that time was so defining for many years of my childhood. I didn’t know. I was so ambitious as a small child, and I think maybe that did come from wanting my life to be different.”

In 2022, Williams spoke about the difficulties she faced back then on the Diary of a CEO podcast. Her parents split up when she was a baby, and her father is no longer in her life. “I had a traumatic relationship with my dad, and ever since I can remember I have struggled sleeping,” she told host Steven Bartlett. She described a teacher noticing her struggling at school and asking if she ate breakfast in the mornings. Williams said she didn’t. She was eight. The teacher called her mum. “I would look around at other kids and be, like, ‘Why don’t they seem to understand this pain or dread or fear? Joy – when does that come for me?” she said on the podcast.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

after newsletter promotion

“I have very close friends that I had not told,” Williams says today. “What I said on that podcast was all I’ve said about it to a lot of people, other than my family and my therapist. I even had boyfriends who didn’t know. So my reluctance to want to talk about it again is because my relationship to fame, and my relationship to success, was hugely defined by my childhood experience, and so that being explored in such a public setting now feels a little bit … terrifying?” She winces.

“I think it reached a lot of people who were in the same position, and I’m really happy that it did.” I’m curious to know why she chose that moment to finally speak about what had happened to her. “I always wanted to,” she says. “I think part of the reason why I was so good at playing Arya was because of how I’d grown up.”

She says journalists would often ask her how she was able to access such difficult emotions as a younger, less experienced actor. “I always felt like it was something I couldn’t say. I could access these emotions because I felt them myself, every one of them, for really extended periods of time.” What emotions? “Anger and fear.” She lets out a bitter laugh. “Stonewalling. I know that feeling of shutting down. These things that you don’t really start to understand about yourself until a lot later.” Being a teenager, she says, is already so fraught with emotion.

By the time she recorded that podcast, “I had done a lot of therapy,” she says, “and so was feeling a lot clearer about a lot of things.” It was Bartlett’s initial question that cracked them open for her. “He said, ‘What happened to you as a child that defines how you are?’ or something. It’s literally the only question that someone would have to ask me for me to answer honestly.” I was struck by her candour and vulnerability in that interview, I tell her. “I just thought that by releasing it, it was the last step in being free from it. Which kind of turned out to be true,” she says.

I wonder what she makes of Bartlett now. “Mmm,” she says, eyebrows raising, her mouth tightening into a horizontal line. In recent years, Bartlett has become a controversial figure, who has been criticised for amplifying medical misinformation and platforming manosphere-adjacent guests such as fellow podcaster Chris Williamson, who blamed declining birthrates on “women’s socioeconomic emancipation into the workforce”. Bartlett has aired the views of “experts” who claimed that Covid vaccines were “a net negative for society” and that cancer could be treated by a keto diet. It’s not a show that seems particularly aligned with liberal values.

“At the time, it felt like he had a podcast that felt fresh and different,” Williams says. “After, I felt slightly like I had been part of a podcast that gets a lot of views based on uprooting trauma. When I saw the trailer to the episode, I felt slightly icked out by how he had clipped it. But ultimately I can’t control that. Now I just feel like it’s quite dangerous, some of these conversations that are being had and taken out of context.”

Still, speaking about her experiences publicly was “a huge, defining moment of change” for Williams. “The first half of my 20s was just hell, but I think maybe it is for a lot of people,” she says. “I think that has more to do with the fact that Game of Thrones was ending, and I didn’t know what I was going to do next, and I just needed a break, to be honest with you. And then it also has to do with delayed teenage awkward years, and figuring a lot of things out that I felt like maybe I couldn’t do much earlier than that. And also Covid, and also an industry strike,” she adds with a shrug. The pub is getting noisy, filling up with finance bros who have just finished work.

“But post-2023, every day has been getting better,” she says. What happened in 2023? “I started seeing my friends again. I moved out of London. I was living alone. I was back with my dog. Everything was different,” she says. Williams is too discreet to confirm whether this change was sparked by the breakup of her long‑term relationship with fashion designer Reuben Selby. “At that point, it was time to … ” She smiles as if she’s got a secret. “Just choose myself,” she says. “What always comes into my mind is Kim Cattrall,” she adds, paraphrasing a quote the actor gave to the Guardian that became a popular meme. “‘I don’t want to be anywhere, not even for an hour, where I’m not enjoying myself.’ That’s truly how I’ve been the last three years.”

For Williams, choosing herself means “a lot of quiet, a lot of reading, and writing, and yoga, and running, and exercise, and swimming, and cycling, and walking the dog. Walking the dog for, like, hours a day.” In other words, being in her body. “Exactly, because then I know what I want. And that can be going out with my friends all weekend, or it can be a fun dinner in London where you miss your last train home, or it can be going to the cinema alone.” This summer, it has meant going to Primavera Sound and seeing singer Ethel Cain play, having barbecues with her friends and watching the World Cup in her local pub.

When I ask Williams what her career ambitions are now, a misty, faraway look comes over her. She does say her dreams out loud, but she’d rather not say them in print, she says. “My ambition is to work with people who have proven themselves to be really talented,” she says. “I’ve worked in the industry for quite a long time, and even though I love working with debut directors, there’s a stark difference in our experience now, which is noticeable. Working with people who are more experienced brings a different atmosphere on set.” She’s also been pouring her time into her production company, Rapt. It has meant reading a lot of scripts. “I cannot tell you the amount of postpartum horrors that people are making,” she says. “Whenever there’s one great movie, you’ll get seven scripts like that on your desk.” She and her co-founder, Lowri Roberts, are having fun writing their own feature film, too. “It’s a dark comedy. It’s a satire about the end of the world,” she says.

Williams has frequently been cast in dark, dramatic roles: “But I don’t really think that’s how I am most of the time,” she says. “I think when I’m in bad situations, I’d be more likely to laugh than to cry. I don’t know if I’m really in the camp of ‘plan for the worst’. I’ve had periods of my life where I’ve been so overcome by the fear of what could go wrong that, particularly now, I’m more in a phase of ‘anything can be fixed’.”

Not that there’s much that needs fixing. She is dating and “so happy” about it, though she is coy when pressed about the details. Has she been enjoying playing the field? “No! I’m in love,” she says, smirking. “That’s all I’ll say.” Does it feel different from other times she’s been in love? “Yes, which is good. There’s lots of laughter,” she says, giggling. The vibe this summer, she says, has been “hot, in all senses of the word”. She grins. “I got myself a fan. I am a late adopter of the fan.” Before that, she says, she was “just sweating”. These days, she’s too busy enjoying herself a la Kim Cattrall to be constantly bracing for the worst. “Life is actually quite fun, but we all torture ourselves over the agony of what could be.”

Practical Magic 2 is out in cinemas on 11 September.

Tupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the case

The Guardian Sun, 06 Sep 2026 05:00:56 GMT

Police received information nearly immediately after the killing. It took Las Vegas police 27 years to make an arrest

For years, US law enforcement officials blamed their failure to solve hip-hop star Tupac Shakur’s murder on the lack of cooperation from key witnesses, and on gang members’ “snitches get stitches” culture.

But testimony in a much-delayed murder trial, which concluded this week, almost 30 years after Shakur’s death, highlighted just how much law enforcement officials knew about the shooting, and how early.

On Monday, a Southside Compton Crips gang leader and drug dealer, Duane “Keffe D” Davis, was convicted for orchestrating Shakur’s killing. Davis told investigators in 2008 that it was his nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, who pulled the trigger. Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998.

The lack of resolution in Shakur’s murder had resonated painfully not just with the artist’s own family and friends, but with many Black Americans.

Even though Shakur was one of the most famous Black men in the world, a star whose movements attracted enormous media attention, his killing remained officially unsolved for almost three decades, said Jody Armour, a law professor at the University of Southern California. “If even he could be murdered on a major Las Vegas boulevard and the case could sit around and languish, one naturally wonders what happens when the victim is just a 19-year-old Black man in Compton, or South Central, or Chicago.

“Tupac spent much of his career insisting that America did not adequately value Black life,” Armour added. “His own homicide became another exhibit in that argument.”

The fact that the Las Vegas jury reached a verdict in the Shakur case so swiftly – after less than three hours – “suggests that the evidence that had existed for some time was persuasive enough for them to convict, and calls into some question why it didn’t happen sooner”, Mark Chutkow, a former federal prosecutor, said.

And indeed, witnesses in the trial put a new spotlight on allegations of police corruption and incompetence, the mixed motivations of investigators, and law enforcement turf wars that went on for years behind the scenes of the homicide investigation.

Though it would take Las Vegas police 27 years before they made their first arrest in Shakur’s murder, testimony at Davis’s trial revealed that police received information almost immediately about what prompted the killing, and who might be behind it.

Surveillance footage played at the trial showed Shakur, the Death Row Records founder, Marion “Suge” Knight, and their associates, some affiliated with the Mob Piru Bloods, assaulting Anderson at the MGM hotel in Las Vegas, an attack that Davis would later say prompted him and his nephew to seek revenge on Shakur.

Reggie Wright Jr, the former head of security for Shakur’s record label, testified that in the hours immediately after Shakur was shot in Las Vegas, he made multiple phone calls to a police lieutenant in Compton, California, warning him that Shakur and Knight had “got into it at the MGM with some guys from the Southside Crips” and “There’s going to be trouble in Compton.”

The immediate communication between the Death Row Records security chief and the Compton police on the night of Shakur’s shooting was no surprise: Wright Jr had been a Compton police officer until he retired earlier that year, and he was calling his father, Reginald Wright Sr, then the head of Compton’s gang unit.

The elder Wright quickly passed on the information about Shakur’s Las Vegas shooting to then-Compton gang homicide detective Robert Ladd, who testified that police in Compton immediately braced for retaliatory violence on their streets. “We expected war,” he said.

The violence that exploded over the next 10 days – three killings and 10 attempted murders, including a shooting that left a 10-year-old girl in critical condition – left Ladd convinced that the information Compton police had received about who shot Shakur had been accurate.

“There was no doubt in my mind that the Southside Crips were responsible, because the Mob Piru had to retaliate, and they had 54 other gangs to choose from, but they went right after the Southside Crips,” Ladd testified.

In response to the violence in Compton, Ladd testified, police “rounded up” a large number of local gang members on both sides of the conflict in October 1996, including Anderson, Davis’s nephew. They also invited the Las Vegas police to interview the arrested men. The alleged gang members were “all the players that we heard about that were involved in the shooting of Tupac Shakur”, with the goal “to try to help Las Vegas PD with their investigation”, Ladd testified. Compton officers also collected a large number of firearms, hoping to find the weapon used to murder Shakur, he said.

While Las Vegas sent two detectives to Compton and they did interview Anderson, nothing came of the interview, Ladd testified.

The trial was not the first time the former Compton detective has spoken publicly about the Shakur case: Ladd went public about his frustrations with how Las Vegas police handled the case in a 2002 Los Angeles Times investigation, saying that Compton police had told Las Vegas police a week after the attack that they believed Anderson was the shooter, but that the Las Vegas police rejected the theory.

When Compton police gave Las Vegas police a chance to interview Anderson and other gang members they believed to be involved in Shakur’s murder, “Las Vegas expressed no interest whatsoever in talking to any of them,” Ladd said in 2002, saying that their interview with Anderson lasted only 20 minutes.

Anderson was publicly identified as a potential suspect in Shakur’s killing less than a month after the shooting, and was widely rumored within Compton to be the one who killed the hip-hop icon. Anderson, his lawyer and his family repeatedly denied he was involved in the killing, but those close to him told the Guardian after his death that the allegations that he shot Shakur shaped his daily life, and that strangers would sometimes recognize him as Shakur’s killer.

In 1997, while Anderson was still alive, Tupac’s mother, Afeni Shakur, filed a civil lawsuit accusing him of murdering her son.

In an audio recording heard in a Las Vegas courtroom 29 years later, Davis described Anderson as the one who fired the shots that killed Shakur.

There were reasons, of course, that Las Vegas police might be skeptical of Compton police, and particularly about information they were sharing about Shakur’s killing.

It wasn’t just that Compton itself had a reputation for political corruption, and that Compton’s police department, battered by scandals and conflicts with the city’s mayor, would soon be disbanded by the city council.

The fact that a former Compton police officer was in charge of security for Death Row Records, and that he had been paid to protect Knight, Shakur and the label’s other artists while they engaged in high-profile gang disputes, concerned Las Vegas detectives because they feared that his father, the head of Compton police’s gang unit, might pass information along to Knight. Knight himself was known for associating with Mob Piru gang members. He would also continue to make headlines for his donations to Compton city officials.

At the trial, Wright Jr himself testified that he had grown up in a Compton neighborhood that was considered Mob Piru territory, had known many gang members since childhood, and that he had already been employed by Knight as the head of security for Death Row Records during “my last year or two of being a police officer”.

As his private security business grew, Wright testified, he would hire off-duty and retired police officers daily to provide security for Death Row Records’ studio and to accompany the label’s artists to events. He had “about ten officers working a day”, he testified.

The testimony of “Mob James” McDonald, a 61-year-old who said he had done security and enforcement for Knight, reinforced just how closely Wright and the officers he employed worked alongside the Mob Piru gang members that surrounded Suge Knight.

“His security did, like, the right thing. My security did what they ain’t going to do. You get what I’m saying?” McDonald testified.

It was two Mob Piru gang members who first told Wright that Shakur had been shot, he testified.

In his memoir, Compton Street Legend, Davis accused Knight, the then Death Row Records executive, as having “police hitmen”, and “crooked ass police on his payroll”, and named Reggie Wright Jr and his father specifically. Wright and his father would later be indicted on federal drug-trafficking and money-laundering charges.

When it came to the Shakur homicide investigation, Las Vegas detectives had feared that Wright’s father, the gang lieutenant, or other Compton officers might pass along information to Knight, or try to protect him, the Los Angeles Times reported in 2002. Compton’s police chief at the time removed Wright Sr from the case and replaced him with another officer to address these worries, the Times reported, but it did not assuage the concerns.

As conspiracy theories flourished in the absence of any official narrative of Shakur’s death, the police, and Reggie Wright Jr himself, were regarded as potential suspects in the star’s death, something Wright denied on the stand this past month.

Testimony in Las Vegas left no doubt that some witnesses to Shakur’s killing did not want to work with law enforcement to convict the hip-hop star’s assailant, and that they preferred to seek street justice instead.

Garry Dale, a former Las Vegas police officer, testified that Shakur himself, lying wounded inside the ambulance, would not identify his shooter when asked, saying only something to the effect of, “No, we’ll take care of it.”

Other witnesses described a fear of being perceived as snitches, and even facing violent retribution, if they cooperated with police or prosecutors. “Mob James” McDonald repeatedly told prosecutors, “You better treat me as a hostile witness”, and refused to answer some questions, saying “Me or anybody else bringing up the dead is wrong.”

But as they investigated the ongoing conflict between the Southside Crips and Mob Piru, law enforcement officers also found themselves caught in their own bureaucratic turf wars.

One of the most outspoken retired officers on the Shakur case is former Los Angeles police detective Greg Kading, who served on the law enforcement taskforce that heard Davis’s 2008 confession to his involvement in Shakur’s killing.

The Los Angeles-based taskforce was originally set up to solve a different murder: the 1997 shooting of Christopher “Biggie Smalls” Wallace, which, like Tupac’s murder, languished for decades without any official resolution.

Wallace’s mother, Voletta, eventually sued the LAPD, alleging that police officers had been involved in the murder. “Desperately trying to cover its ass,” the LAPD set up a multi-agency taskforce to investigate the Wallace murder, Kading wrote in his 2011 memoir, Murder Rap: The Untold Story of the Biggie Smalls & Tupac Shakur Murder Investigations.

In an account that largely mirrors the one Las Vegas prosecutors brought to trial, the book describes how, in a 2008 interview with the taskforce, Davis unexpectedly confessed to his role in Shakur’s murder. The book also alleges a motive and a gunman for Wallace’s murder, which remains officially unsolved. The book ends with Kading’s removal from the taskforce, which eventually shut down without bringing the evidence it had gathered in either hip-hop killing to trial.

“It’s my belief that the LAPD carefully weighed its options and decided that, all things considered, it best suited them to let sleeping dogs lie,” Kading wrote.

It wasn’t that the LAPD wanted to hide the identity of the killers, Kading argued – it was that the specifics of the murder trials in the cases, and the accompanying media coverage, might be messy and difficult for the department’s reputation. In the end, it was more bureaucratic ass-covering, not conspiracy, that stood in the way of justice, he argued. “Rather than manning up to bring these killers to justice, it chose to hedge its bets, letting the investigation die an unnatural death rather than risk the potentially damaging, but ultimately insubstantial, flak that would surely come its way.”

Kading did not testify in the Las Vegas trial. Daryn Dupree, a career Los Angeles police detective who served with Kading on the taskforce, did, and suggested a different motivation for the apparent law enforcement priorities in the case: Davis was a relatively small fish to federal law enforcement officials involved in the taskforce, which had tried, and ultimately failed, to hook a much bigger fish.

After Davis’s initial confession in 2008, the taskforce focused on trying to verify allegations by Davis that Sean “Diddy” Combs, who ran the rival record label Bad Boy Records, had commissioned the hit on Shakur and offered payment, Dupree testified

Despite flying Davis to New York to attempt to verify his link to Combs, the investigators were unable to get the evidence they needed, Dupree said.

The higher-level officials overseeing the Los Angeles taskforce also made the decision to delay sharing intelligence from their investigation with Las Vegas police, Dupree testified. That choice would probably have “led to a lot of frustration” once Las Vegas learned about it, Chutkow, the former federal prosecutor, said.

At the federal level, law enforcement officials on the taskforce were “chasing the money”, and trying to build a racketeering case against both Suge Knight’s Death Row Records, which had signed Shakur, and Combs’s Bad Boy Records, Dupree testified. The FBI, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Drug Enforcement Administration were trying to solidify that both record companies had been originally funded by drug sales.

“I’m from the hood,” Dupree said. “Everybody knows that those record companies were started with narcotics. So the feds were looking at a Rico [a case using the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act]. We cared about the murders.”

In finally bringing Davis to trial for orchestrating Shakur’s murder, Las Vegas prosecutors relied heavily on two fairly old pieces of evidence: Davis’s 2008 confession to the Los Angeles taskforce, and his public description of the shooting in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.

In the end, the only reason the case was solved was “because the defendant implicated himself”, said Shirin Bakhshay, an assistant professor at UCLA law school. “This is not amazing police work that uncovered, after 30 years, the facts of the case. This was a guy who thought he was out of the window of any sort of danger – who didn’t understand the legal implications of what he was doing.”

When Davis was finally arrested and indicted for murder in 2023, Steve Wolfson, the Clark county, Nevada district attorney, told reporters, “In this case, justice has been delayed, but justice won’t be denied.”

But the delay in securing any official justice in Shakur’s murder “festered for a long time”, Armour, the USC law professor said, and a guilty verdict after 30 years “isn’t going to repair America’s deplorable record of racial injustice in the criminal justice system”.

“It will give at least some sense of closure,” he said. “It will put to rest some of the conspiracy theories that have cropped up around this case.”

While Shakur’s killing had acquired an almost mythical status, and the theories around it were sweeping and dramatic, Armour said, the case prosecutors ultimately made in court was not: Shakur was “a 25-year-old artistic genius, who died largely because one group of young men beat another young man in a casino lobby, and the humiliation demanded retribution”.

From Nish Kumar to the Bayeux tapestry: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 05:00:29 GMT

Our premier political comedian heads out on tour, while the 70-metre-long woven story of 1066 arrows its way to Britain for the first time

Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex PassOut now Widely popularised by an episode of Friends in which Ross makes an ass of himself with Isabella Rossellini, the notion of the “celebrity sex pass” completes some sort of cultural loop here as another Friends star, Jennifer Aniston, comes full circle to play a version of herself, the subject of Tom’s (Michael Cassidy) get-out-of-jail lust freebie. A romcom from David Wain (Wet Hot American Summer).

The IncomerOut now This British comedy follows a pair of isolated siblings, Isla (Gayle Rankin) and Sandy (Grant O’Rourke), whose parents disappeared 30 years ago. Having fended for themselves ever since, they aren’t eager to welcome Daniel (Domhnall Gleeson), who has been given the task of relocating them from their remote Scottish island home.

Super NatureOut now Filmed on Super 8mm film via cameras sent to 40 collaborators across 25 countries and five continents, this nature documentary is the brainchild of director Ed Sayers, and edits together footage of all creatures great (including rhinos) and small (snails).

Late FameOut now Willem Dafoe and Greta Lee star in Kent Jones’s adaptation of a posthumously published novella by Austrian modernist author Arthur Schnitzler. Dafoe plays a post office worker and former poet living in downtown Manhattan who is flattered by the attention of a group of wealthy young writers who apparently want to revive his career. Catherine Bray

Hilary Duff6 to 15 September; tour starts Dublin After breaking a decade-long musical hiatus with February’s Top 5 album, Luck … Or Something, the artist formerly known as Lizzie McGuire keeps up the momentum with this arena tour. Probably best to save your voice for 2003 teen-angst classic So Yesterday. Michael Cragg

Melanie MartinezThe O2, London, 11 September; touring to 12 September With the follow-up to March’s alt-pop opus Hades apparently due by the end of the year, the gloriously OTT New York curio brings her head-spinning show to the UK. Expect elaborate set pieces, skin-singeing flames and theatrical, dark-hued anthems. MC

Tête-à-Tête: The Opera festivalThe Cockpit, London, 8 to 20 September It may be annual, but this showcase by the Cornwall-based new opera powerhouse is always one of a kind. This year’s crop of novelties features Orpheus and Mary, Queen of Scots, folk horror, morris dancing and Old Norse: a typically colourful retort to anyone who thinks that opera is dead. Flora Willson

Emma RawiczLondon, 5 September; Manchester, 9 September; Gateshead, 10 September The whirlwind evolution of UK sax original Emma Rawicz since her 2022 debut album at 19 now finds her leading her own exciting orchestra, working with A-list players, and gigging all over Europe. She brings the big band to Ronnie Scott’s (5 September), then follows that up with shows with her fusion-angled Inkyra quintet. John Fordham

Monika SosnowskaSouth London Gallery, London, 10 September to 22 November Ultra-minimal installation and half-tonne hanging sculptures all about architecture and its impact on everyday life by this Polish artist, who uses a whole raft of industrial materials to look at the legacies of modernism and communism.

The Bayeux TapestryThe British Museum, London, 10 September to 11 JulyThe world-famous Bayeux tapestry is finally making its long-awaited journey back to England for the most hyped, hotly anticipated and sure-to-sell-out blockbuster exhibition in a decade.

A Mughal SongbookThe Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge, 8 September to 7 MarchA fascinating, colourful, melodious look at the ornate pages of the Plowden songbook, a rare manuscript of songs from the Mughal empire, which ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from 1526 to 1857.

Tschabalala SelfTrafalgar Square’s fourth plinth, London, from 10 September We’ve had a big thumb, a giant ship in a bottle and a huge dollop of cream; now the fourth plinth is going to be home to something more traditional for public sculpture: an enormous human figure, striding positively forwards in a blue dress, by American artist Tschabalala Self. Eddy Frankel

Scottish Ballet: EmergenceTheatre Royal, Glasgow, 10 to 12 September; touring to 3 October A visually arresting ballet by Crystal Pite is the main draw here. Pite’s Emergence, from 2009, uses the impact of the corps de ballet en masse to great effect. There’s also a premiere from Julia Cheng, award-winning choreographer of Cabaret and Fiddler on the Roof. Lyndsey Winship

Nish Kumar9 September to 27 November; tour starts Belfast Impassioned but never pious, righteous but never smug, Kumar’s ability to temper strident takes with goofy likability means he’s fast becoming our premier progressive political comedian. New show Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy sees the 41-year-old mine laughs from the threat of autocracy and the ageing process. Rachel Aroesti

Bloodsport: After Helen of TroyTheatre Royal Stratford East, London, to 10 October Brilliant new(ish) playwright Ava Pickett (1536) imagines what might have happened when Helen returned home from Troy, after a war fought in her name. Starring Michelle Dockery and Laura Aikman. Miriam Gillinson

Tartuffe (Remixed)Marylebone theatre, London, to 24 October Mark Rylance stars alongside an ensemble of Intermission Youth graduates in Darren Raymond’s modern take on Molière’s classic comedy – which sees, in this case, a Nigerian-Jamaican family’s wedding plans blown apart by the arrival of a mysterious guest. MG

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Last SeenApple TV, 9 September In what is quite the career gear change, Colin from Accounts star Patrick Brammall sloughs off his warm and fuzzy romcom associations to lead this chilling drama with Maxine Peake about a police dispatcher convinced he’s answered a call from his daughter, abducted a decade earlier.

The PaperSky One & Now, 10 September, 9pm Season one of this feelgood and impeccably performed US Office-universe comedy saw ambitious editor Ned (Domhnall Gleeson again) take the Toledo Truth Teller from depressing clickbait factory to award-winning bastion of actual journalism. Now he’s searching for a showstopping scoop to cement his reputation.

Britain’s Forgotten GirlsBBC Two & iPlayer, 9 September, 9pm Alessia Camoirano Bruges’s 2022 film about the Italian mafia’s recruitment of young teenagers via social media was nominated for an Emmy; now the documentarian turns her attention to the vulnerable children abused and trafficked by drug-dealing gangs in the UK, and asks why the authorities have done so little to help.

The Drop: A Snowfall SagaDisney+, 9 SeptemberThis spin-off from the critically acclaimed Damson Idris series Snowfall shifts focus from LA’s 1980s crack epidemic to the following decade’s west coast hip-hop scene. Gail Bean’s Wanda is now clean and ready to capitalise on rap’s thrilling rise – something that requires a savvy navigation of street politics and nerves of steel. RA

Halloween: The GamePC, PS5, Xbox; out 8 September Play as a hapless teenager or take on the role of masked psychopath Michael Myers in this multiplayer gorefest set during the original film’s timeline. It looks like an absolute scream.

ValheimPC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox; out 9 September The acclaimed Viking-inspired survival adventure is finally getting a full release after several years in “early access”. Survive in a hostile purgatory with up to nine pals as you conquer beasts, gather resources and, of course, build pretty houses. Keith Stuart

Kasabian – Act IIIOut now Flamboyant rock wizard Serge Pizzorno and his band of merry men are back with their ninth album. Co-produced by Mark Ralph (Years & Years, Clean Bandit), Act III mixes bright pop moments (Superpowers) with more noodly new wave songs such as the festival-ready Great Pretender.

Natalie Imbruglia – Algorithm Out now Pop’s other Ramsay Street resident turned singer returns with this seventh album. The follow-up to 2021’s Firebird tackles Imbruglia’s ADHD and OCD diagnoses, and features the peppy soft-rock of single Upside Down, plus the Robyn-esque electropop bop, Just Drive.

Mykki Blanco – Cafe ParadisoOut now Inspired by a life lived in transit, and influenced by New York, Paris and Tangier (where the American rapper and performance artist is now based), Cafe Paradiso is billed as a record for “artsy kids”. They should find a lot to love in the scuzzy art-rock of Butt Sex.

Adéla – PrimaOut now With the Bangerz-esque current single Ain’t in LA all over TikTok, the Slovak alt-pop experimentalist releases her long-awaited debut album. As you’d imagine for someone who auditioned to be in girl band Katseye, pop runs through Adéla’s veins, as shown on the bratty KGB and Red Bottoms’ sultry midtempo catharsis. MC

What Music Looks Like Podcast Writer Paul Weedon explores how artful design can enhance music, speaking to artists such as Adam Smith on his immersive stage visuals for the Chemical Brothers and Laura LiPuma on her 1980s work with Prince.

InCinematicYouTube Video essayist InCinematic presents fascinating and often niche takes on the efficacy of different creative techniques in cinema. A recent highlight explores Leslie Nielsen’s deadpan delivery in Airplane! and the experimentalism of The Lion King.

Hamza: African Birds of PreyBBC iPlayer Wildlife cameraman Hamza Yassin takes his infectious enthusiasm for nature to Kenya in this beautiful film where he goes in search of some of Africa’s most threatened birds of prey, such as the crowned eagle. Ammar Kalia

Five Great Reads: After the flood, leaving Maga, and sex doll ethics

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 22:17:54 GMT

Guardian Australia’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

This week, we have selected stories that will move you. A dispatch from a disaster zone, where rescue teams are sifting through scattered, buried remnants, a feature about walking away from a community that once welcomed you, and a piece on running just to see how far you can go.

Enjoy.

In the aftermath of the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, thousands remain missing and access to aid remains hindered by treacherous conditions. On the ground in some of the worst-hit areas, our south Asia correspondent, Hannah Ellis-Petersen, and journalist Gaurav Pokharel write that while the scale of the damage caused by the flood is unfathomable, so too is the human suffering as communities almost wiped out of existence reckon with what comes next. Notable quote: “Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”

Scattered fragments: The ruins of the lives of thousands are now buried in and among the debris. “Kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses” remind rescue teams of the hundreds still missing.

How long will it take to read: Three-and-a-half minutes.

Further reading: Trapped workers could still be alive, families hope DNA can be used to find their loved ones, and desperate relatives of the missing fear attention is already drifting away from the ongoing crisis.

Donald Trump and his “Make America Great Again” (Maga) base of supporters have come to dominate American politics. For many Trump followers, the movement built on lies and conspiracy theories offered a shared identity. For others, it became something closer to religion. But after more than 10 years, some devotees are finally walking away, making amends, and offering support to others who are reckoning with their role in Trump’s America.

What drew people into the Maga “cult” and why did they leave? Rich Logis found a second family in the Maga community. He found belonging, camaraderie and a common enemy. But after the politicians he lionised platformed Covid anti-vaxxers he started to diversify his news sources. Logis slowly began to realise that what he believed was false and he had been “complicit in dividing this country”.

Notable quote: “My loyalty wasn’t to Trump. My loyalty was to God and the church.”

How long will it take to read: Four-and-a-half minutes to read, and less than one minute to share with a friend who has fallen down a rabbit hole.

Further reading: You can learn more about Life after Maga, and how the non-profit Leaving Maga is fighting Trumpism like a disease.

Mary Austin was the quiet girlfriend of rock band Queen’s flamboyant figurehead. They dreamed of marriage until they both finally spoke the unspoken. Thirty-five years after his death, Austin’s new book lays out Mercury’s life in lyrics.

‘No, Freddie, I think you’re gay’: Austin and Mercury had been living together for four years when they both realised Mercury was only attracted to men. But rather than destroying their relationship, Austin says the revelation felt like a relief. They continued living together for the next 18 months and, as Queen and Mercury became a global phenomenon, Mary and Freddie became better friends.

Mercurial money: Austin has inherited half of Mercury’s estate (now estimated at about £150m). Asked where the money will go when she dies and if much of it will go to charity, she said, “It’s going to go to my children.”

How long will it take to read: Just over 13 minutes. Enough time to listen to Bohemian Rhapsody two times through.

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Further reading: Check out Freddie Mercury’s “splendid things”, or pick up a copy of Mary Austin’s book from the Guardian Bookshop.

On a quiet country road south of Sydney, two distressed citizens stumbled across what they assumed was the mangled corpse of a woman stuffed into a suitcase. But the woman was not a woman at all and, after forensic analysis revealed it was a sex doll, questions about the booming sex doll industry have garnered global attention.

A flourishing trade: Estimates show that the global sex doll market is valued at more than US$6bn. But as the industry grows, Madison Griffiths asks, does it matter how these dolls get treated?How much? Lifelike sex dolls are now increasingly customisable and you can walk away with one for about US$1,790. But Caitlin Roper, the Australian author of Sex Dolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, calls these kinds of dolls “replica female sex slaves”. How long will it take to read: Just under four minutes. Further reading: The rise of “sex robots”, how police mistook a sex doll for a “body”, and what can we learn about male desire in a sex doll factory?

In a remarkable feat of physical and mental endurance, the Australian endurance athlete Phil Gore ran 6.71km every hour for an entire week just to see how far he could push himself.

Finding your limit: Having already set the world record in 2025, Gore knew he had “a lot more left to give”. But the rules of backyard ultra running require the final runner to stop one lap after the second-place runner drops out – limiting the potential boundaries of the winner. Gore wanted a challenge that would push him further. This time around, competing only against his own body and mind, Gore says, “that’s what I’ve done. Maybe [there is] a little bit of disappointment that I wanted my limit to be a bit further away.”

Fuel fit for a champion: Running for a week straight requires calories. A steady stream of “speckled snakes and Nerd clusters, jelly cups, custard pouches, simple sugars like that” kept Gore going for days.

How long will it take to read: Just over two minutes.

Further reading: What happens when you don’t finish a race, and why would anyone run an ultramarathon anyway?
