Premier League, Italian GP, WSL and US Open tennis – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 14:43:02 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

After the off-field fun of the transfer window the Premier League returns – and it is also the opening weekend of the Women’s Super League. David Tindall and Tom Bassam bring you all the buildup and breaking news. Join our Matchday live community by sending your thoughts and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

It’s day four of a rain-affected round of County Championship fixtures as the season enters its final month. Tanya Aldred will bring you all the action from around the grounds.

Matthias Jaissle’s Newcastle have taken four points from what should have been a tricky opening pair of fixtures, against Newcastle and Tottenham, so will be confident of a victory that would take them temporarily top of the table. Bournemouth are yet to win and are cursing their inability to see out games, having conceded a 92nd-minute winner against Manchester City and a 91st-minute equaliser against Everton. David Tindall is on liveblog duty, Louise Taylor reports from St James’ Park.

There are five 3pm Premier League kick-offs for Rob Smyth to keep his eye on in the blog. Brentford face Sunderland, Brighton welcome Leeds to the south coast, Fulham and Crystal Palace meet in a London derby, Manchester City take on Coventry in a battle of the Sky Blues and winless Tottenham travel to the City Ground to face Nottingham Forest. And we’ll have live updates from the Championship, Bundesliga and beyond.

Philip Cornwall is at the wheel as F1 screeches on to the track at Monza, where Max Verstappen has won three of the last four editions of the Italian GP. His Red Bull doesn’t look quick enough to challenge this time around however, and Lando Norris in the McLaren has taken the last two poles of the 2026 season, breaking the Mercedes stranglehold at the front of the grid. Giles Richards reports from the track.

The third round continues at Flushing Meadows, where plenty of big names are in action in the women’s singles – Elena Rybakina, Naomi Osaka, Coco Gauff and Iga Swiatek all continue their campaigns on a bumper Saturday. Katy Murrells brings you all the action on the blog, while Tumaini Carayol reports from New York.

The Greatest Rivalry series has done a decent job of living up to its name thus far with the Springboks taking the opener and the All Blacks levelling things up at Ellis Park last weekend. Now for the third Test. Daniel Gallan helms the blog and Gerard Meagher reports.

One of these teams have won two out of two in the league, without having conceded a goal. The other have lost two out of two and are yet to score. And it’s not the way round you would have expected at the start of August. Billy Munday is on the blog to see if Villa can break their duck, while Ross Heppenstall reports from an MKM Stadium that is sure to be rocking for the undefeated hosts.

John Brewin is on hand to review Saturday’s action and preview Sunday’s games in the Premier League, WSL and beyond. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your notions and queries.

England have dominated the series thus far, cruising to back-to-back six-wicket victories to clinch the series with a game to spare. Can they make it a clean sweep on Sunday? Tanya Aldred and James Wallace are on over-by-over duty, while Raf Nicholson reports from Worcester.

Kimi Antonelli arrives at his home grand prix at the top of the drivers’ championship and hoping to end a long drought for the home fans at Monza – no Italian has won the Italian Grand Prix since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966. Michael Butler provides lap-by-lap coverage on the blog, while Giles Richards is at the track.

It’s a new season in the WSL and last season’s runners-up, Arsenal, will be hoping to get off to a winning start after improving their squad with some star signings. They travel to Broadfield Stadium to take on Brighton, who are still reeling after the departure of head coach Dario Vidosic this week. He has been hastily replaced by Arturo Ruiz, who led Real Sociedad into the qualifying stage of the Women’s Champions League. Rob Bleaney will bring you live updates.

Deadline day was a tough one for Everton, who failed to land the striker they so badly need. David Moyes’s side are unbeaten in their first two Premier League games, however, and might fancy their chances against a United side still finding their feet. Tim de Lisle helms our liveblog, while Andy Hunter and Will Unwin will be at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The final major of the year reaches the fourth-round stage (or the last 16 if you prefer). Seven Americans made the last 32 in the men’s singles – can any of them push into the latter stages at a tournament that has not had a US winner in the men’s singles since Andy Roddick in 2003? Daniel Harris is in the liveblog hotseat and Tumaini Carayol reports from Flushing Meadows.

Perhaps the game of the weekend in the Premier League, with Xabi Alonso’s new-look Chelsea taking on Mikel Arteta’s not-much-changed Arsenal. Both sides have won two out of two in the league so far, so something will have to give. Rob Smyth is on liveblog duty, while David Hytner, Jacob Steinberg and Barney Ronay are all at the Emirates for reports, reaction and analysis.

Inside the Battle to Save One Pioneering General From Hegseth’s Purge

The New York Times September 06, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Gen. Christopher T. Donahue’s vision for fighting future wars won him powerful supporters around the world. Could they save his career?

By Adam Entous and Greg Jaffe

Reporting from Washington

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth decided in early 2025 to spike Gen. Christopher T. Donahue’s nomination to be the top U. S. military officer in Europe.

Mr. Hegseth believed that President Trump wanted heads to roll for the deaths of 13 U. S. service members in a suicide bombing at the Kabul airport during the U. S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021. General Donahue was not responsible for security at the bombing site. But he was a top commander at the airport, and so Mr. Hegseth decided he needed to go.

It fell to Joe Kasper, Mr. Hegseth’s chief of staff, to try to convince him that he was wrong.

Mr. Kasper asked a senior Pentagon official to prepare a card with a half-dozen bullet points laying out the facts in General Donahue’s defense, current and former officials said. He took it with him in March of last year as he and Mr. Hegseth sped through traffic to the White House for a press event.

For those few minutes in the car, Mr. Kasper knew he would have his boss’s undivided attention.

Sirens were blaring. He handed Mr. Hegseth the card.

These were the facts of General Donahue’s three-decade career: He had seen more combat in his 20-plus deployments than just about any officer in the U. S. military. A star in the clandestine world of special forces, he had spent years in the shadows hunting terrorist leaders. And then as the world and warfare changed, he changed with it.

He had played a central role in the U. S. military’s efforts to help Ukraine hold off a much larger Russian force, a job that inspired his vision for a new kind of combat that married divebombing drones, robotics and artificial intelligence.

Now his fate lay in the hands of Mr. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who had two deployments as an Army officer to Iraq and Afghanistan. Mr. Hegseth had come to the Pentagon vowing to weed out the “small” and “feeble” generals who he believed had failed in those wars.

What played out in the 16 months after the car ride was a clash between Mr. Hegseth and General Donahue’s supporters, who viewed him as a generational talent.

That clash, and its outcome, was described to The New York Times by more than 40 people at the Pentagon, in Congress and around the world, nearly all of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retribution.

It amounts to one of the most consequential chapters in Mr. Hegseth’s campaign to drive out those he sees as out of step with his priorities, a leadership purge that his critics say is driven by ideology, identity and suspicion of those with tenuous ties to former military leaders that he does not like. And it shows the intensity of the behind-the-scenes battle to save one general.

The more General Donahue’s allies pushed, the more Mr. Hegseth’s opposition seemed to harden.

The Pentagon declined to answer questions about General Donahue, saying in a statement that all senior military leaders serve at the pleasure of the president and the defense secretary.

In the spring of 2025, General Donahue was commanding ground forces in Europe. Mr. Hegseth was new to the Pentagon. To the extent he was familiar with General Donahue, it was largely through the prism of the Afghanistan withdrawal and a grainy photo that indelibly linked the general to the war’s tragic end.

General Donahue was the last U. S. soldier to leave Afghanistan. As he stepped onto a hulking military cargo plane, an Army photographer snapped his picture using his cellphone camera and night vision device.

The green-and-black image rocketed around the world. Senior Pentagon officials said Mr. Hegseth seemed to be fixated on the photo, mistakenly referring to it as a “selfie.”

The first item on the card that Mr. Kasper handed to Mr. Hegseth in the car clarified that the photo was not a selfie and that General Donahue had nothing to do with its distribution. Other bullet points noted that Marines, not General Donahue’s paratroopers, were in charge of the gate where the suicide bombing occurred.

The defense secretary glanced at the card and passed it back to his chief of staff.

“I don’t care,” Mr. Hegseth told Mr. Kasper.

At first, General Donahue wasn’t supposed to go to Afghanistan for the withdrawal. The Pentagon said it just needed roughly 2,000 of his paratroopers from the 82nd Airborne Division to help with security at the Kabul airport.

Then, on Aug. 16, 2021, shortly after the paratroopers started arriving, thousands of Afghans, desperate to escape Taliban insurgents, swarmed the runways, preventing planes from taking off and landing.

General Donahue’s paratroopers watched in horror as Afghan special operations units, who were waiting to be evacuated, beat back the civilians so that flights could resume.

Amid the chaos, General Donahue got new orders: Get to Kabul as fast as possible.

Three decades had passed since General Donahue graduated from West Point. He was in his mid-20s when his leadership skills and football player’s build caught the eye of a senior officer in Delta Force, the Army’s elite counterterrorism unit.

He survived the selection process and disappeared into a world of secrecy and fake personas. Deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria and other hot spots followed as he rose to become Delta’s top commander.

The skill that often set General Donahue apart from his peers on those battlefields was his ability to win the trust of local partners. It had been on display in Afghanistan in May 2019 when he began leading special operations forces in the country and won over his Afghan counterpart, Brig. Gen. Sami Sadat.

Together, they leveraged airstrikes, special operations advisers and commandos to punish Taliban insurgents and retake territory that had been lost. “We didn’t feel like we cracked the code; we did crack the code,” General Sadat said.

But their battlefield gains were fleeting. In February 2020, Mr. Trump cut a deal with the Taliban to curtail U. S. military support to Afghan forces and begin the American withdrawal.

General Sadat remembered sitting by General Donahue’s side in their command post watching a drone feed as the Taliban rolled over an Afghan unit. “He was very angry, frustrated and ashamed,” General Sadat said.

Eighteen months later, the Afghan president had fled the country and the government had collapsed. General Sadat reconnected with General Donahue, who was already on his way back to Afghanistan, and told him that his Afghan forces had dissolved.

“Brother, we need your help,” General Sadat recalled telling him.

General Donahue landed in Kabul on Aug. 17.

Around 2 a. m., he met with Qari Hamdullah Mokhlis, a Taliban commander whom General Donahue’s commandos had been trying to find and kill as recently as 2020. The general’s former target was now his partner.

“You don’t like me; I don’t like you,” General Donahue’s paratroopers recalled his telling the Taliban commander. “But we’re going to have to work together.”

The biggest threat to both was the Islamic State terror group, which was determined to turn the withdrawal into a blood bath, according to U. S. intelligence. The U. S. military would control the airport and its entry gates. U. S. commanders wanted the Taliban, who had set up checkpoints outside the airport, to let American citizens and allies pass through, and keep out would-be suicide bombers.

General Donahue’s paratroopers began preparing for a major attack. They cleared the roads leading to the airport’s field hospital so they would be able to rush wounded to get care.

The intelligence identified Abbey Gate, a major airport entry point controlled by the Marines, as the most likely target. The Marines were planning to leave and turn over control of the site to General Donahue’s troops.

On Aug. 24, General Donahue visited the gate and saw thousands of desperate Afghans crowding the Marines who were trying to maintain order and screen them.

The chaos and proximity between the Afghans and the Marines made it an ideal target for a suicide bomber, General Donahue told his paratroopers.

The plan was for General Donahue’s paratroopers to take control of Abbey Gate from the Marines on Aug. 27 and shut it down. But General Donahue thought it was too risky to wait. He met with the senior U. S. commander at the airport and recommended shutting the gate immediately.

British forces, which were using the entryway to evacuate their citizens and allies, asked the Americans to keep it open. Pentagon leaders “grudgingly” agreed, a senior U. S. official recalled.

The Marines were still in control of Abbey Gate at 5:48 p. m. on Aug. 26 when the suicide bomber struck. Eleven Marines, one Navy medic and one Army soldier, along with scores of Afghans, were killed.

General Donahue could hear and feel the blast at his headquarters on the other side of the runway. “I need to know the numbers and types of casualties,” he told his staff. The situation was so dire that medics began pumping blood from healthy soldiers into the veins of the wounded.

On Aug. 30, America’s longest war came to a bitter end. General Donahue took a parting glimpse at the Kabul airport and then hurried onto the big, gray plane. It was the last one out and, in keeping with Army tradition, he was the final soldier to board. The Army photographer captured the moment at 11:46 p. m. using his iPhone and the night vision monocle attached to his helmet. When the plane landed in Qatar, General Donahue called his wife.

His paratroopers overheard the conversation.

“We’re out,” he said.

“I know,” she said.

“How did you know?” he asked.

“Everybody knows,” she said.

She sent him the photo, which was now posted on news sites around the world. General Donahue, taken aback, showed the photo to members of his team. He had spent most of his career in the shadows. Now he was everywhere.

“This is not good,” he said.

On the 2024 campaign trail, Mr. Trump blasted the Biden administration for the withdrawal and the Abbey Gate deaths, calling the episode “the most embarrassing moment in the history of the United States.” He wondered why no generals had been fired for it.

He did not mention the deal he had cut with the Taliban that set the collapse in motion.

The withdrawal first became a career-threatening problem for General Donahue in November 2024. Markwayne Mullin, then a Republican senator from Oklahoma, put a hold on his nomination to lead U. S. ground forces in Europe, effectively blocking him from taking the job.

The hold set off a scramble among senior Army officials, members of the special operations community and some of General Donahue’s supporters in Congress. Mr. Mullin, after meeting with General Donahue, relented.

For General Donahue, it would prove to be a fleeting victory. His career and vision would soon collide with Mr. Hegseth, who resigned from the Army after being singled out for tattoos that the service deemed extremist. “The military I loved, I fought for, I revered spit me out,” Mr. Hegseth wrote in a 2024 book.

Mr. Hegseth went on to blame the Army’s generals, whose ranks he believed were “bloated.” It was time, he wrote, to “clean house.”

Before he was confirmed as defense secretary, Mr. Hegseth met with Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort and emerged from their talk believing the president-elect shared his vision.

“He wants fewer generals!” Mr. Hegseth told aides.

General Donahue, in his 50s and one of the military’s youngest four-star generals, seemed to be on the ascent. Three years earlier, he created a new headquarters to funnel intelligence, technology, planning and strategy to the Ukrainians.

It worked, and the Ukrainians retook large swaths of their territory. But in the years that followed, the U. S. military and its NATO partners couldn’t provide the Ukrainians with enough shells and missiles, so the undermanned Ukrainians improvised. They replaced scarce and costly shells and missiles with cheap drones.

General Donahue and like-minded military leaders were convinced that U. S. support to the Ukrainians was a worthwhile investment: It was bleeding the Russians and preparing the U. S. military for future wars.

Mr. Trump and Mr. Hegseth did not see it that way. They spoke of curtailing U. S. support and forcing Kyiv to cut a deal with Moscow.

In February 2025, Mr. Hegseth traveled to Europe. The trip began with a tense conversation with Gen. Christopher G. Cavoli, General Donahue’s boss who, as the head of European Command, led all U. S. and NATO forces on the continent. General Cavoli, who was retiring that summer, told Mr. Hegseth that he would soon need to choose his replacement.

The front-runner for the job was General Donahue, who was standing by with his troops in Poland. It was Mr. Hegseth’s last stop. The meeting — their first and only — was brief and positive.

In Washington, Mr. Hegseth received a binder with candidates’ photos and bios. General Dan Caine, the incoming chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, had scribbled an effusive endorsement with a black Sharpie next to General Donahue’s picture, the officials said. The two officers had worked together earlier in their careers.

Mr. Hegseth initially agreed that General Donahue would take over European Command. But Mr. Hegseth later told his staff that Mr. Trump wanted punishment for the deaths at Abbey Gate.

After Mr. Kasper’s failed attempt in the car to salvage General Donahue’s nomination, the chief of staff met General Donahue in his office.

The top job at European Command was now off the table, Mr. Kasper explained. General Donahue looked dejected. But he still had his Army post and a purpose, which he described to a former colleague.

The headquarters he established in Germany in 2022 to aid the Ukrainians should serve as “the laboratory where we test new ideas and capabilities and then rapidly share them across the force,” he said.

He saw the war as a historic opportunity, the colleague recalled. In the waning days of its defeat in Vietnam, the Army had sent a general to the Middle East to study how the outnumbered but innovative Israelis defeated Arab armies in the 1973 Yom Kippur War. That general’s report had transformed the Army.

“This should be our new model,” General Donahue told the former colleague.

He began to turn his vision into a detailed plan using a dry-erase board, officers recalled. His command would take Ukrainian advances in cheap, mass produced drones and drone interceptors, and build on them with new tactics and high-tech systems unique to the U. S. military, like precision-guided missiles, Patriot batteries and intelligence from satellites. All of this would be plugged into an artificial intelligence-enabled command and control system that would identify and track thousands of potential enemy targets in real time.

The system would then be shared across NATO to defend against Russia but could be replicated in the Pacific and elsewhere. The officers in the room initially called it “the Global Killing Machine.” Its proper name became the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.

He pitched the plan to Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll over beers at a bowling alley at his base in Germany, said Pentagon officials.

Mr. Driscoll was taken with it.

Gen. Randy George, the Army’s chief of staff, was going to retire in the summer of 2027. Now that the European Command job was off the table, General George, Mr. Kasper and Mr. Driscoll cooked up a new idea. General Donahue could take over for General George when he stepped down.

The Army chief of staff job would allow General Donahue to bring the vision he had sketched out in Europe to the entire force.

But Mr. Hegseth had other plans. He wanted to nominate General Christopher LaNeve, his senior military adviser, to the chief of staff post.

Mr. Driscoll had a strained relationship with Mr. Hegseth. He tried to advance his preferred candidate by arranging a meeting between Vice President JD Vance, his close friend and Yale Law School classmate, and General Donahue, officials said.

Mr. Vance might be willing to push Mr. Trump to overrule Mr. Hegseth, Mr. Driscoll reasoned.

But Mr. Hegseth learned of the meeting and blocked it, officials said.

Mr. Hegseth had set in motion a plan to reduce General Donahue’s job in Europe from a four-star to a three-star position this summer. The move was in line with the Trump administration’s policy of shifting the military’s focus from Europe to Asia. For Mr. Hegseth, it also had the benefit of forcing General Donahue to retire, if he did not get another four-star position.

In late February, the drone threat that General Donahue had been preparing for in Europe became a deadly reality for U. S. forces in the Middle East.

Mr. Trump had launched an extensive attack on Iran, and Iran responded with volleys of Shaheed drones, similar to those used by the Russians. U. S. troops were not ready.

One attack struck a U. S. Army base in Kuwait, killing six soldiers.

Overnight, the Pentagon sent frantic messages to commanders around the world, desperate for drone interceptors.

General Donahue had already distributed the command’s stock to NATO partners. But he knew someone who had more of them: Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi, the commander in chief of Ukrainian forces.

They had grown close over the previous four years in frequent secure video conference calls that began with the same salutation — “my friend” or “my brother” — and ended with General Donahue saying, “What else can I do for Ukraine?” the Ukrainian general recalled.

“Afterward, he would genuinely try to do something,” General Syrskyi said.

Now the situation was reversed. The U. S. military was the one needing help. General Donahue asked General Syrskyi for drone interceptors and Ukrainian officers with experience using them in battle. They would join their Europe-based American counterparts and teach troops in the Middle East how to defend themselves.

“I called the president of Ukraine, explained the situation, and told him that I believed providing this assistance was the right thing to do and that it would not compromise Ukraine’s defense,” General Syrskyi said.

As this was happening in early March, General George called General Donahue to tell him to put in his retirement papers. Mr. Hegseth wanted him out.

General George said he would try to convince Mr. Hegseth to extend General Donahue’s command six months until December 2026. The Army chief asked for 30 minutes with Mr. Hegseth to discuss General Donahue and other issues, but Mr. Hegseth kept postponing the meeting.

On April 1, Mr. Hegseth fired General George in a phone call that lasted 15 seconds, officials said.

General George could no longer help him. There was now one last slim hope for General Donahue: his supporters in the Senate. They were frustrated by Mr. Hegseth’s lack of transparency, and they valued senior officers like General Donahue for their frank assessments.

One of General Donahue’s supporters was Senator Tim Sheehy, a former Navy SEAL and Republican of Montana. Mr. Sheehy’s combat record and pro-Trump reputation gave him extra credibility with Mr. Hegseth. He had succeeded in persuading Mr. Hegseth to drop his objections to a handful of senior officers, particularly those Mr. Sheehy had served with in combat.

But his efforts to save General Donahue were going nowhere.

In a meeting with Mr. Sheehy, General Caine explained why: The senators’ campaign was only causing Mr. Hegseth’s opposition to grow, reinforcing his perception that General Donahue was too powerful, independent and connected.

A spokesperson for the chairman disputed that he used those words to describe Mr. Hegseth’s perception of General Donahue.

Mr. Sheehy stopped pushing.

Senator Joni Ernst, an Iowa Republican who had deployed to Iraq and served 22 years in the National Guard, had been General Donahue’s most insistent champion. She continued to look for a way to help him.

She believed Mr. Hegseth had promised her that he would allow General George, a fellow Iowan, to finish his full term. And she felt betrayed when Mr. Hegseth fired him.

Now she was determined to block Mr. Hegseth’s choice to lead the Army. Instead of General LaNeve, she suggested three alternatives to the White House. Her top choice was General Donahue.

But a senior White House official told her that Mr. Hegseth would never nominate General Donahue for the job.

With less than a month left in General Donahue’s career, Ms. Ernst asked him if he would be interested in taking over the four-star command in Austin, Texas, focused on transforming the Army.

It would give him a new platform to spread the vision that he had made a reality in Europe. But he had a big concern.

“Do you honestly think Secretary Hegseth would work with me if I was there?” General Donahue asked, according to a congressional official familiar with the exchange.

“Honestly, no,” Ms. Ernst replied.

General Donahue retired on Aug. 27, surrounded by people he had fought alongside.

We have been covering Pete Hegseth's purge of senior military officers for much of this year. But something about Pete Hegseth's effort to force out General Donahue seemed different and revelatory. Donahue was widely known as one of the Army's best battlefield leaders and seemed to embody everything Hegseth said he wanted in a general. He had many supporters in Washington and around the world. So why did the effort to save him fail? We spent the last few months digging into this question.

Adam Entous is a Washington-based investigative reporter for The Times, focused on national security and intelligence matters.

Greg Jaffe covers the Pentagon and the U. S. military for The Times.

A Transplanted Pig Kidney Is Still Working After a Record-Setting 9 Months in a Patient

Wired September 03, 2026

A woman has lived with a pig kidney for more than nine months without needing dialysis, a record-setting achievement.

The woman underwent the operation at Massachusetts General Hospital on November 22 last year. As of Thursday, the kidney has been functioning for 285 days, according to Cambridge, Massachusetts-based eGenesis, the biotech company that used Crispr gene editing to make the organ fit for human transplantation. Previously, the record for a person living with a transplanted pig kidney was 271 days, set by Tim Andrews.

Most people in need of a kidney transplant wait three to five years on average to receive one, though it can take longer depending on blood type and other factors. While they wait, patients often need dialysis, in which a person’s blood vessels are hooked up to a machine that removes excess fluid and waste from the bloodstream. Dialysis typically requires four-hour sessions three times a week and can damage blood vessels over time, making the procedure hard on the body.

Pig kidneys could offer an alternative until a human organ is available. Pig organs are similar in size and function to human organs and are being investigated as a way to ease the shortage of human donor organs. To make them more suitable for humans, scientists are genetically editing them to prevent immediate rejection and reduce the risk of pig viruses being passed on to transplant patients.

Patients' health gets worse the longer they're on dialysis, “and their odds of getting a human transplant aren't rising fast enough to meet their declining health,” says Mike Curtis, CEO of eGenesis. The company used Crispr to remove certain pig genes that could cause an immune response and add a handful of human genes.

“What we saw with Mr. Andrews was a radical improvement in his overall health while he was on the pig kidney versus if he had stayed on chronic dialysis,” Curtis says.

The woman who has crossed the nine-month mark is the fifth person to receive an eGenesis kidney through a special regulatory pathway known as expanded access. The Food and Drug Administration allows patients with serious or life-threatening conditions to gain access to experimental treatments when there are no good alternatives.

Andrews’ case shows that pig kidneys may provide a temporary solution. He received a pig kidney in January 2025 and had it removed in October last year after a period of decreasing kidney function. He returned to dialysis but received a human kidney transplant in January this year. A second person has also successfully received a human transplant after having a pig kidney for eight months, according to eGenesis.

Curtis says the company is learning more with each transplant. In a paper published on Thursday in The Lancet medical journal, the surgical team that performed the transplants details Andrews’ experience. They determined that Andrews’ pig kidney eventually failed due to thrombotic microangiopathy, which means tiny blood clots formed in the transplanted organ.

The team is using that information to adjust the immunosuppressant medications that pig kidney recipients receive and how frequently they need to take those drugs. People who receive human organ transplants also need to take immunosuppressive drugs to prevent their body from rejecting the transplanted organ. Organ rejection can happen at any time following a transplant, ranging from minutes after the surgery to many years later.

Kidneys are the most-needed organ, with more than 95,000 people waiting to receive one in the US. But due to a shortage of donor organs, fewer than 28,000 kidney transplants were performed in the US in 2025.

The FDA has given eGenesis the green light to conduct a more formal trial in up to 33 patients with kidney failure who are between 50 and 70 years old and on the wait list for a human kidney. That trial will not happen until 2027, but eGenesis plans to perform additional transplants under the expanded access pathway in the meantime. Their next goal is to get a transplanted pig kidney to function for a year.

Nobody Is Saying Why OpenAI and Anthropic Had Outages Today

Wired September 03, 2026

Frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI all experienced rare outages on Thursday morning, creating downtime for their corresponding AI chatbots. SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, said on Thursday afternoon that the issues with Grok resulted from “an outage at our Memphis compute center this morning.”

The issues initially appeared to be linked because they coincided—perhaps the result of a shared third-party service provider—but neither OpenAI nor Anthropic cited an external source in comments to WIRED on Thursday. SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. But the company said as part of its public comments on Thursday: “We’d also like to apologize to our impacted compute partners.” Anthropic and xAI announced a “compute partnership” with SpaceX in May.

OpenAI spokesperson Kathleen Chaykowski tells WIRED: “A routing error starting around 7:43 am PT on Thursday, September 3, made ChatGPT and Codex unavailable for some users across platforms. As of about 8:17 am PT on Thursday, a solution was successfully implemented and is continuing to be monitored.”

Anthropic declined to comment on the episode. The company began alerting about a “partial outage” at 6:23 am PT on Thursday that involved “elevated errors on requests to Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.” Shortly after, the company said it had “identified the cause” and that “a fix has been deployed.” The company marked the issue as resolved by 9:16 am PT. Claude Sonnet 5 seemed to briefly have similar issues shortly after 9 am PT.

xAI reported Grok outages across all of its platforms and services beginning at 6:30 am PT when the company posted “investigating outage” on its service status page. “Grok is experiencing issues. We are working on restoring service as quickly as possible,” the page said. At 10:05 am PT the episode was marked complete. “We have resolved the situation, and traffic is healthy again,” the company wrote.

There were scattered reports of a possible Google Gemini outage on Thursday morning as well, but the company did not confirm this or record any incidents on its service status dashboard. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment ahead of publication.

Typically, multiple outages in the same sector at the same time would point to a cloud provider, content delivery network, or other third-party vendor having issues affecting multiple customers. But OpenAI and Anthropic did not point to a potential shared cause, and major players in the internet infrastructure space—including Cloudflare, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure—did not report outages on Thursday.

GPT-6 Astra Is Here—and OpenAI Thinks It May Kick Off the AGI Era

Wired September 03, 2026

OpenAI announced Thursday the launch of its next generation AI model, GPT-6 Astra, which the company claims is state of the art at navigating computers and web browsers, writing software, and solving difficult math problems.

It plans to make GPT-6 Astra available to paid customers in the coming days, starting with a limited set of organizations, including enterprise clients in its Daybreak early access program, followed by ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise plan subscribers. OpenAI did not say whether GPT-6 Astra will be available to free users of ChatGPT.

In a press briefing with reporters, OpenAI executives made it clear that they feel very confident about the company’s latest AI model. President and cofounder Greg Brockman says he personally believes the world is now in the era of artificial general intelligence, or AI systems that are generally smarter than humans.

“It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” Brockman told reporters. “I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it's going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model."

OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Astra at a critical moment for the company. The ChatGPT maker is trying to rapidly advance its technology and boost sales ahead of a planned initial offering while simultaneously avoiding compromising on safety and security. OpenAI is also facing stiff competition from Anthropic, its most important rival, which is also working on an upcoming IPO.

In a blog post, OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra the “world’s best computer use model,” claiming it can navigate computers and web browsers on behalf of humans far better than its predecessors. AI companies have historically struggled to make models that can reliably browse websites, fill out forms, and manipulate software tools quickly and accurately enough to replace humans. In tests, OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra was able to book DMV appointments, search for job listings, and apartment hunt faster than the average person could.

The company also claims GPT-6 Astra is also the most safe and aligned AI model OpenAI has ever released. Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told reporters that the company is monitoring GPT-6 Astra’s chain-of-thought—the model’s internal scratchpad it uses to work through problems—to ensure it is deployed safely. However, Pachocki said that making sure advanced AI models don’t cause unintended harm is increasingly a challenge, and may present a bottleneck to further AI progress.

“We kind of take this visibility for granted, and we are seeing that as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging,” said Pachocki. “We think confidence in monitoring may constrain further development, because we would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We would withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence.”

OpenAI Cut Off a Billion-Dollar Customer to Avoid Elon Musk

Wired September 03, 2026

In a late-night blog post last Friday, OpenAI said it would wind down its partnership with Cursor, the startup behind one of the most popular AI coding tools on the market. The reason OpenAI gave for the decision is effectively that it can’t trust Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX recently acquired Cursor in a $60 billion deal.

In doing so, OpenAI walked away from one of its most important customers. Cursor has long paid OpenAI fees to offer the ChatGPT-maker’s models to developers using its AI coding editor. At the start of 2026, Cursor was one of OpenAI’s top five customers in terms of revenue, people familiar with the matter tell WIRED. By the spring of this year, OpenAI estimated Cursor would bring in more than $1 billion in annualized revenue for the ChatGPT maker, based on the partnership’s performance at that time, the people said.

The figures, which have not been previously reported, indicate the financial loss OpenAI is willing to take on to avoid doing business with Musk. OpenAI declined to comment. Representatives for SpaceX and Cursor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.

“We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts,” said OpenAI in the blog post.

As OpenAI prepares to go public next year, it’s trying to show investors a more stable business—ideally one that doesn’t rely so heavily on the goodwill of Musk. OpenAI reportedly now generates more than $40 billion in annualized revenue, drawing on several different lines of business, including subscriptions, ads in ChatGPT, and selling access to its AI coding tool, Codex.

Losing a major customer like Cursor may not hurt OpenAI financially as much as it once would have, but it was certainly a difficult decision. The company acknowledged in its blog post that ending the partnership may damage its standing with developers—a community it has spent years carefully working to win over—by cutting off a major channel they use to access OpenAI’s models.

Michael Truell, Cursor’s founder and CEO, who is now leading teams at SpaceX, responded publicly to OpenAI’s announcement hours later on Friday in a post on X, claiming that the ChatGPT-maker’s models only “serve about 5% of Cursor user traffic.” The comment seemed designed to imply that OpenAI’s models weren’t very popular with developers using Cursor, and wouldn’t meaningfully affect its business.

OpenAI’s head of core products, Thibault Sottiaux, was quick to point out that token usage is “not a proxy for revenue nor value created,” and asked Truell to “share the math” behind the 5 percent number.

WIRED previously reported that Cursor leaders hoped to remain a platform for third-party AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic, even after the SpaceX acquisition. Some AI insiders considered that wishful thinking, assuming that Cursor and OpenAI’s breakup has long been a foregone conclusion. As OpenAI builds Codex into a large AI coding business, it increasingly finds itself competing with Cursor for customers. Nevertheless, the companies have operated relatively peacefully, as partners and competitors, for well over a year.

Evidently, that arrangement was no longer possible with Musk in control of Cursor. OpenAI may have determined that its Cursor partnership was not worth the risk that SpaceX might distill its best AI models. The company noted in its blog post that, earlier this year, Musk seemingly said that xAI—now a part of SpaceX—used OpenAI’s models to train its own. The apparent admission came during Musk’s deposition in his lawsuit against OpenAI, in which he claimed that Sam Altman and Greg Brockman had stolen a charity they created together roughly a decade ago. A federal jury dismissed the suit earlier this year.

OpenAI and Cursor have a long, complicated history of their own. OpenAI’s startup fund was one of the first investors in Cursor, participating in its 2023 seed round. At the time, the idea that a young startup could compete with Microsoft’s popular AI coding tool, GitHub Copilot, seemed like a pipe dream. But in the years since, Cursor’s popularity with developers became undeniable.

WIRED previously reported that OpenAI approached Cursor about an acquisition at one point, though the talks never reached an advanced stage. By the summer of 2025, Truell appeared prominently in OpenAI’s marketing materials for the launch of its long awaited GPT-5 AI model.

Cursor isn’t done with third-party AI models just yet. In the wake of OpenAI’s announcement, Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown said his company would continue to make Claude models available in Cursor. I’m not sure that’s out of the goodness of their heart—Anthropic may have to play nice with Cursor because it depends on Musk’s SpaceX for $45 billion of data center capacity. Last year, Anthropic had no problem cutting off the AI coding startup called Windsurf when OpenAI was rumored to be acquiring it. (Windsurf was ultimately bought by another startup, Cognition.) At the time, Anthropic cofounder Jared Kaplan told me, “It would be odd for us to sell Claude to OpenAI.”

I guess it’s fine to sell Claude to SpaceX, though?

Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade Fanless Laptop Takes Thin and Light to the Extreme

Wired September 03, 2026

Lenovo is well-known for its creative, if wacky, concept laptops, usually involving some sort of display trickery. But at the IFA Berlin 2026 consumer electronics trade show, the company showed a proof of concept that actually looks production-ready.

The Project AeroBlade Concept laptop is built around a new active cooling technology from Frore Systems that uses air pressure—instead of fans, heatsinks, and large vents—to expel heat from the CPU. That means thinner laptop designs and quieter operation, and the space savings allow for larger batteries. According to Lenovo, it could reimagine how future high-performance laptops are designed.

Lenovo is the first computer manufacturer to unveil a laptop that uses Frore’s AirJet Mini fanless air-cooling technology. Frore is known for its liquid-cooling tech that’s used in data centers, but the AirJet is designed for consumer computers.

Dubbed the Lenovo Active Flow Thermal Solution, the AirJet module pulls ambient air that’s inside the laptop to create 2,000 Pascals of back pressure (around 124 miles per hour). This high-speed air is then spread onto a copper base layer through tiny jets in the AirJet module, which Frore claims will disrupt the boundary layer that causes heat buildup and throttling. Without a boundary layer, the processor’s heat is dissipated out the back. Lenovo had a motherboard sample from the AeroBlade concept laptop that showed four embedded AirJet modules, located along the top of the laptop.

Frore says each AirJet module can create 10 times the back pressure of a regular laptop fan and can pull and expel air without needing many vents. Lenovo claims the Active Flow Thermal Solution uses the same power as a traditional fan, but it’s debris- and water-resistant.

While Lenovo may be the first to demo a laptop using AirJet, it’s not an exclusive partnership, so we could see other laptop makers employ it.

The circuit board is surrounded by AirJet Mini modules.

With its typical, unassuming laptop design, nothing about the AeroBlade Concept screams that it’s a concept. But at 10 mm thin and weighing 1.8 pounds, you can’t help but think there’s something special. With a magnesium-aluminum body, it’s so lightweight that it makes some of the current lightest laptops, like the Asus Zenbook A14 or MacBook Air, feel downright heavy. I spent longer than I should have just lifting it up and down, and marveling at its portability.

I expected Lenovo to show a non-functioning sample or one I couldn’t touch, but what I demoed felt like a production unit. Indeed, Lenovo told me it’s a “very mature and refined product in terms of sample stability.” The laptop has an OLED screen and USB-C ports that support Thunderbolt 4.

The engineering sample uses an Intel Lunar Lake processor, which suggests the cooling tech can support higher-performance CPUs, though with support for up to 20 watts of thermal design power (TDP), it may not suit really demanding machines (there is a more powerful version of the AirJet, called the AirJet Pro). We won’t fully know how effective this design will be until it’s in the real world. If it goes into production, Lenovo says that class of chipset won’t necessarily be what’s inside, or whether the AirJet tech will end up in a future variant of the company’s existing laptops and mini PCs.

Lenovo didn’t reveal any details like battery life, pricing, or availability. Still, the product feels so finished that I can’t help imagining an imminent release, especially since some of Lenovo’s concepts have made it into production.

The Project Swan concept features a rollable display that expands horizontally from 14 to 17 inches.

Alongside Project AeroBlade, Lenovo’s wackier concept of the year is Project Swan. Like its rollable gaming laptop that debuted at CES 2026, Project Swan expands horizontally from 14 to 17 inches with the push of a button. The company says it took what it learned from previous projects and refined it. While Lenovo mentions it's suitable for travel in its press release, at 3.5 pounds, it's noticeably heavy. That means this model has fewer motors, but they’re more durable. While still very much a “watch this space” product, it’s an exciting showcase of how a compact laptop could provide the visual real estate of a larger machine.

I Got a Brief Look at Guild Wars 3, and I’m Excited

Wired September 03, 2026

Hardly a year goes by without me whistling the Guild Wars 2 loading theme, rewatching clips of the original to soak up that Pre-Searing Ascalon nostalgia, or subjecting my wife to yet another Grawl impression. (Gui-la-la!)

That's how monumental ArenaNet's MMORPG has been in my life. So you can understand my excitement when the game developer announced Guild Wars 3 earlier this summer, with a beta set to launch in late 2027.

I spent countless hours playing Guild Wars in middle school and high school, and an ungodly amount of time playing Guild Wars 2 with my roommates in college. Guild Wars always felt like the dark horse in the MMORPG world, never reaching the scale and attention of World of Warcraft or Final Fantasy XI, yet maintaining a massive user base with a cult-like following. (It uniquely did not require a monthly subscription.) You wouldn't hear anyone talking about it in the school cafeteria like you would the other two titles (I was not a Cool Kid). Still, it always had a grand scale of wonder, adventure, and lore that drew me in—props to my older brother for discovering the game and its many discs, and building a PC to run it.

Guild Wars 3's setting predates the events of Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, which means you don't really need to know anything about the series to dive in. It marks the first time the franchise is heading to console with a PlayStation 5 release alongside PC. And while developers typically wind down support for predecessor titles ahead of a sequel, ArenaNet plans to maintain both the original Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2 for years to come. (It recently released the original game as Guild Wars Reforged with system enhancements and a mobile port.)

Details on the game—built on Unreal Engine 5 and in development for 4 years—are limited, but ArenaNet gave me a brief glimpse of early alpha footage showcasing gameplay components that have me excited to jump back into the world of Tyria.

Gliding is already a movement mechanic in Guild Wars 2, but when you stop and start running, the transitions are awkward and slow. All of that is becoming more fluid in Guild Wars 3, alongside some new range of movements. In some ways, it brings the game closer to an action RPG.

You can jump into a ravine, start gliding, and now wall-run to reach your desired destination, all in a series of fluid movements with no awkward transitions, though there is a stamina bar as a limiter. Colin Johanson, ArenaNet’s studio head, says this unlocks “truly expressive and free-formed joy of movement.” Much of this centers on character momentum—using speed, weight, and directional inertia—a philosophy massively multiplayer online games have historically avoided due to network latency and server-client synchronization issues.

Momentum doesn't only affect how you get around, but combat as well. For example, you can build up speed to ram into enemies and smash them into cliff walls to stun them—they can do the same to you—or use momentum to kick them off a ledge, King Leonidas-style. (What happens to their loot if they fall off a cliff? ArenaNet hasn't figured that out just yet.)

While the basic movement mechanics are the same across all character classes, each class has a unique spin on it. The Warrior class, for example, can sprint up a wall and use downward momentum to plunge their weapon and slam the ground, causing area-of-effect damage to nearby enemies.

I recall enjoying many of the collaborative fighting mechanics when Guild Wars 2 first debuted—like an Elementalist dropping a fire ring on the ground so an ally could shoot arrows through it to inflict burning damage. That's still a crucial component in GW3.

Warriors can angle their shield to act as a launchpad for allies, catapulting them into the air for elevated strikes. Rangers have an ability that creates an ice vortex, and a Warrior can jump in, ride the vortex's lift high, then plummet down to cause big (icy) damage. Some of these moves are GW3's new “contextual skills," which only show up during specific contextual windows. If a Warrior is in the air, that's when they can use the skill to bomb down and hit the ground with power.

In one encounter against spiders, a Warrior set his weapon on fire, which in turn lit his allies' weapons. They sliced through the spiders quickly, and the fire also spread through the webs to clear them out. Players can adjust and customize their builds on the fly in the open world, though some build aspects are restricted until they're back in main hub locations.

“Customizing your build to defeat different enemies more easily is also an important part of the Guild Wars franchise,” Johanson says. “It's one of the key pillars of Guild Wars 1, and we're bringing it back more heavily in the combat system in Guild Wars 3.”

Conditions you place on enemies are multiplayer stackable, so if one player starts freezing an enemy, the cold effect builds, and the enemy's animation slows down; their attacks are slower. As more people put more cold on the enemy, they'll move slower and slower until they become a block of ice that blocks their moves for a short period. If the enemy is low on health, a character with a knock ability like a Warrior can slam into the ice block and, if it kills the enemy, shatter them into tiny ice cubes, causing damage to nearby foes.

There's lots ArenaNet didn't talk about in this gameplay showcase, like the spirit mounts from the game's initial teaser—Johanson says there will be more to share in the future. Also, how will PS5 players, who can't really take advantage of the game's text-based chat systems on PC, communicate? But he confirmed that there will be a player-versus-player (PvP) mode, along with “high-trust coordinated dungeon-like experiences.” In general, combat will feature a “heck of a lot less” user interface over the screen than a traditional MMO.

ArenaNet says the scale is different compared to Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, with the former sitting at the smaller scale of the MMO market and the latter sitting on the opposite end. “Internally, we call Guild Wars 3 more of a meaningful MMO, where it's more about each player on-screen really matters and makes a difference,” Johanson says.

That's because GW3 uses an evolved version of the megaservers from GW2, allowing for fewer loading screens and an open-world cap of roughly 20 players in active combat zones—a number that scales up significantly higher in social hubs, like cities and towns.

“We've seen very few new MMOs in the last decade, and the overwhelming majority of us are still playing the same games from 10 to 20 years ago,” Johanson says. “We see MMO fans constantly clamoring for something new and saying this genre desperately needs something new to move it forward right now, and I think that is when ArenaNet is at its best.”

Expect a slow trickle of information over the next year as the beta launch for Guild Wars 3 approaches. Until then, I'm going to dust off Guild Wars 2, which has been seeing its own sudden influx of new players. As the Norn say, “May the spirits guide you.”

We Just Got Our First Real Look at AI PCs With Nvidia’s RTX Spark ‘Superchip’

Wired September 03, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Three months ago, Nvidia took the wraps off its RTX Spark “superchip” and a handful of future laptops that would use it. It felt like a consequential moment in the history of the PC, despite all the questions that remained.

And now, as announced at the IFA 2026 tech show in Berlin, we’ve had our first hands-on look at one of these laptops, as well as some announcements around RTX Spark-powered mini desktop PCs. Demand for running agentic AI workflows like OpenClaw locally on your computer keeps rising, and these new PCs look like they are designed specifically to feed it.

The laptop in question is the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1, a 16-inch laptop with a 360-degree hinge. As I assumed it would, this thing looks incredibly premium, aiming to be a MacBook Pro competitor in every aspect. The OLED touch display has a sharp 2880 x 1800 resolution and a 120-Hz refresh rate. The whole chassis is surrounded by rounded metallic edges and some very thin display bezels. Other high-end features we don’t typically see include a six-speaker sound system and a 9.2-megapixel webcam.

But here’s the important bit: It’s 0.69 inches thick, just 0.03 inches shy of the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That’s possible thanks to Nvidia’s Arm-based chip under the hood, which combines a Grace CPU with “up to 20 cores” and a Blackwell RTX GPU with “up to 6,144 cores.” The CPU, GPU, and memory are packaged together into a single system-on-a-chip (SoC), sharing more in common with Apple silicon than a conventional Windows laptop. Based purely on core count alone, that would theoretically put the integrated GPU capability of this chip somewhere between an RTX 5070 Ti and an RTX 5080 as found on laptops available today. Those specs also indicate that lower-powered configurations will be sold, though we don’t know how broad the performance range will be. There was no mention of battery-life claims, though presumably one benefit of using an Arm-based SoC (rather than a discrete GPU) is greater efficiency and, thus, better battery life.

Personally, I don’t prefer laptops this large with 2-in-1 capabilities and number pads, so I’m happy that Lenovo is also offering a 15-inch model, the Yoga Pro 9n. While it wasn’t available to see in person, that’s the model I’m more interested in checking out. It shares a lot in common with the 16-inch model, such as the rounded edges, higher-resolution webcam, and very large haptic touchpad. But it has a smaller 15-inch OLED screen with a resolution of 2560 x 1600 and is thinner at 0.66 inches (at its thinnest point). Another unique feature is its Force Pad touchpad, which lets you use a stylus (such as the Yoga Pen Gen 2) to write or draw directly on it.

Interestingly, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 can only be configured with up to 64 GB of memory, which is less than I thought these AI-focused PCs would offer. I suppose what makes the Yoga Pro 9n a “Pro” model is its configuration options up to 128 GB of memory, as it otherwise seems to have the same performance.

Lenovo’s device is just one among a new line of RTX Spark-powered laptops coming this fall, including the Dell XPS 16, Asus ProArt P16, and Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra. These larger laptops all seem focused on pleasing the creator and AI enthusiast demographic, though only one 14-inch model has been announced so far: the HP OmniBook X 14.

The point of all these new PCs is to offer hardware that can capably run on-device AI models locally. That means less dependence on the cloud and more ability to run full agentic AI workflows without worrying about privacy. That’s crucial when an AI model handles sensitive personal data like your financial information, email accounts, or anything else you feel comfortable providing.

Acer announced its own mini PC solution, the Acer SFF RTX Spark, following up on Asus’ ProArt Mini PC shown off earlier this summer. Both are around the same size as the Mac Mini, but offer a “petaflop of AI performance,” up to 128 GB of memory, and the same RTX Spark superchip at its core. These mini PCs are interesting, coming just a week after the announcement of Apple’s M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio. These small, efficient desktop computers are going to (and already are) play an important role in the adoption of local AI.

Nvidia isn’t the only player here. Lenovo announced an AMD-powered ThinkCentre X Ultra, which also puts 128 GB of memory at the disposal of agentic AI models, alongside AMD’s Ryzen Max+ Pro 495 chip. This is another popular chip being used for local AI, such as on the Framework Desktop. You can even buy the AMD Developer Kit with 128 GB of RAM right now. The expected starting price of the ThinkCentre X Ultra is $3,699, which should give you an idea of how expensive these systems are getting. And note that’s the base model, not the maxed-out, 128-GB version.

Price remains the most crucial missing element. RAM has never been more expensive or more necessary, so I wouldn’t expect any RTX Spark systems to be cheap. The most affordable MacBook Pro (aside from the M5 base model) is $2,349, which gets you the M5 Pro and only 24 GB of RAM. For a 128-GB MacBook Pro, you’re currently looking at $6,139.

Nvidia’s Hugging Face Acquisition Is a $12.9 Billion Bet on Open-Source AI

Wired September 03, 2026

Nvidia has agreed to acquire Hugging Face, which makes online developer tools and maintains a massive library of open-source data sets, for nearly $13 billion. While the deal had been rumored for weeks, the companies made it official Thursday morning.

The deal signals Nvidia’s seriousness about being steeped in the software side of generative AI development as well as in infrastructure. Nvidia already offers customers a suite of free, customizable open-weights AI models, known as Nemotron. As part of its announcement, Nvidia committed to maintaining Hugging Face’s current open standards, suggesting that the chipmaker is positioning itself as an even greater resource for developers looking to access cutting-edge, nonproprietary tools.

The move also underscores Nvidia’s position that open-weights models are better for the tech industry than closed, proprietary AI models like those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic. Earlier this month, Nvidia rallied more than 80 companies to sign an open letter asking the US government to defend open-weight AI models. Nvidia also launched an initiative called SAFE, or Shared AI Findings Exchange, that encouraged tech companies to “confidentially collect and analyze AI incidents and near misses, identify recurring control failures and publish evidence-based operating recommendations that reduce systemic risk.”

“Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in the press release announcing the deal. “AI advances faster when people can build together.”

Nvidia’s embrace of open-source software and open-weights AI might seem like an abrupt turn, especially given that CUDA, the software layer for its highly coveted GPUs, is itself proprietary. But as frontier AI labs and some of the large hyperscalers, including Amazon and Meta, seek to build their own custom chips, Nvidia has begun to position itself as a maker of not just GPUs but also high-performance CPUs, and has widened its software offerings in order to keep developers building on Nvidia’s platforms.

Business Insider previously reported that the two companies were in talks, and The Information later reported that a deal had been reached.

Hugging Face was founded a decade ago by three French entrepreneurs in New York City, who wanted to launch an AI “companion” app. That didn’t catch on, but the team’s efforts to build their own natural language processing (NLP) tools inspired their next move: making complex tech tools more accessible to developers. Hugging Face eventually became a platform for developers to freely share source code, data sets, and, in the generative AI era, large language models.

“Open-source AI is at an inflection point,” wrote Hugging Face cofounder and CEO Clément Delangue in a post on X announcing the acquisition. “Thanks to the community, we’ve shown that it can be a complement, and even an alternative, to closed-source APIs. But for it to happen at larger scale, it needs more compute, more support, more collaboration and more visibility.”

According to PitchBook data, Hugging Face had raised nearly $400 million in venture capital funding as of December 2025. Some of its backers include Betaworks, Lux Capital, Sequoia Ventures, Coatue, and Addition. Notable individual investors include Greg Brockman, Richard Socher, and the NBA player Kevin Durant.

Hugging Face has more recently been front and center after its platform was hacked by AI agents from OpenAI. The incident sparked a broader conversation across the tech industry about the safety, security, and manageability of the autonomous agents being touted by top AI companies.

In a 2023 interview with CNBC Delangue predicted that the number of developers working with AI models would soar, and estimated that within five years, “you’re going to have like 100 million AI builders. And if all of them use Hugging Face all day, every day, we’ll obviously be in a good position.”

Obviously, Nvidia seems to agree.

Scientists Have Found the Most Convincing Evidence Yet of a Dark Matter Particle

Wired September 03, 2026

More than a kilometer underground, in what used to be a gold mine, inside a tank filled with tons of liquid xenon, “something” struck the nucleus of an atom. The tiny collision left an unusual energy signature that researchers are still unable to explain, but the scientists behind the experiment believe this could be the most convincing physical evidence of dark matter to date.

Dark matter is one of the most important and elusive substances in astrophysics. Though it makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe, we can’t observe it directly because it doesn’t interact with light or much else. Most of the evidence for its existence comes from its gravitational effects, the mass of dark matter having tugged on the atoms of the early universe to form stars, galaxies, and the vast web of intergalactic structures visible today.

But the enigma of dark matter is complex. Scientists don’t even know what it is made of, whether it’s a single type of particle or an entire set of particles that interact with one another in ways we do not yet understand. The most fantastical explanations even suggest that it consists of black holes. One of the most widely studied theories on dark matter has dubbed its components WIMPs, short for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, meaning the particles have a mass and thus a gravitational pull but otherwise interact weakly with conventional matter.

If WIMPs exist and are part of the dark matter of our galaxy, enormous quantities of them could be passing through the Earth continuously without leaving a trace. However, it is possible that, very occasionally, one might interact with an atomic nucleus and transfer some of its energy to it, which is why an inexplicable collision is exciting in the world of particle physics.

In the strange disturbance recorded at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in South Dakota, the detector monitoring the tank recorded that a xenon nucleus received energy and recoiled. Though researchers have not yet been able to satisfactorily explain the cause, some models suggest a WIMP could produce such a reaction.

The scientists stated that this single event is statistically too small to be considered the discovery of a new particle. In 220 days of observations conducted between 2023 and 2024, only one such anomaly occurred. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves. We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input,” Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown University and a member of the team leading the project, said in a press release.

The team behind the experiment has published their study as a preprint, meaning it has not yet been peer reviewed. They have, however, presented the results to the scientific community at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics Conference in Japan.

Discoveries made around dark matter tend to elicit this kind of restrained excitement. When in November 2025 a team of Japanese astronomers announced that they had seen signs of dark matter in the Milky Way, they too advised the research community not to count their chickens.

But even if cautious, there are reasons for enthusiasm. If the impact was caused by dark matter, there is enough evidence for researchers to begin characterizing the responsible particle. For example, the team has already calculated that, under the WIMP models they analyzed, the particle is about 200 times more massive than a proton. The impact could help us understand how this type of matter interacts with conventional matter.

The team has also been examining other possible explanations. Paradoxically, in experiments as sensitive as this one, atypical events are not all that uncommon. That’s why SURF has various methods of filtering out background noise and detecting interference caused by known particles or radiation. This event withstood that scrutiny. So far, the researchers have not found an explanation among these known sources that fits what they observed.

“We understand our detector and the backgrounds so well that even a single outstanding event, like the one we found, is important,” said Sam Eriksen, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol and the study’s lead author. “We expect dark matter events to be extremely rare, so only a handful could mark the first detection of WIMP dark matter.”

The Best Laptop Backpacks I’ve Tested for Work, Travel, and Everyday Life

Wired September 06, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Though I’ve been working from home for the past 15 years, both freelance and full-time, this often means needing to be available 24/7, so I typically carry my laptop everywhere I go—including sports practices, day trips, and vacations.

I have used many laptop backpacks in this time, and the dividing line between a work backpack that’s comfortable and fits seamlessly into your daily routine and one that’s aggravating at every turn is a fine one. If you’ve got limited closet space, it also helps if the backpack can pull double duty and be used for travel and/or hiking. The backpacks below are ones either I or another WIRED reviewer have used extensively in real life, taking on planes, hiking trails, vacations, and work trips.

Everlane

Amazon

Aer

Troubadour

Everlane

Everlane

I took this backpack on a weeklong work trip, where I bitched about it endlessly to everyone who would listen. However, I must fairly and objectively conclude that this bag offers tremendous value for the money. It's a light, attractive, rucksack-style backpack that's sleek and understated enough for work, and it's under $120. The 27-liter capacity accommodated enough gear for a full day's worth of travel, from a scarf for the plane to a water bottle, snacks, and other in-flight accouterments. It has a slim profile and lies close to your back, so it's not hard to carry and won't swing into people on the subway. The pockets are very minimal—just an exterior laptop pocket, an interior tablet sleeve, an interior zip pocket, and two large catch-all pockets—but they work if you already put your belongings in pouches anyway.

Certain design elements just felt cheap. I didn't like the curved zipper that gives you access to the main compartment—zippers that don't run straight are doomed to get stuck. One of the catch-all pockets is annoyingly located on the cover flap, where anything inside will flap and bang around. The luggage pass-through is a bare piece of webbing. However, it all works: it's light, affordable, and looks nice. The fabric is also water-resistant, so you can wear it in the rain! For most people, that's all that really matters. —Adrienne So

Thule

Amazon

Thule

Thule's newest addition to its already solid backpack lineup was made specifically for schlepping gear to and from work on a daily basis, and it shows. The silhouette is sleek and aerodynamic, making it suitable for bike commuting (there's even a loop on the front to attach a bike light), and it's just big enough for a laptop, several notebooks, and maybe a jacket without feeling too big or bulky. The water bottle holder on the side is stretchy for a variety of sizes.

I also love the amount of organization inside for smaller things like pens and notebooks (the flap folds down for access to the interior, too, so you can access these things next to your desk), as well as the hidden yet easily accessible small pocket under the flap for wallet, keys, and phone. It's not the roomiest pack, so you're not carrying gym gear in this or taking it on an overnight trip, but if you're just going to and from the office with basics and a laptop, this is the most well-engineered option I've tried.

Aer

Aer

Aer has a lock on the tech-minimalist aesthetic with its no-frills, black Cordura bags; this is the larger version of the popular City Pack. Though there is a newer version of the Travel Pack—the Travel Pack 4 is supposedly more streamlined—my husband and I have both been using this bag constantly for two years and have zero complaints, which is rare. It's also still in pristine condition, despite going on at least 10 work trips between the two of us.

Any backpack need you might have, the Travel Pack can probably cover it, from hiking to one-bag travel. The front zip pocket has built-in organization for all your pens, cords, and notebooks, and the main compartment opens clamshell-style for packing cubes or gym gear. It covers all the bases without feeling too fiddly. However, note it's not the lightest pack and would likely be frustratingly bulky for commuters.

Troubadour

Troubadour

I have never received as many approving comments on a backpack as I have when I tested this one on a three-day work trip (I was told by three people in a day that I sold them on it). It's a good-looking, structured bag with vegan leather accents and gigantic padded back panels and padded shoulder straps. There are little details like vegan leather pull tabs on the interior pockets, so you're not fumbling around for the pocket opening (I have never had this problem, but you do you). The fabric is also waterproof, and you can buy optional accessories like a rain cover.

I really liked the interior organization—for example, the padded, suspended tech pocket has two pockets, one for your laptop and one for your iPad or Kindle. However, all those padded panels and good-looking accents come at a price—this bag is disproportionately heavy. I couldn't go on a 20-minute bike ride without stopping to give my shoulders a break. Other details seem like they were designed by aliens who had never seen backpacks before. My tiny 18-ounce Owala tips right out of the water bottle pocket because its lip slants forward. The capacity is surprisingly small for how bulky it is, and a 100-percent plastic backpack just should not cost $249. However, everyone else loves this backpack, so here it is. —Adrienne So

Comfrt

Shop

Comfrt

Given that Comfrt is primarily known for its viral “airplane mode” hoodies, I was impressed with this au courant puffy backpack’s finish and construction for the price. (Though note there's no warranty, just a 30-day return policy.) My teen son has been testing it now for about three weeks, packing it to the gills and throwing it into his locker and on the ground for after-school sports. Though it looks like it might be fragile, the water-resistant polyester exterior still has nary a scratch or tear.

The straps are well-padded, the laptop compartment in the back is lined with a minky fabric, and there's a hidden pocket for valuables. It's also got a luggage pass-through and two generously sized pockets on either side for water bottles or whatever else (my son keeps a Shark ChillPill in one). Best yet, this pack fits far more than it seems like it will at 25 liters—more than some of the similar-sized backpacks on this list. It's perfect for high school or college students who need to pack in textbooks as well as incidentals and gym clothes. Color options include black (shown), navy, espresso, and pink.
